summary.tldr:
Anthropic’s S-1 filing reveals that its seven co-founders—Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah—plan to sell 3,378,378 shares each during the company's upcoming IPO. With an initial price range of $70 to $78 per share, each founder is expected to cash out approximately $250 million at the $74 midrange. The IPO has already attracted significant interest from board members, with Reed Hastings committing to purchase $300 million in shares via his donor-advised fund and Christopher Liddell committing to $3 million.

Despite the share sale, the founders will retain significant control over the company. Post-IPO, they will collectively hold 51.1% of the voting power through a combination of Class A shares and individual Class F supervoting shares. While the founders will hold roughly 22% of the total outstanding Class A shares, their total equity stake is diluted by nonvoting Class N shares held by major investors including Amazon and Google. The company, founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees, continues to emphasize its focus on AI safety as a core differentiator.
takeaways: **Founder Payout:** Each of the seven co-founders will sell 3,378,378 shares, netting between $236 million and $264 million depending on the final IPO price.
**Voting Control:** The founders will maintain a collective 51.1% voting majority through Class F supervoting shares, ensuring they retain control despite the share sale.
**Board Participation:** Board member Reed Hastings has signaled intent to purchase $300 million in shares, while Christopher Liddell has committed to $3 million.

**Equity Structure:** Post-sale, the founders will hold approximately 22% of the total outstanding Class A shares, with additional equity held by institutional investors like Amazon and Google in nonvoting Class N shares.

title: Oura to acquire AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625M
author: Aisha Malik
contentSnippet:
Oura announced on Tuesday that it’s acquiring AI-native primary care company Counsel Health for $625 million. The deal comes a few weeks after Oura postponed its up to $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market.”

Counsel Health is an AI-powered healthcare platform that combines a chat-based medical experience with access to licensed physicians. Its service was integrated into the Oura app in June.

Users can connect with Counsel’s medical AI to get personalized medical advice, and chat with a physician when needed, all within the Oura app. Now, the companies plan to expand on their existing partnership to build across preventative care, acute care, and specialty and chronic care.

While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating. By acquiring Counsel Health, Oura is looking to expand its business and help users access medical care.

“Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care, and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale in a press release .

Counsel Health raised a $25 million Series A a year ago, led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and GV. PitchBook estimates it had raised a total of $36 million.

Following the acquisition, Oura says Counsel will continue serving existing and new enterprise partners, with the goal of expanding its AI-native care model to more people beyond Oura’s membership.

Counsel CEO Muthu Alagappan will join Oura as chief clinical AI officer, alongside the company’s 70 employees, Bloomberg reports.

“At Counsel, we’ve built medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions,” Alagappan said in the press release. “Oura’s data gives clinicians objective context, trended biometrics, and member engagement to deliver more informed care. From the start, our teams bonded over a joint vision, shared culture, and mission, further solidifying as we negotiated our deal over the past few months.”

The deal is expected to close before the end of 2027.

Oura also announced that its revenue grew 153% year-over-year to $533 million for the quarter ended on September 30. For its fiscal year 2026, O

summary.tldr:
Oura has announced the acquisition of AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625 million. This move follows Oura's indefinite postponement of its planned $2.2 billion IPO, citing market uncertainty. Counsel Health, which previously raised approximately $36 million in total funding—including a $25 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and GV—provides a platform that integrates chat-based medical AI with access to licensed physicians. The service was already integrated into the Oura app as of June 2024.

The acquisition aims to transition Oura from a passive biometric tracking company into a proactive healthcare provider, covering preventative, acute, specialty, and chronic care. Counsel CEO Muthu Alagappan will join Oura as Chief Clinical AI Officer, bringing his 70-person team to the company. The deal is expected to close by the end of 2027. Oura intends to maintain Counsel’s existing enterprise partnerships while scaling the AI-native care model to a broader user base.

Financially, Oura reported $533 million in revenue for the quarter ending September 30, representing 153% year-over-year growth, and approximately $1.75 billion in revenue for fiscal year 2026, a 92% year-over-year increase. The company is currently valued at $11 billion, following a $900 million late-stage funding round in October 2025. This expansion comes as Oura faces increasing competition in the smart ring market from rivals such as RingConn and Ultrahuman.
takeaways: **Acquisition Terms:** Oura is acquiring Counsel Health for $625 million, with the transaction expected to close by the end of 2027.
**Leadership Transition:** Counsel Health CEO Muthu Alagappan will join Oura as Chief Clinical AI Officer, along with the startup's 70 employees.
**Financial Performance:** Oura reported $1.75 billion in revenue for fiscal year 2026 (92% YoY growth) and a valuation of $11 billion as of October 2025.
**Counsel Health Funding:** Prior to the acquisition, Counsel Health had raised approximately $36 million, including a $25 million Series A led by a16z and GV.
**Strategic Integration:** The acquisition builds upon a June 2024 integration that allowed Oura users to access Counsel’s medical AI and licensed physicians directly within the Oura app.

title: The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
author: Robert Hart
contentSnippet: As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. He also wears a cool leather jacket. Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI. Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. That makes it a gatekeeper to hardware that has become a key bottleneck in global AI development. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute. For China, the US’s main rival at the frontier of AI, that bottleneck is even tighter. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged. Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI. Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American S

summary.tldr:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing scrutiny following reports of an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. While no public evidence suggests Huang provided trade secrets or illicitly directed restricted hardware to China, the revelation has raised concerns regarding national security and the stability of the US AI supply chain. Nvidia currently serves as the primary gatekeeper for high-end AI compute, with companies like OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic heavily dependent on its GPUs to maintain their competitive edge against Chinese development.

Experts from the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) and the Jamestown Foundation warn that the scandal could destabilize Nvidia, potentially distracting leadership and slowing the rollout of critical hardware. Beyond the risk of intellectual property theft, analysts suggest that access to Huang—who maintains close relationships with US policymakers and Silicon Valley executives—could provide Beijing with strategic insights into American industrial policy, infrastructure expansion plans, and private perspectives on geopolitical tensions. While China has reportedly utilized black-market channels to acquire restricted chips, the scandal is expected to accelerate legislative efforts in Congress to tighten export controls and oversight of the semiconductor industry.
takeaways: **Market Impact:** Nvidia shares have experienced a decline following the public disclosure of the affair, raising concerns about the company's governance and operational continuity.
**Supply Chain Risks:** Analysts note that companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang, have reportedly facilitated approximately $7 billion in Nvidia chip sales to China.

**Strategic Intelligence:** Beyond hardware, experts suggest the primary risk involves the exposure of sensitive US policy discussions, export control strategies, and private industry planning through Huang's high-level access.
**Legislative Fallout:** The scandal is expected to increase the likelihood of stricter US congressional legislation regarding AI chip export controls and oversight.
**Industry Dependency:** The US AI sector remains highly concentrated, with major labs like OpenAI and Anthropic facing significant hurdles if Nvidia's execution is delayed by ongoing investigations.

title: PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery
author: Tim Fernholz
contentSnippet:
David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI) , used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing.

“I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?”

The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution.

The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said.

More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving.

“A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?”

That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding.

“An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.”

For now, the company’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound — “where the perfo

summary.tldr:
Physical Superintelligence (PSI), a startup lab, has utilized Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve the 18-year-old Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a significant open problem in quantum query complexity. The proof, which demonstrates that certain quantum speedups are not possible, was autoformalized in the Lean programming language and verified by external researchers. The achievement marks a shift in scientific research, with PSI staff member David Turturean suggesting that AI-driven discovery may soon render traditional academic paper publication obsolete.

PSI, led by CEO Matt Pines, operates as a "neolab" that builds specialized AI harnesses, memory systems, and simulation infrastructure to tackle scientific problems. While the company currently generates revenue by applying these tools to optimize data center physics—specifically heat, power, and water management—its long-term objective is to translate theoretical physics breakthroughs into tangible technologies. The firm emphasizes the necessity of bridging the gap between computational results and real-world experimental validation, acknowledging that while AI excels in formalizable domains like mathematics, physical sciences require empirical verification.
takeaways: **Core Achievement:** PSI solved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a long-standing problem regarding the speed advantages of quantum computers over classical systems.

**Technical Validation:** The solution was autoformalized in Lean, a formal proof assistant, and vetted by a team of external experts, including Scott Aaronson, who co-authored the original conjecture.
**Current Business Model:** PSI currently derives revenue from optimizing data center performance by simulating physical variables such as heat, power, water, and sound.
**Methodology:** The company focuses on building "harnesses"—integrated systems of tools, memory, and simulation infrastructure—to allow AI to explore scientific problems with both breadth and depth.

**Industry Context:** PSI is actively participating in emerging academic discussions regarding the standards and transparency required for AI-generated scientific proofs, with advisory support from Northeastern University professor Jim Halverson.

title: OpenAI rolls out new business profiles, making ChatGPT just a little bit more like Google
author: Lucas Ropek
contentSnippet:
In an effort to make ChatGPT an even better consumer discovery engine, OpenAI is launching a host of new features designed to help companies control how users interact with their businesses.

On Tuesday, the company rolled out a Business Hub that will serve as a place where companies can create business profiles that — in a feature that greatly resembles the kind of profiles that Google and other search engines already offer — allow enterprises to verify and update information about their products and services. The feature is currently in beta.

Eligible companies will also be able to create and launch a specialized business agent, which gives ChatGPT users the ability to ask questions about the business and its products.

“As people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI,” the company said on Tuesday. “Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT.”

In a move that calls to mind Google Analytics , the Business Hub will also give users access to limited business insights. These insights will reveal how ChatGPT users interact with their products — including profile views, business mentions, website clicks, and other metrics.

Businesses will have to verify their profiles through a formal process, although the company did not share specifics of what that process would entail. Benji Shomair, OpenAI’s VP of Monetization, told journalists on Monday that there are “multiple verification methods that we use for different types of business in different markets.”

OpenAI previously tried to position ChatGPT as an e-commerce hub by which users could buy products directly. This effort — which used a commission fee system — was viewed as a potentially huge source of revenue and a way to make ChatGPT a more direct Amazon competitor. However, that project ultimately failed to take off and, in March, the company retired the effort , which had even included a “checkout cart” feature.

With the integration of business profiles and intelligence, ChatGPT seems to be attempting to become more like Google, which — since the advent of the internet — has been the place where web users go to understand the companies they want to shop at. It remains to be seen whether this initiative will bear better results than the one that sought to

summary.tldr:
OpenAI has launched a new Business Hub in beta, enabling companies to create verified business profiles within ChatGPT to manage product and service information. This initiative allows enterprises to deploy specialized AI agents capable of answering user queries regarding their specific offerings, effectively positioning ChatGPT as a discovery engine for consumer research and decision-making.

Beyond profile management, the Business Hub provides companies with analytics dashboards—reminiscent of Google Analytics—that track user interactions, including profile views, business mentions, and website click-through rates. Verification for these profiles is mandatory, with VP of Monetization Benji Shomair noting that OpenAI employs multiple, market-specific verification methods to authenticate businesses.

This pivot follows the discontinuation of OpenAI’s previous e-commerce strategy in March, which had attempted to integrate direct purchasing and checkout carts to compete with Amazon. By shifting focus toward business discovery and intelligence, OpenAI is realigning its platform to function more like a search-based business directory, though the long-term commercial viability of this model remains to be proven.
takeaways: **Business Hub Beta:** A new platform feature allowing companies to verify profiles and manage product information directly within the ChatGPT interface.
**Specialized AI Agents:** Eligible businesses can now launch custom agents designed to field user questions about their specific products and services.
**Analytics Dashboard:** Provides businesses with metrics on user engagement, specifically tracking profile views, mentions, and website clicks.
**Strategic Pivot:** The initiative marks a departure from the failed e-commerce/checkout cart project retired in March, moving toward a discovery-based model similar to Google Business profiles.

title: 14-year-old creates tool for AI agents to band together like a team
author: The Register AI
contentSnippet: Built by a 14-year-old developer, a new tool called Autark treats AI agents as a virtual team that can work without constant prompting. Users put tasks in an inbox, where a manager agent delegates them to other agents that carry out the work and report their results. Agents can also ask clarifying questions if tasks are too vague. “Agents do not wait for a prompt,” Autark’s website explains. “A schedule, a timer, a new task, a message or an event wakes them up. They decide what to do, do it, and can plan their own next step.” As one would hope from a product like this, Autark is model agnostic and can be set up to connect to OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Kimi Code through those services’ CLI tools. Local models are also supported. Your mileage may vary if you choose to use anything besides Codex or Claude Code, though, as Autark’s website mentions support for other models is built in but hasn’t been tested in a live run yet, as Autark is still under active development as an open-source tool. Real teenage engineering Autark is the brainchild of teenage Austrian developer Stanislaus Hees. He’s still in school, and tells The Register he’s deeply interested in AI and came up with Autark after being unhappy with existing AI tools. “I could get help with individual tasks, but I still had to organise the work, remember what was unfinished and keep pushing it forward,” Hees said of his time using Claude Code and Codex. “I wanted a system that could take responsibility for ongoing work, not just respond to my next message.” He developed Autark - or, more accurately, prompted AI coding tools to do it for him - to come up with a tool that could fulfill that want. You know what that means: It’s capable, but that capability also makes it dangerous. Autark’s page on access and data makes clear what’s at risk if you give it unfettered access to a PC, and why you don’t want to let the thing run roughshod over a system. “It can do everything,” the page explains, because “Autark does not put walls around its agents.” There’s no sandboxing in Autark, no approval prompts, and no permission gates. It doesn’t stop agents from spending all the money they can get their hands on, deleting files, or sending unsolicited emails, either. Agents run with the privileges of the machine's user, with approval checks and permission restrictions disabled or byp

summary.tldr:
Autark is an open-source tool developed by 14-year-old Austrian developer Stanislaus Hees designed to orchestrate AI agents into a self-directed virtual team. The system functions by utilizing a manager agent that delegates tasks from a centralized inbox to subordinate agents, which then execute work, plan subsequent steps, and request clarification for vague instructions without requiring continuous human prompting. The tool is triggered by events such as timers, schedules, or new messages, aiming to shift AI interaction from reactive single-turn responses to autonomous, ongoing project management.

Technically, Autark is model-agnostic, designed to interface with existing CLI tools including OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Kimi Code. While local model support is included, the developer notes that integration with non-Codex or non-Claude models remains untested. The architecture prioritizes autonomy over safety, explicitly lacking sandboxing, permission gates, or approval prompts. Agents operate with the full system privileges of the host user, meaning they possess the capability to delete files, send emails, or execute financial transactions without oversight.
takeaways: **Core Functionality:** Autark uses a manager-agent architecture to delegate tasks and manage workflows autonomously based on triggers like timers or new messages.
**Model Compatibility:** The tool is designed to connect to CLI-based AI coding assistants including OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Kimi Code.
**Security Profile:** The software operates without sandboxing or permission restrictions, allowing agents to execute any action available to the host user's system account.
**Development Status:** Created by Stanislaus Hees, the project is currently under active development and is available as an open-source tool.

title: Autonomous treasury agents: How Trovata built an AI-native solution on Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore
author: Kushal Mangtani
contentSnippet: Corporate treasury teams face a persistent challenge: fragmented banking data scattered across dozens of bank portals, manual reporting trapped in spreadsheets, and legacy Treasury Management Systems (TMS) that can’t scale for modern enterprise needs. For treasury teams these manual processes create delays, errors, and an inability to make real-time cash decisions when they matter most. Trovata is an AI-native cash and liquidity management platform with direct connections to over 10,000 banks, serving enterprises globally from a single cloud-based platform. In 2023, Trovata launched the first generative AI built specifically for treasury. Now, with Trovata’s latest AI-native updates, they’ve evolved from delivering insights to deploying autonomous agents that act on behalf of treasury teams. Trovata’s customers have seen measurable results: $1M+ in annualized cost savings, over 5 hours per day saved per accounting team, a 77 percent reduction in annual TMS costs, and treasury reporting reduced from hours or days to under a minute. In this post, we explore how Trovata built autonomous treasury agents on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the architecture secured with role-based access control (RBAC) that supports bank-branded AI deployment, and how agentic workflows are transforming corporate treasury from manual operations to real-time decision-making at enterprise scale. Solution overview Trovata operates as an AI-native treasury operating system, providing direct connections to over 10,000 banks through a single system for cash reporting, forecasting, analysis, and money movement. Treasury teams today face a three-pressure problem: Fragmented banking data across multiple portals, requiring manual aggregation and reconciliation. Manual reporting and reconciliation consuming hours or even days of skilled team members’ time. Legacy TMS applications that lack cloud-native architecture and AI capabilities needed for modern operations. Trovata’s evolution from its first generative AI for treasury in 2023 to its AI-native capabilities with autonomous agents represents a fundamental shift. The solution moves from static insights to persistent agentic workflows that operate continuously on behalf of treasury teams. Critically, Trovata AI is built directly into the treasury operating system. It’s not a generic chatbot layered on top, but embedded intellige

summary.tldr:
Trovata, an AI-native cash and liquidity management platform, has transitioned from providing generative AI insights to deploying autonomous treasury agents built on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The platform integrates with over 10,000 banks to centralize fragmented financial data, replacing legacy Treasury Management Systems (TMS) with a cloud-native architecture. These agents are designed to perform continuous, persistent workflows rather than acting as simple chatbots, enabling automated cash reporting, forecasting, and money movement.

By embedding these agents directly into the treasury operating system, Trovata reports significant operational improvements for enterprise clients. Documented outcomes include over $1 million in annualized cost savings, a 77 percent reduction in annual TMS expenditures, and a reduction in reporting time from hours or days to under one minute. The architecture utilizes role-based access control (RBAC) to ensure security and supports bank-branded AI deployment, allowing treasury teams to shift from manual data reconciliation to real-time, automated decision-making.
takeaways: **Platform Scale:** Trovata maintains direct API connections to over 10,000 global financial institutions.
**Operational Efficiency:** Clients report saving over 5 hours per day per accounting team through agentic automation.
**Cost Impact:** Implementation of the platform has resulted in a 77 percent reduction in annual legacy TMS costs.
**Technical Foundation:** The system is built on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, featuring integrated role-based access control (RBAC).

title: ChatGPT is getting verified AI ‘Business Agents’
author: Jay Peters
contentSnippet: ChatGPT is going to let you chat with verified “Business Agents” that represent a brand to help you with things like comparison shopping. The feature, available first to “eligible” e-commerce and online service businesses in the US, is launching as part of a suite of business-focused features in ChatGPT being announced today in beta. You can start talking with a Business Agent if a business that has created one appears in a response from ChatGPT. While chatting with a custom agent, you can ask about a business’s offerings and ask follow-up questions, like asking about differences between two different products. Businesses can specify a Business Agent’s instructions and provide business context so that the agent knows how to respond. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/Business-Agent-Setup.png?quality=90&strip=all] Chats with Business Agents will be clearly labeled and separate from your main ChatGPT conversation, OpenAI says. To help people know that they’re talking with an agent that actually represents the business, companies will be able to claim their organization and get verified through a feature called Business Hub. (OpenAI isn’t sharing specifics about its verification methods because there are different methods for different businesses, VP of monetization Benji Shomair said in a press briefing.) Business Hub will also let companies see insights such as mentions in ChatGPT responses and top “discovery topics” where their business pops up. “Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT,” OpenAI says in a blog post. “We’re starting with the foundations: accurate business information, useful insights and conversations that help people make informed decisions.” As things evolve, “we’ll explore more ways for businesses to connect with customers — directly or through agents and in ChatGPT and beyond. Our goal is to make ChatGPT more useful for people making decisions, and give businesses new ways to participate and grow.”

summary.tldr:
OpenAI has launched 'Business Agents' for ChatGPT, a new feature allowing e-commerce and online service businesses in the U.S. to deploy verified AI representatives to interact directly with users. These agents are designed to assist with tasks such as product comparison and answering specific queries about a company's offerings. Businesses can configure these agents by providing custom instructions and proprietary context, ensuring the AI adheres to brand-specific guidelines during customer interactions.

To ensure authenticity, OpenAI is introducing a 'Business Hub' where companies can claim their organization and undergo a verification process. While specific verification protocols remain undisclosed, the Business Hub provides companies with analytics, including tracking how often their brand is mentioned in ChatGPT responses and identifying the top 'discovery topics' that lead users to their business. These agent-led conversations are visually distinct from standard ChatGPT threads, appearing in separate, clearly labeled interfaces to maintain transparency for the user.
takeaways: **Geographic Availability:** The Business Agents feature is currently limited to eligible e-commerce and online service businesses operating within the United States.
**Verification Mechanism:** Companies must claim their organization via the new 'Business Hub' to receive verification, though OpenAI has not disclosed the specific criteria used for this process.
**Analytics Suite:** The Business Hub provides participating companies with data on brand mentions and 'discovery topics' to track how their business is surfaced in AI responses.
**User Interface:** Conversations with Business Agents are separated from standard ChatGPT chat history and are explicitly labeled to distinguish them from general AI interactions.

title: The indie game community is in disarray over AI and Big Walk
author: Jay Peters
contentSnippet: Some Independent Games Festival (IGF) jurors published a statement yesterday saying they would not vote for games that use generative AI in “any capacity.” Soon after, the developer of indie hit Big Walk has published a statement saying it “sparingly” used AI in the “final stretch” of the game’s development to “help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs.” According to the jurors’ statement, a copy of which was posted by Austin Walker, while this year’s IGF entries have been “incredible,” there has been “a significant increase” in the number of games “developed with generative AI tools,” leading to “fairly intense discussion and disagreement” with no “universal consensus.” The statement includes a list of beliefs, including that generative AI has “negative effects,” that AI-generated code is “not an exception to these harms,” and that use of AI tools is “not a forgone conclusion in our industry.” IGF jurors that signed include Telling Lies and Immortality creator Sam Barlow and Celeste composer Lena Raine. The jurors say that the statement doesn’t speak for IGF as an organization or for all IGF jury members, noting that some voiced concern about being able to safely sign “without professional blowback.” [Media: https://bsky.app/profile/austinwalker.bsky.social/post/3mzvyqaxnzc2w] One contentious title was apparently Big Walk, the co-op adventure game from Untitled Goose Game developer House House. In a statement to Aftermath and posted on its website, House House said that “In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.” House House said its “primary use case” of LLMs was “to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code,” including fixing an issue with shadows by modifying LLM-suggested code. House House noted it turned to the “LLM chatbot” after researching the problem “extensively” and even speaking to an engineer at Unity. The studio said it disclosed its AI usage as part of its IGF submission, though it has not disclosed AI usage on Big Walk’s Steam page because “the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.” “This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, h

summary.tldr:
A group of Independent Games Festival (IGF) jurors has issued a statement declaring their refusal to vote for games utilizing generative AI in any capacity, citing concerns over the technology's negative industry impact. The statement, signed by notable figures including Sam Barlow and Lena Raine, highlights a growing divide within the indie community regarding the integration of AI tools in development. While the jurors clarified that their stance does not represent the official policy of the IGF organization, they noted that many members fear professional repercussions for publicly opposing AI usage in submissions.

The controversy intensified following disclosures regarding 'Big Walk,' the upcoming co-op adventure game from House House, the studio behind 'Untitled Goose Game.' House House confirmed that they used LLMs to troubleshoot technical issues and bugs during the final stages of development, estimating that less than 0.1% of the game's total code involved LLM-generated snippets. The studio disclosed this usage in their IGF submission but not on their Steam page, noting that the platform does not require such disclosures. House House acknowledged the lack of an internal AI policy during development as a failure and expressed support for efforts to limit the harms of generative AI in the industry.

Sam Barlow clarified that 'Big Walk' was not the specific catalyst for the jurors' statement but served as a complex edge case for evaluating 'minimal' AI usage. The jurors emphasized that their position is intended to define the values of the IGF awards as an alternative to mainstream development rather than a call to boycott specific titles or developers. The discussion remains ongoing as the community grapples with establishing standards for AI transparency and ethical development practices.
takeaways: **IGF Juror Stance:** A group of jurors, including Sam Barlow and Lena Raine, declared they will not vote for games using generative AI in any capacity.

**Big Walk AI Usage:** Developer House House estimated that less than 0.1% of 'Big Walk' code involved LLM-generated snippets, used primarily for troubleshooting third-party code and shadow-related bugs.
**Disclosure Practices:** House House disclosed their AI usage to the IGF but did not list it on their Steam page, citing a lack of platform requirements for such disclosures.
**Policy Failure:** House House admitted they lacked a formal AI policy during the development of 'Big Walk' and committed to establishing a more comprehensive policy for future projects.
**Juror Motivation:** The jurors stated their position is focused on defining the identity of the IGF awards rather than economically targeting specific developers or games.

title: Anthropic launches Claude Meetings to turn workplace discussions into plans and tasks
author: Aisha Malik
contentSnippet:
Anthropic announced new workplace features on Tuesday, including Claude Meetings, which brings Claude into video calls to begin working on tasks while participants are still talking. The company also unveiled Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets.

The launch of Anthropic’s new productivity-focused features comes just a few weeks after OpenAI unveiled a series of workplace tools that allow users to collaborate with ChatGPT to do things like visualize company information and create presentations, as both companies compete to turn their products into office suites of sorts to take on Microsoft and Google. Meta is also joining the competition with its Muse AI agent, which can build mini-apps on the fly to help users complete specific tasks.

With Claude Meetings, teams can add Claude to a video call as a visible participant. Claude then follows the conversation and gets to work on tasks in real time. As participants talk, it can draft the plan being discussed, map out a timeline on a whiteboard, answer questions in the meeting chat, and access connected work apps to retrieve information, such as last year’s figures. After the call, the meeting notes, action items, and other materials Claude created are available in claude.ai.

The work that comes out of a meeting usually starts after everyone hangs up, but with this new feature, teams can turn discussions into actions in real time, Anthropic says.

Claude identifies itself as a meeting participant and posts a notice in the meeting chat. It won’t join calls with external guests unless authorized by an admin, and will automatically leave if an external guest joins.

Claude Meetings is launching in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. At launch, it works with Google Meet, with support for additional plans expected to follow.

As for Claude Whiteboards, Anthropic describes the feature as a collaborative board where teams can talk through a plan and have Claude turn it into an organized visual workspace with timelines and deadlines.

The company notes that many people already brainstorm with Claude, but that in order to share their results with others, they would have to copy-paste them somewhere else. Now, a team can work directly with Claude on the same board in real time.

When the brainstorm is done, Claude can turn the board into a doc or a slide deck. Additionally, Whiteboards also work inside Claude Meetings, so

summary.tldr: As participants talk, Claude can draft the plan being discussed, map out a timeline on a whiteboard, answer questions in the meeting chat, and access connected work apps to retrieve information, such as last year's figures.

title: Anthropic has its own AI-powered office suite now
author: Hayden Field
contentSnippet: For years, Anthropic has been known for its focus on enterprise and coding tools that attract high-flying corporate clients, inspiring competing frontier labs — like OpenAI, SpaceXSI, and Meta — to copy its strategies. Earlier this year, Claude Code went through its own particular hype cycle. And now, Anthropic is trying to expand its footprint to other knowledge workers with an AI-powered suite of office tools. At an event in San Francisco on Tuesday, Anthropic unveiled new tools for non-technical workers who spend a lot of time attending meetings, brainstorming new ideas, and analyzing metrics: Claude Meetings, Claude Sheets, and Claude Whiteboards. The tools allow for Claude to join a meeting, take notes, lay out ideas on a shared whiteboard, edit spreadsheets alongside employees, or turn a presentation into a one-minute explainer video. The new “Artifacts,” or Anthropic’s version of graphical UI, come two and a half years after Artifacts first debuted, and join existing tools like Claude Docs, Slides, Design and Motion. Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Meetings are all now available in beta, with the first two available to all paid plans and Meetings available for Teams and Enterprise subscriptions. The company also announced that Claude Data (formerly known as Claude Dashboards when it was introduced in beta in October) is now generally available to all paid plans. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/Claude-Artifacts-All-Press.png?quality=90&strip=all] Nicholas Lin, who works on product at Anthropic, told The Verge in a pre-briefing that Claude Code “changed how engineers work a year ago” — and now, the company is looking to knowledge workers as “the gap we’re hoping to close.” “I think there’s still a lot of friction when it comes to adopting AI for non-developers,” he said. The company also unveiled new interactive connectors that allow for users to open apps from partnered companies, such as HubSpot, Adobe, and Atlassian, inside Claude. The company launched Model Context Protocol about two years ago, and its marketplace of tools has grown to more than 9,000 plugin options; now, Lin says, the company is looking to make those connections a lot deeper, so that users don’t have to switch tabs to access the services they use every day and instead just embed them into Claude. For example, with the new tools, people can a

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has expanded its enterprise product suite with three new AI-powered tools for non-technical knowledge workers: Claude Meetings, Claude Sheets, and Claude Whiteboards. These tools, which leverage the company's Artifacts graphical UI, allow users to automate meeting note-taking, collaborate on spreadsheets, and visualize brainstorming sessions directly within the Claude interface. Additionally, the company announced the general availability of Claude Data (formerly Claude Dashboards) for all paid plans. These releases represent a strategic shift to capture the broader knowledge worker market, moving beyond the developer-centric focus of previous tools like Claude Code.

To reduce context-switching, Anthropic introduced "interactive connectors" that embed third-party applications directly into the Claude environment. Users can now access native integrations for platforms including HubSpot, Adobe, and Atlassian. This expansion builds upon the Model Context Protocol, which now supports over 9,000 plugin options. While Claude Sheets and Whiteboards are available to all paid plans, Claude Meetings is restricted to Teams and Enterprise subscriptions. The move positions Anthropic to compete directly with Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s ChatGPT, both of which offer similar meeting-transcription and spreadsheet-integration capabilities, as the company seeks to demonstrate revenue growth and product engagement ahead of a potential IPO.
takeaways: **New Toolset:** Anthropic launched Claude Meetings, Claude Sheets, and Claude Whiteboards to target non-technical knowledge workers.
**Availability:** Claude Sheets and Whiteboards are available to all paid plans, while Claude Meetings is limited to Teams and Enterprise tiers.
**Interactive Connectors:** New integrations allow users to run third-party apps like HubSpot, Adobe, and Atlassian natively within the Claude interface.
**Ecosystem Growth:** The Model Context Protocol now supports over 9,000 plugin options for the Claude platform.
**Strategic Context:** The product expansion is part of an effort to increase revenue and engagement metrics ahead of a highly anticipated public offering.

title: How TCS built an agentic test orchestrator with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Varun Valsan
contentSnippet: This post was co-written with Varun Valsan from Tata Consultancy Services (TCS). Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) runs large-scale testing for Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) clients, where the slowest part of a release is rarely writing application code. The larger constraint is the chain of work that follows: interpreting requirements, designing scenarios, writing and maintaining automation, preparing execution environments, investigating failures, and assembling evidence for review. BFSI clients need to increase testing throughput while preserving the controls expected in financial services. The objective wasn’t to replace quality engineers. It was to remove repetitive translation and execution work so that engineers could spend more time on risk analysis, exploratory testing, and release decisions. These industry needs generated four specific requirements for TCS. First, every test must be grounded in project-specific context rather than generic prompts. Second, it had to cover both API and browser-based UI testing to match how BFSI applications are built. Third, security is paramount, so every tenant’s data and knowledge store must be isolated. Finally, it must provide a repeatable path from requirement ingestion to test evidence and reporting, so the gains hold across teams and releases. In this post, we show how TCS built an agentic test orchestrator that turns requirements into executable, governed tests, and what it changed for its BFSI testing teams. Why conventional automation and systems weren’t enough TCS already uses traditional test automation for its clients, and it does improve execution speed. But it leaves the slow work untouched: teams must still create the scenarios, convert them into scripts, maintain locators and dependencies, and diagnose failures. When a linked user story changes, scripts generated for an earlier story can quickly become stale. A single generative AI prompt also doesn’t provide the control needed for a multi-stage engineering workflow. TCS therefore designed the Agentic Test Orchestrator to decompose testing into specialized tasks. Each task has its own agent, tools, validation rules, and context. A deterministic supervisor routes work, while an execution workflow controls retries, error classification, persistence, and reporting. title: Amazon Bedrock tokenomics data lake
author: Steph Gooch
contentSnippet: If you need an observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock workloads, you’re not alone. When you’re running thousands of model invocations a day across multiple accounts, after a request is sent you might be wondering, what happened? You can see the aggregate bill, but you can’t see what happened inside each call. You might start to ask questions: what prompt was sent, what the model returned, how many tokens it used, which model handled it, and whether the response was any good! If you’re a platform or machine learning (ML) engineer looking after a fleet of Amazon Bedrock workloads across teams, that’s a real problem. You can’t debug a spike, you can’t spot wasteful prompts, and you can’t tell one team’s usage from another’s. We built something to help: a centralized observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock invocations. In this post, I cover what native data you have and how we designed the lake. I also show how to use it to see your prompts and derive the per-invocation cost. The AWS CloudFormation templates, AWS Lambda code, and SQL queries are all in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository . This post walks through the architecture and deployment steps. The repo has everything you need to deploy it. What Amazon Bedrock visibility do you have today? Amazon Bedrock offers model invocation logging , and it’s genuinely powerful. You turn on invocation logs in the settings in each AWS account you are using Bedrock . It delivers a full record of requests and responses to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch . The data exists, but it’s locked inside individual accounts. What you really want is a single, fast, queryable view of every invocation across your whole organization. That’s what the data lake gives you. What is the Amazon Bedrock observability data lake? A centralized Amazon Bedrock invocation log data lake pulls raw model invocation logs from your linked accounts into Amazon CloudWatch . Subscription log filters then forward those records to your central account. The central account processes the data through Amazon Data Firehose , and exposes them through Amazon Athena as one clean table you can query across your organization. Figure 1: Amazon Bedrock invocation observability data lake architecture across a central account and linked accounts Everything is deployed as Infrastructure as Code us

summary.tldr:
If you need an observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock workloads, you’re not alone. When you’re running thousands of model invocations a day across multiple accounts, after a request is sent you might be wondering, what happened? You can see the aggregate bill, but you can’t see what happened inside each call.

You might start to ask questions: what prompt was sent, what the model returned, how many tokens it used, which model handled it, and whether the response was any good! If you’re a platform or machine learning (ML) engineer looking after a fleet of Amazon Bedrock workloads across teams, that’s a real problem. You can’t debug a spike, you can’t spot wasteful prompts, and you can’t tell one team’s usage from another’s.
takeaways: We built something to help: a centralized observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock invocations.
In this post, I cover what native data you have and how we designed the lake.
I also show how to use it to see your prompts and derive the per-invocation cost.
The AWS CloudFormation templates, AWS Lambda code, and SQL queries are all in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository .

title: NVIDIA Expands Open Source Commitment With OpenShell Donation and New AI Infrastructure
author: Warren Barkley
contentSnippet: Kubernetes, the open source system that manages how applications run across thousands of AI factories, has become the foundation for AI, and the demands on it are only growing. To help meet them, NVIDIA is deepening its commitment to open source at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon , the flagship conference for the Kubernetes and cloud-native communities. NVIDIA is contributing NVIDIA OpenShell , an open source runtime for securing and governing autonomous agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), a nonprofit that is part of the Linux Foundation and the host of KubeCon. As a CNCF Sandbox project, OpenShell will be governed by the organizations building it into their products and strengthened by the expertise of security professionals worldwide. NVIDIA is also contributing to Agent Substrate , an open source Google-led framework for operating long-running agent workloads at scale on Kubernetes that has been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox. Additionally, NVIDIA announced new components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform : NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine , NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes and NVIDIA Snapshot . These tools help teams deploy, manage and scale GPU infrastructure on Kubernetes for AI factories. Together, these advancements mark a step forward in making Kubernetes the leading foundation for AI workloads at scale — empowering developers to build safer, more efficient AI infrastructure for the future. Securing AI Agents in the Open NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF puts security infrastructure for autonomous agents in the community’s hands to build, inspect and improve — accelerating development and hardening its safeguards. “The cloud-native community has a new infrastructure challenge: giving agents secure environments in which to operate,” said Jim Zemlin, CEO of the Linux Foundation. “NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF gives developers a shared foundation to build on and an opportunity to shape how agent security evolves. title: Zyphra Releases ZONOS3-Mini: Open-Source TTS With 100M Active Parameters
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Zyphra has released ZONOS3-Mini , an open-source text-to-speech model built for real-time use on local devices. The ZONOS3-Mini text-to-speech model is a sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) with 800M total and 100M active parameters. It supports zero-shot voice cloning and word-level delivery control. Weights ship under Apache 2.0. For AI devs, size is the key point. It runs in a browser tab, on a laptop or on a server GPU. TL;DR Size: 800M total parameters, about 100M active per token (64 experts, top-2 routing); 32,768-position context; up to 10 minutes of audio per generation. Runs on: NVIDIA GPUs via SGLang-Omni, Apple Silicon via MLX, CPU/CUDA/Metal/Vulkan via ggml, and phones or laptops via WebGPU in the browser. Performance: Ranks first among open models on Zyphra’s ZTTS2-Eval Capability Index (self-reported). Best: 80 ms median time to first audio on one H100 at 8 concurrent requests, and 457 seconds of audio per second peak throughput. Worst: Under 570 ms time to first audio in the browser on a Pixel 9, versus under 150 ms on an M3 MacBook Air. Bottom line: Best: frontier-level open TTS quality at 100M active parameters. Worst: every benchmark is run by Zyphra itself, and reference-clip cloning scores far lower than embedding mode. What is ZONOS3-Mini? ZONOS3-Mini is a compact zero-shot voice-cloning TTS model from Zyphra that runs in real time on-device. Zyphra trained it on 112 NVIDIA H100s in 2.5 days. It follows ZONOS2 , which used 8B parameters and an 86 Hz codec. That size limited where ZONOS2 could be deployed. How does the ZONOS3-Mini architecture work? Zyphra changed 3 layers of the stack : A new codec : Zyphra trained Zyphra Audio Codec 1 (ZAC-1) to replace the Descript Audio Codec. ZAC-1 runs at 15 Hz with 10 codebooks of 4,096 entries: 1 semantic and 9 acoustic. Zyphra reports a 10x word error rate reduction versus a DAC-trained model under similar data constraints. A causal iSTFT head renders each frame to 44.1 kHz audio as soon as it is generated. A hybrid MoE backbone : The model card lists 11 layers with model dimension 1,024. Sequence mixing follows a 3:1 ratio: 9 Gated DeltaNet layers and 2 global attention layers. Zyphra also adds latent MoE, Q balancing and attention residuals. A new speaker encoder : Voice representation moves from the Qwen3-TTS speaker encoder to MECT-B2. The model accepts a raw reference clip of up to 60 seconds,

title: Anthropic Launches Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2: Same Model, Different Safeguards
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Anthropic just released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 . Claude Fable 5.2 is a frontier model from Anthropic for long-horizon coding, research and agentic work. Mythos 5.2 is the same underlying model with fewer cyber and biology safeguards. It beats Opus 5.5 on most evaluations and costs less than the 5.1 models. TL;DR Size: 1M-token context window, 128K max output. Runs on: Hosted API only. Claude Platform, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure. No open weights. Performance: Ahead of Opus 5.5 on almost every benchmark Anthropic reported. Best: RoboDojo Sim 64.9%, more than double GPT-6 Astra (29.8%). Worst: AutomationBench 51.4%, behind Gemini 4 Carbon (53.9%). Bottom line: Best: Opus-level coding at roughly half the cost per task. Worst: Fable still blocks most cybersecurity work. What is the difference between Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2? They are one model. Fable 5.2 adds classifiers that block high-risk cybersecurity tasks and most research biology. That lets Anthropic offer it to all users. Mythos 5.2 drops those blocks. Access runs through the Cyber Verification Program and the Life Sciences Verification Program . When Fable blocks a query, users get an answer from Opus 4.8 (cyber) or Opus 5 (biology). Anthropic reports about 55% fewer blocks than Fable 5.1. That splits into roughly 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. How does Claude Fable 5.2 perform on benchmarks? Anthropic published one table comparing Fable 5.2 with Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Carbon. All scores are self-reported. Key results: FrontierCode 2.0 (agentic coding): 49.1% at Xhigh effort, vs 45.5% for Opus 5.5. FrontierSWE v2: 69.9%, vs 65.5% for GPT-6 Astra. Remote Labor Index: 41.3%, vs 21.3% for Opus 5.5. Humanity’s Last Exam (with tools): 74.2%, vs 67.7% for Opus 5.5. OSWorld 2.1 (partial offline set): 89.3%. CVE Rediscovery (Mythos 5.2): 89.6%, vs 81.3% for Opus 5.5 without safeguards. Fable 5.2 does not lead everywhere. Gemini 4 Carbon wins AutomationBench (53.9% vs 51.4%). title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. [...] If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

title: Don't Blame The Preferences: Examining The Emergence of Sycophancy in LLM Training
author: Chao Peter Yang, Catherine Zehr, Pranav Bijith, Brandon Fain
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI sycophancy, the tendency of large language models (LLMs) to flatter users and affirm their beliefs, can undermine accuracy and contribute to misinformation, dependence, and overconfidence. Although prior work has benchmarked sycophancy in released models and proposed mitigations, its origins during training remain poorly understood. Preference alignment methods such as RLHF and DPO are often blamed, but their effects are rarely compared with earlier training stages. We investigate sycophancy across the training pipelines of three model families and three benchmarks. We find that sycophancy is largely established by the end of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), rather than introduced by preference alignment. Across all nine model benchmark combinations, SFT checkpoints attain at least 92% of preference aligned models' sycophancy scores and at least 85% of final models' scores; on average, they are about as sycophantic as final models. Preference alignment increases sycophancy in only four of nine cases, by an average of 4.2 percentage points when it does. To probe the underlying causes, we isolate model representations associated with sycophancy using mechanistic interpretability and measure their activation on training datasets from each stage. SFT datasets show roughly the same average activation as other training data but contribute substantially more examples, and the highest-scoring individual datasets all come from SFT. Our findings suggest that addressing sycophancy requires interventions throughout the training pipeline, particularly in data selection and augmentation for pre-training and SFT.

title: Veterans' Mental Health Crisis Severity Annotation: Do LLMs Agree More Than Human Experts?
author: K M Sajjadul Islam, Pranav Yaramalla, Nadiyah Johnson, Mark Flower, Praveen Madiraju, Zeno Franco
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable approach for annotating mental health and crisis-related social media content, but their reliability in safety-critical tasks remains unclear. This study evaluates LLM-based crisis-severity annotation of veteran-related social media posts against annotations from eight Veteran Subject Matter Experts (SMEs). Using 149 tweets and five severity categories, we evaluate 15 open-source and 10 proprietary LLMs across eight prompt variants, examining annotation performance, inter-model agreement, prompt sensitivity, and high-severity crisis detection. Human reviewers showed higher ordinal than nominal agreement ({\alpha} = 0.494), indicating that disagreements often occurred between neighboring severity levels. In contrast, selected LLMs demonstrated substantially higher inter-model consistency, with ordinal agreement ({\alpha}) reaching 0.8336 under the baseline prompt. Proprietary models generally showed better agreement with expert annotations and greater stability than open-source models. GPT-5.6-Terra achieved the best overall performance, while the open-source Qwen2.5-7B showed the strongest performance in identifying Acute Crisis with Suicidal Ideation cases. However, higher model consistency did not necessarily correspond to agreement with human judgments or reliable detection of rare high-severity cases. Label-flipped demonstration experiments also revealed model-specific sensitivity to misleading in-context examples, while explanatory demonstrations did not consistently improve performance. Overall, LLMs show promise as scalable complements to expert annotation, but require careful evaluation before use in high-stakes mental health applications.

title: LoRazor: Trimming Adapter Execution for Efficient Multi-LoRA Serving
author: Xiang Li, Pengcheng Wang, Azam Ikram, Saurabh Bagchi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LoRA offers a parameter-efficient adaptation strategy, supporting multi-user workloads via customized adapters on a shared backbone. However, serving concurrent requests with different adapters introduces substantial computation and memory-management overhead. We ask the research question: Do all requests need their adapters throughout the whole generation process? Our motivational study reveals that employing LoRA adapters at every decoding step is unnecessary, releasing them early has limited impact on accuracy while substantially accelerating generation. Although skipping adapters early offers theoretical workload reduction, translating these computational savings into concrete throughput gains requires tailored GPU kernels. We present LoRazor, a multi-LoRA serving framework that combines early adapter release with active-row aware GPU kernels. LoRazor determines when to permanently release a request's adapter and continue decoding with the backbone alone. By dynamically resizing LoRA kernel launches as adapters are released, LoRazor trims idle GPU blocks. Across two backbones and four tasks, LoRazor achieves up to 3.02x request throughput and 2.53x output-token throughput over vLLM multi-LoRA, with a mean relative task-accuracy decrease of 2.89%.

title: AYO: A Safe and Privacy-Preserving Platform for Studying Children's Interaction with LLMs
author: Huiwen Alex Yang, Rachel Skwersky, Bill D. Thompson, Celeste Kidd
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Children and adolescents are increasingly interacting with generative AI and large language models (LLMs), yet little is known about how these interactions may influence their development, beliefs, and behavior. Existing research has relied heavily on surveys, while direct study of children's interactions with LLMs presents substantial challenges related to safety, privacy, consent, and experimental control. We introduce AYO (AI Youth Open Science), an open-source platform designed for safe and systematic research on children's interactions with conversational AI. AYO provides a child-friendly interface, configurable age-based safety guardrails, researcher monitoring, and privacy-preserving data practices. These capabilities enable cross-sectional, longitudinal, and experimental research on how children use and respond to LLMs and how AI design may shape trust, epistemic judgment, curiosity, and other aspects of development. AYO provides the infrastructure to generate evidence that guides safer AI systems, educational practices, and policies for children growing up with AI.

title: META-IR: Meta-Introspective Reasoning for Adaptive Safety Alignment in LLM
author: Mahabubur Rahman Miraj, Hongyu Huang, Nankun Mu, Chao Chen, Shanqin Yi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks and harmful-content prompts, particularly under adversarial distribution shifts where static alignment pipelines fail to generalize. Although introspective methods such as STAIR strengthen refusal consistency, they depend on fixed self-evaluation policies that cannot rapidly adapt to evolving manipulation strategies. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces META-IR, a meta-introspective reasoning framework that enhances safety alignment through meta-learning-driven adaptation. It employs a dual-loop architecture: an inner introspective loop that performs structured risk analysis, self-assessment, and reflective correction via SI-MCTS, and an outer meta-learning loop that optimizes the introspection policy across diverse jailbreak task families to enable rapid generalization to unseen attacks. A dynamic jailbreak simulation module further exposes the model to progressively harder adversarial prompts, enabling continual self-improvement without human supervision. Experiments across multiple models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2-7B-Instruct) and a broad suite of safety, helpfulness, generalization, and introspection metrics demonstrate that META-IR substantially improves adaptation speed, robustness, and reasoning stability compared with all baseline models. These results establish META-IR as an effective pathway toward building LLMs capable of sustained, adaptive safety alignment under dynamic and evolving threat environments.

title: The Infrastructure Divide: Analyzing Community Stance on Data Center Development via Reddit
author: Yoko Koyama, Gongfan Chen, Mansi Saxena
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid expansion of AI-driven data center construction has outpaced public engagement: an estimated $64 billion in U.S. data center projects were blocked or delayed by local opposition between May 2024 and March 2025, yet the concerns driving this resistance remain poorly characterized. Prior engagement methods such as surveys and hearings are introduced late in the planning process, and no study has systematically mined social media to measure community stance at scale. To address this gap, this study presents an LLM-powered opinion-mining framework and applies it to 798 Reddit posts and 102,328 associated comments spanning a decade. An open-source large language model, guided by a Chain-of-Stance prompting framework and three domain-specific labeling rules, classified stance at 83% of the human inter-reviewer agreement ceiling. Opposition dominated discourse volume rather than disapproval: against posts outnumbered favor posts 2.6:1 and generated 8.5 times more comments, and this gap widened significantly over 86 weeks. Topic modeling of opposition arguments resolved into four reproducible clusters, resource consumption and scarcity (42.8%), contested siting processes and secrecy (34.2%), political opposition to data centers (13%), and political and corporate accountability (8%). Engagement analysis revealed that posts with emotional or provocative political framing attracted the most engagement, while key technical concerns (e.g., water, power) were dispersed across lower-engagement comment threads. These findings give local leaders, developers, and policy makers a quantified, continuously updatable basis for prioritizing concerns and policy levers, supporting a shift from opposition to negotiated, verifiable partnership for data center development.

title: Homeopathic Learning: Diluting poisoned fine-tuning data can strengthen its effect
author: Matt Clarke, Jan Dubi\'nski, James Chua, Simon Schrodi, Owain Evans, Alex Cloud
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study homeopathic learning, a phenomenon where poisoned training data with little effect on its own can create a hidden backdoor once clean, contrasting data is added. In our experiments, a model fine-tuned only on a "poison" dataset associated with a trait T (such as speaking German or being misaligned) does not learn T. Surprisingly, adding similarly formatted "clean" data not associated with T causes the model to learn T. This effect requires that the poison data have an identifying "trigger" feature that is absent from the clean data. We demonstrate this effect in a variety of settings: subliminal learning of backdoor behaviors, inoculation prompting of reward hacking transcripts, generalization from archaic bird names, and an MNIST classifier with mislabeled data. We propose a simple regression model as an explanation. In the poison data, the task and trigger always co-occur, and regularization favors attributing T to the task. Clean data without the trigger causes T to be attributed to the trigger instead. Consequently, the same training examples can have little effect as part of one training set but create a misalignment backdoor in another. This finding exposes a potential limitation of safety methods that audit or filter training data in isolation.

title: What Is the Value of AI-Involved Art? Evidence From a Juried In-Person Exhibition
author: Wisdom Obinna, Hexuan Wang, Cecile Duncan, Kristelia Garcia, Nina Grgi\'c-Hla\v{c}a, Toni-Lee Sangastiano, Elissa M. Redmiles
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10150v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What is the value of AI-involved art, and to whom does it belong? We begin to answer these questions using data from an in-person, juried AI art exhibition. Our study involved artists, lawyers, and computer scientists (N=209) as either creators or evaluators of AI-involved artworks. We found that nearly half of evaluators reported willingness to buy an artwork, with pricing correlating with perceived artistic value---creativity and visual appeal---as well as the effort necessary to create it. In contrast, three-quarters of creators reported willingness to sell at prices correlating only with effort rather than artistic value. Both groups viewed prompting users and AI developers as deserving rewards and rights, leaving training data artists behind. Disciplinary training shaped these views: participants with legal training favored distributed reward models. These findings have implications for future research on human-AI creative collaboration and policy debates regarding AI-involved works.

title: WorldMind: Test-Time Scaling for Visual Spatial Reasoning through Latent World Simulation
author: Haoming Wang, Yongjian Fu, Ju Ren, Wei Gao
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have continuous deficiency in spatial reasoning tasks that require \emph{mental spatial transformation}, such as reasoning under hypothetical changes in viewpoint or position, known as perspective-taking tasks. Existing approaches either scale linguistic reasoning or augment VLMs with static geometric representations, but neither directly enables active transformation of the represented scene. World models offer this capability, yet existing systems typically communicate through synthesized RGB images, introducing a latent-to-pixel-to-latent bottleneck. We introduce \emph{WorldMind}, a framework for test-time scaling of spatial reasoning through latent world simulation. Given a query and observation, the VLM selects useful spatial transformations, while a world model executes them and exposes aligned intermediate latent features directly to the VLM. The resulting latent evidence is incorporated into subsequent reasoning steps, enabling iterative spatial simulation without repeatedly decoding imagined states into pixels. To optimize this interaction, WorldMind further employs process-verifiable reinforcement learning that rewards reasoning progress only when the associated action and latent transition are valid. WorldMind thus scales spatial reasoning by allocating additional inference-time computation to active world simulation rather than generating more language or pixels. title: DeepResearch RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Deep Research Report
author: Shudong Liu, Yuting Zhong, Guanhua Chen, Xinyi Yang, Junnan Liu, Lidia S. Chao, Jiaheng Liu, Derek F. Wong
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Empowered by Large Language Models (LLMs), deep research systems integrate online information into research reports through multi-step web searching and information synthesis. Evaluating these reports presents a significant challenge due to their long context, high information density, and domain specificity, necessitating the use of AI evaluation as a substitute for prohibitively expensive human assessment. However, few studies have examined the effectiveness of existing reward models or LLMs in understanding and evaluating such research reports. To bridge this gap, we introduce DeepResearch RewardBench, the first benchmark dedicated to evaluating reward modeling for research reports. We collect diverse report candidates from multiple agents or tool-augmented LLMs. These candidates are scored using query-specific golden rubrics, and we ensure data quality and difficulty through a combination of multi-round filtering and human verification. Our benchmark comprises preference datasets formatted as pairs, triplets, and quadruplets to test ranking capabilities across varying levels of difficulty. Extensive experiments demonstrate that while current reward models handle general coherence effectively, their performance significantly degrades when evaluating research reports. Generative LLMs acting as judges demonstrate comprehensive superiority in this domain, with comparative evaluation proving more effective than direct scoring methods. We anticipate that this benchmark will serve as a vital testbed for the evaluation and advancement of research agents.

title: AutoEMatic: Runtime-Adaptive Mixed-Precision LLM Inference via Automatic Exponent-Mantissa Refinement
author: Akshat Ramachandran, Reena Elangovan, Rangharajan Venkatesan, Charbel Sakr, Tijmen Blankevoort, Brucek Khailany, Tushar Krishna
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing LLM post-training quantization techniques determine precision before inference begins, yet the precision a model requires varies dynamically across prompts, layers, and inference phases. We present AutoEMatic, a full-stack co-design that adapts the precision of weights, activations, and the KV cache at runtime. A lightweight policy selects each layer's precision at every prefill and decode step from two runtime signals: the entropy of the next-token distribution and the magnitude of each layer's update to its hidden states. This runtime adaptation is made practical by AutoFP, a multi-scale floating-point format that derives 2-, 4-, and 6-bit precisions from a single NVFP4 base format. We realize AutoEMatic on two targets: GPU kernels that execute AutoFP on NVFP4 Tensor Cores, and an accelerator whose vector MAC datapath executes all AutoFP formats natively. Across reasoning and agentic benchmarks, AutoEMatic improves accuracy by up to 21.7% over NVFP4 and matches group-scaled FP6 accuracy on most benchmarks, using 4.9 bits per weight versus 4.5 for NVFP4. On GB300 GPUs, AutoEMatic retains approximately 90-98% of NVFP4 decode throughput across the evaluated configurations. Furthermore, the AutoEMatic accelerator reduces latency by 1.6-2.3x and energy by 7-23% compared to an accelerator with NVFP4-only datapath at iso-accuracy.
