title: EmoHarness: Boosting Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Meta-Harness Evolving
author: Fenghai Li, Bingxuan Li, Jiawen Zhang, Yifan Shen
contentSnippet:
Authors: Fenghai Li , Bingxuan Li , Jiawen Zhang , Yifan Shen , Jiateng Liu , Yutong Zhang , Yue Guo

Abstract: Small multimodal models can misjudge emotion when words, voice, and visual cues conflict. We present EmoHarness, which runs such a model, the frozen student, inside a harness: the prompts, settings, and verification code around its calls. A human-written starting harness, the scaffold, numbers the student's visual observations, transcript, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence and has the student weigh candidate emotions against it. In Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), a stronger LLM, the Builder, reads the student's errors and execution traces offline and edits the harness; static checks and validation gates decide which edits are kept, and the Builder never sees evaluation items. On 5,507 MME-Emotion items, EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6-13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders. Transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of this boost (+5.38 to +10.71); the scaffold changes the audio-augmented call by -0.79 to +2.54, partly through extra multi-label predictions, and evolved edits add at most +0.95, although no evolved increment survives Holm correction. The harness's emotion context also transfers to IntentQA, with small gains for three of four students, none of which survives correction. EmoHarness thus boosts small multimodal students chiefly by supplying and organizing audio-derived evidence.

Notes: 18 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Project page: this https URL . Code: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Researchers Fenghai Li et al. introduced EmoHarness, a framework designed to improve emotion recognition in small multimodal models (SMMs) by wrapping them in a 'harness'—a structured system of prompts, settings, and verification code. The system utilizes a 'scaffold' that forces the model to index visual observations, transcripts, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence before weighing candidate emotions. This approach addresses the common failure mode where SMMs misinterpret emotions when verbal, vocal, and visual cues are contradictory.

The framework incorporates Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), an offline process where a stronger LLM (the 'Builder') analyzes the student model's execution traces and errors to iteratively refine the harness. Validation gates and static checks ensure that only effective edits are retained, while the Builder is strictly prevented from accessing evaluation data. Testing on 5,507 items from the MME-Emotion dataset demonstrated that EmoHarness improved task-macro recognition by 7.6 to 13.4 points across four different student models and two Builder models. The majority of these gains (5.38 to 10.71 points) were attributed to the inclusion of transcripts and prosody descriptions, while the evolved edits provided marginal improvements of up to 0.95 points, though these did not survive Holm correction.
takeaways: **Performance Gains:** EmoHarness improved task-macro recognition by 7.6–13.4 points on the 5,507-item MME-Emotion dataset.
**Primary Driver:** The integration of transcripts and prosody descriptions accounted for the bulk of performance improvements, contributing 5.38 to 10.71 points.
**Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE):** An offline iterative process where a stronger LLM edits the harness based on student error logs, though evolved increments did not survive Holm correction.
**Transferability:** The framework was tested on IntentQA, showing small gains for three of four student models, though these results were not statistically significant after correction.
**Methodology:** The system uses a 'scaffold' to force the model to cite evidence from visual, transcript, and prosody inputs before finalizing an emotion classification.

title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
author: Zhengyu Hu, Zheyuan Xiao, Yike Wang, Hamish Ivison
contentSnippet:
Authors: Zhengyu Hu , Zheyuan Xiao , Yike Wang , Hamish Ivison , Haoyu Wang , Yige Yuan , Rulin Shao , Yuetai Li , Niqi Lyu , Yicheng Ding , Shu Yang , Zhichen Zeng , Banghua Zhu , Jiaxin Pei , Kaize Ding , Pradeep Dasigi , Dan Roth , Hannaneh Hajishirzi , Noah A. Smith , Teng Xiao , Radha Poovendran

Abstract: In this work, we study whether frontier agent can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from 6.82% with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to 19.86%. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, Our Infrathon framework provide resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions.

summary.tldr:
Researchers from a multi-institutional team including the University of Washington and Allen Institute for AI have introduced Infrathon, a benchmark designed to evaluate the capability of frontier AI agents to perform long-horizon infrastructure optimization. The study assessed six models over 150 experimental runs, each with a 24-hour budget, consuming a total of over 10,000 GPU-hours. The research aims to determine if agents can autonomously improve real-world AI infrastructure systems over extended timeframes, moving beyond the limitations of short-duration evaluations.

The findings reveal that model performance rankings are highly sensitive to the evaluation horizon, with 135 out of 150 runs demonstrating continued optimization gains during the second half of their 24-hour budgets. Notably, the Claude Opus 5.5 model outperformed human-designed baselines in specific tasks, increasing the mean KV-cache compression ratio from 6.82% (achieved by the Quant-VideoGen codec) to 19.86%. Despite these successes, the study identified significant barriers to sustained agent performance, including task violations, unreliable testing protocols, and a tendency for agents to signal premature completion of optimization tasks.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** Infrathon evaluates AI agents across diverse, long-horizon infrastructure optimization tasks using a 24-hour budget per run.
**Resource Intensity:** The study utilized over 10,000 GPU-hours across 150 individual model runs to assess performance.
**Performance Metric:** Claude Opus 5.5 achieved a 19.86% mean KV-cache compression ratio, significantly exceeding the 6.82% ratio of the human-designed Quant-VideoGen baseline.
**Evaluation Insight:** 90% of experimental runs (135/150) showed continued optimization progress in the second half of the 24-hour window, suggesting short-term benchmarks may be misleading.
**Failure Modes:** Identified primary barriers to agent efficacy include task violations, unreliable testing environments, and premature task termination.

title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". title: InfraRSI: Harnessing Recursive Self-Improvement for Training Infrastructure
author: InfraRSI Team, Yuchuan Tian, Haocheng Mei, Ye Yuan
contentSnippet: While Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) accelerates isolated algorithm and kernel synthesis, distributed LLM training depends on tightly coupled launch settings, operator kernels, and communication schedules, where single edits often hit out-of-memory (OOM) boundaries, compiler conflicts, measurement jitter, or silent numerical drift. We present InfraRSI, the agentic harness that turns open-ended human commands into verified training optimizations via a five-stage workflow: init locks editable scope and a fixed task contract over workload, loss, and timing invariants to prevent reward hacking, doctor profiles baseline phases and calibrates cluster noise, run co-optimizes launch knobs and code patches before re-verifying top candidates against the baseline and logging findings to a cross-hardware experience bank, and report and apply audit source paths, track failed-trial costs, and commit promoted changes. Rather than stepping greedily from a single incumbent, InfraRSI initializes from diverse experience-seeded configurations and fits global execution-time and censored peak-memory models across all trials, including OOMs. Using these models, it prices per-setting memory costs, revises miscalibrated LLM priors from live runs, and pairs memory-hungry optimizations with memory savers and verified code patches. Across four single- and multi-node dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM workloads, InfraRSI achieves a speedup of up to 2.75times and lifts mean Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) from 17.4% to 30.0%, outperforming existing tuners and coding agents while transferring experience across GPUs. As it improves training infrastructure efficiency, InfraRSI forms a two-level Recursive Self-Improvement loop---revising priors online within runs and distilling experience across clusters---to push foundation model scaling.

title: Ostinato: Fast CPU-GPU MoE Inference for Local Agents via Resident Experts in Every Forward Pass
author: Junning Zhu
contentSnippet: Language-model agents increasingly run on workstations with a few consumer GPUs, where large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models keep part of their experts in host memory. With existing CPU-GPU engines, these agents get fast prefill or fast decode, not both: llama.cpp's expert cache skips forward passes of more than 32 tokens to keep the experts of decode cached, so an agent waits 2.1-2.8 s after each tool output, whereas its default layer placement shortens this wait but is 1.5-1.6$\times$ slower in decode. Our key insight is that a short prefill touches too many distinct experts to upload, yet sends 84% of its expert activations (routes) to a stable set of experts that fits in GPU memory. We present Ostinato, a CPU-GPU MoE inference engine that computes these experts on the GPUs in every forward pass without changing what the model computes. Short prefills split their routes, leaving fewer than one of a token's six routed experts per layer to the CPU; long prefills upload each distinct cold expert once; and each decode step runs as one fixed-shape CUDA graph per GPU. On real coding and customer-service agent sessions with DeepSeek-V4-Flash on four RTX 4090D GPUs, Ostinato is the fastest engine in both phases and finishes every session sooner than all six baselines. Against llama.cpp and KTransformers, it cuts the median wait after a tool output by 22-55% and finishes sessions 1.4-2.5$\times$ sooner.

title: BiVerify: Closing the Loop Between Backward and Forward Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction
author: Rui Zou
contentSnippet: Large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning but still produce incorrect solutions to complex problems, indicating the need for more reliable self-correction mechanisms. Mathematical self-correction typically identifies errors through verification, which can proceed backward or forward. The two directions provide complementary verification capabilities. Backward verification checks a candidate answer against the original constraints, bypassing complex intermediate reasoning, but cannot ensure correct reasoning or objective completeness. Forward verification follows the problem conditions and current solution, enabling it to locate reasoning errors and assess objective completeness, but may overlook key constraints in complex solution chains. We propose BiVerify, a dynamically scheduled framework for bidirectional mathematical verification. BiVerify begins with backward verification to screen the answer against the original constraints, followed by forward verification of the reasoning process; subsequent direction switching, state resetting, and re-verification are governed by verification outcomes. Upon failure, the system revises the candidate or verification flow until the same candidate passes both directions. We also introduce shared mathematical tools that separate logical reasoning from precise computation. We systematically evaluate BiVerify on five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks using multiple mainstream DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models. BiVerify exceeds the strongest representative public baseline evaluated in this work by 13.5 percentage points in average accuracy, with the margin reaching 31.2 percentage points on GPT. Further analysis shows that BiVerify's overall performance exceeds that of either verification direction alone.

We propose BiVerify, a dynamically scheduled framework for bidirectional mathematical verification.

title: Google AI Releases Elephant-Goldfish Model Plugin for Spec-First Coding
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Google has open-sourced the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM) plugin , a design-and-review layer for AI coding agents. The Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin makes an agent write a specification before it writes code. Fresh subagents with no conversation history then attack that spec. Google says thousands of its engineers use it . It is quite simple: catch wrong assumptions in a Markdown file, not in a pull request. TL;DR Size: 7 skills, 9 reviewer personas, 6 brainstorm lenses, 5 review stages. No model weights; your agent supplies the LLM. Runs on: any harness that can spawn fresh subagents: Antigravity, Claude Code 2.1.271+, Claude Cowork, Codex, ChatGPT. Uses your existing model quota. Performance: no accuracy benchmark published. Evidence is adoption and end-to-end harness test runs. Best: Codex 0.163.0 completed 15 native fresh-context reviewers in order. 2 live tests passed in 573.13s. Worst: the Claude Cowork run stopped after stages 5 to 7 on a usage limit. Issue #237 reports AGENTS.md leaking into Codex reviewers. Bottom line: best thing, forced independent review before code. Worst thing, heavy token use and unverified isolation on some hosts. What is Google’s Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin? EGM is an Apache 2.0 plugin of skills, reviewer personas and document standards. It is not a new language model. The method comes from Dave Rensin’s essay on elephants and goldfish. The Google Open Source blog frames it as a fix for AI “slop” and session context collapse. The README states it is not an officially supported Google product . How does the Elephant-Goldfish workflow work? The Elephant is a long session holding project context and earlier decisions. It drafts the spec and writes no code. Each Goldfish is a stateless subagent. It reads only the draft and the files it references. You resolve trade-offs and approve the design. The core loop has 3 commands: /egm-brainstorm clarifies the idea, then runs a 6-lens Goldfish swarm. Lenses cover YAGNI, token cost, UX, migration, observability and tech debt. Output: concepts_brief.md . /egm-draft turns the brief into a design doc under docs/designs/ , section by section. /egm-review runs the Goldfish review. /egm-drift-report later compares code with the spec. author: Michal Sutter

title: MoE Routing Strategies Explained: Top-K, Expert-Choice, Sigmoid Gating and Dynamic Routing (2026 Guide)
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Every Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model repeats one decision for every token: which experts should process it. That decision belongs to the router. MoE routing strategies shape quality, load balance and serving cost in every major open model. This guide explains the 7 routing strategies used in production, and the models that use each one. TL;DR Size: Routers choose from 8 experts (Mixtral) to 384 (DeepSeek-V4-Pro), activating 1 to 8 per token. Runs on: Routing cost shows up in multi-GPU expert parallelism, where each choice becomes all-to-all network traffic. Performance: Sigmoid scoring with aux-loss-free bias balancing is the dominant 2026 recipe for frontier open MoE models. Best: Loss-free balancing cut MaxVio from 0.72 to 0.04 at 1B, with lower perplexity. Worst: Expert choice leaks future tokens in causal models; one test showed a roughly 10% abnormal loss drop. Bottom line: Best thing: bias-based balancing adds no interfering gradients. Worst thing: no router removes the need for serving-time load fixes. What is MoE routing? MoE routing is the mechanism that sends each token to a small subset of expert networks. A router scores every expert, keeps the top candidates and weights their outputs. Only the selected experts run. Mixtral 8x7B , for example, gives each token access to 47B parameters but uses 13B active parameters. video created by marktechpost.com The 7 MoE routing strategies used in production 1. Softmax top-k token choice Each token scores all experts with a linear layer and keeps the k highest. A softmax over those k scores sets the mixing weights. Mixtral picks 2 of 8 experts. gpt-oss-120b picks 4 of 128. Qwen3-235B-A22B picks 8 of 128. An auxiliary loss usually keeps expert load even. Used by: Mixtral, gpt-oss, Qwen3. 2. Top-1 switch routing with a capacity factor Switch Transformer showed that routing each token to 1 expert preserves quality and cuts router compute. Each expert gets a fixed buffer: tokens per batch divided by experts, times a capacity factor. Overflow tokens skip the layer through the residual connection. Llama 4 Maverick also sends each token to 1 routed expert, plus a shared expert. Used by: Switch Transformer, Llama 4 Maverick (with a shared expert). 3. title: Analysis of the Effect of Doppler on Direct-to-Cell: Real-World Performance and Proposed Improvements
author: Yuxi Chen
contentSnippet: Direct-to-cell (DtC) satellites serve unmodified LTE phones today from low Earth orbit, where the satellite's motion creates Doppler shifts of tens of kHz. Since large offsets such as these cannot be compensated adequately by the user equipment (UE), the satellite pre-compensates the Doppler shift of each beam, but it can do so for only one reference point in the beam. A UE elsewhere in the beam still has to compensate a residual offset; previous field studies report residuals of up to 10 kHz, beyond the $\pm$7.5 kHz that the 15 kHz subcarrier spacing can resolve. In this paper we corroborate this effect with our own detailed measurements of Starlink transmissions and further correlate ineffective handover performance to inadequate residual offset compensation. We analyze the Doppler compensation problem with detailed standard-specific simulations and propose a compensation method at the UE, based on the location of the UE with respect to the beam reference point used for the Doppler compensation and the known satellite location, that improves the efficiency of handover. With UE cell-specific pre-compensation, the neighbors are identified, read correctly and handed over to in time rather than lost to radio-link failure.

title: When Is High-Bandwidth Flash Cost-Effective for LLM Inference?
author: Zhiyu An
contentSnippet: Can high-bandwidth flash (HBF) make LLM inference cheaper than adding GPUs? By storing weights closer to the GPU than SSD, HBF may reduce the number of GPUs needed for model capacity. However, this integration is only justified if it meets service targets and its cost is recovered. We simulate this integration using public component data across nine dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, five workloads, two GPU platforms, and 1--100 GPUs. At fixed demand, HBF reduces the minimum GPU count to meet a service target in 98 of 468 comparisons; majority of them are paused and short sessions, 63 remain cost-effective at half a GPU price per HBF stack. For single short-chat users, HBF enables large MoEs, e.g. DeepSeek V3 and Kimi K2, to meet a relaxed service target on one RTX~4090 GPU, where conventional serving fails. At fixed GPU count, HBF improves throughput in 48\% of matched comparisons below 16 GPUs and 13\% at larger counts. Even at 100 RTX~4090-scale GPUs, cascaded HBF raises offline throughput by 16.4--26.5$\times$ for three large MoEs. We found savings and throughput gains arise in different scenarios.

title: Spatial Harness: Grounding Spatial Reasoning in Executable World States with Physics Engines
author: Chentao Cao, Zhanke Zhou, Sangni Duan, Bo Han
contentSnippet: Spatial reasoning requires understanding how objects and observers are arranged in a scene and how their relations change with viewpoint or movement. Vision-language models (VLMs) typically perform both steps through model-internal reasoning, forming an implicit scene interpretation from partial views and imagining the consequences of spatial transformations. A misread scene can lead to a wrong answer, while even a correct interpretation does not ensure that imagined transformations satisfy spatial constraints. We introduce Spatial Harness, which represents scenes as explicit and executable world states to ground spatial reasoning in physics-engine feedback. A Perceiver integrates scene constraints extracted from the question with specialized visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame. The resulting state is instantiated in a physics engine, where a Reasoner executes viewpoint changes and uses computed measurements and rendered views to guide reasoning. We evaluate on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs. On MindCube, Spatial Harness improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%, surpassing pySpatial by 7.52 percentage points. Given identical annotated object and camera poses, it reaches 98.25% versus 71.81% for model-internal reasoning. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/Spatial-Harness

title: How Much Training-Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?
author: Cong Yu, Ziting Wang, Songlin Jiang, Sitong Zhang
contentSnippet: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least 1.93times as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality 1.62times sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at https://github.com/benyucong/train-inference-mismatch-opd

summary.tldr:
On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained.

Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair.
takeaways: OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget.
Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision.
In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods.
Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address.

title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! title: Terry Pratchett's Study
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News. Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin... But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it. title: AutoC2V: Synthesis-Guided LLM Training for QoR-Optimized C++-to-Verilog Generation
author: Guanqi Lyu
contentSnippet: High-level synthesis (HLS) can translate C/C++ kernels into register-transfer level (RTL) designs, yet generating high-quality hardware still relies heavily on manual pragma tuning and repeated synthesis evaluation. We propose AutoC2V, a C++-to-Verilog generation framework driven by real synthesis feedback that enables large language models (LLMs) to directly generate RTL with improved quality of results (QoR) from synthesizable C++ kernels. We construct training data from real synthesis results, including synthesizable C++ source code, the corresponding Verilog RTL, QoR metrics, and optimization objectives. Using this dataset, we align the model toward synthesis-aware RTL generation through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To reduce the high cost of repeatedly invoking real synthesis during GRPO, we design the QoR Prediction Reward Model (QoR RM), which predicts latency and resource metrics by encoding RTL into long-context semantic representations, thereby providing low-cost and continuous QoR reward signals for policy optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that AutoC2V not only substantially improves RTL functional pass rates, but also achieves superior latency and resource optimization compared to the unfine-tuned base model, representative HLS optimization approaches (HLSPilot, LLM-DSE, and AutoDSE), and advanced general-purpose commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek v4 Pro, and GLM-5.2). These results indicate that combining real synthesis data with efficient QoR reward modeling can further improve the ability of LLMs to generate high-quality RTL.

title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement with Statistical Guarantees
author: Zihe Gao
contentSnippet: Recursive self-improvement offers a promising path toward AI agents that improve through experience by refining their own harnesses without retraining their underlying large language models (LLMs). Making this self-improvement process reliable, however, requires more than generating new updates: agents must decide which changes are worth keeping. A greedy gate that accepts updates based solely on higher validation scores can mistake an observed gain for genuine progress and lead to performance degeneration, whereas overly conservative statistical gates may reject beneficial updates and hinder performance improvement. We introduce Trustworthy Recursive Updates with Statistical Testing (TRUST), a framework that adapts an online multiple hypothesis testing procedure to control the rate of false evolution across rounds, with an LLM analyzing historical context to help determine how much evidence is required to update the incumbent. Under interpretable assumptions, we prove that TRUST limits the proportion of accepted updates that result in unacceptable performance loss. We further derive a lower bound on the final performance gain. Across the benchmarks HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS with the models DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.8-Flash, TRUST reduces the average ratio of accepted inferior updates from the greedy gate's 45.59% to 2.78%, while achieving higher final scores than the state-of-the-art statistical gate baselines for recursive self-improvement. These findings demonstrate that TRUST strikes a balance between statistical reliability and performance gain in recursive self-improvement.

title: DFT-Agent Bench: Scaffold Effects and Execution Provenance in Autonomous DFT
author: Shijie Liu
contentSnippet: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for first-principles materials simulation. We report empirical findings from DFT-Agent Bench, a benchmark of 200+ Quantum ESPRESSO tasks spanning relaxation, electronic structure, equation-of-state, and elastic-tensor pipelines over multiple material tiers. Each task carries a QE-derived ground truth with public-reference cross-checks where available, and a provenance audit checks whether the required QE execution contract was met. Under one execution harness, we compare a near-bare ReAct baseline with a bundled v5.1 scaffold on two models. The complete scaffold improves bands+DOS by +0.08/+0.11 and d-electron vc-relax by +0.17 on both models, while high-scoring relaxation and equation-of-state cells leave little room for improvement. The elastic result is model-dependent (0.18 to 0.40 for deepseek-v4-pro and 0.62 to 0.59 for claude-opus-4-8). A fixed 100-task analysis with retrieval disabled supports the aggregate pattern: the fully frozen DeepSeek comparison gains +0.17, while the Opus comparison gains +0.10 against a historical pool baseline (p < 0.001). The provenance gate catches incomplete or unmarked executions that can receive high rubric scores; it is an execution-contract check, not a test for intentional fraud. These results characterize the evaluated DFT workflows. The anonymous review artifact contains the frozen diagnostic slice, prompts, scorer, and solver revisions: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/231e31re91287h/README.md.

title: MotionGraphicsBench: Evaluating Motion Graphics Generation with Programmatic Verification
author: Jiaju Ma, Ashvini Kumar Jindal, Chuhua Wang, Sumithra Bhakthavatsalam
contentSnippet: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, compared with 83.3% for a GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline, and outperform the baseline in both approval and rejection recall. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 6.0% to 67.7%. Across 15 models evaluated at their highest available reasoning effort with 32 attempts per instance, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We release our benchmark at https://huggingface.co/datasets/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of large language models (LLMs) to generate motion graphics from static SVG inputs and natural language prompts. The dataset consists of 100 instances derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, specifically isolating motion generation from graphic creation to simulate professional designer workflows. Unlike traditional benchmarks that rely on VLM judges or reference comparisons, MotionGraphicsBench utilizes deterministic, human-readable verification programs to assess whether generated animations meet specific spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements.

In performance testing, the programmatic verification approach achieved 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, outperforming a GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline which scored 83.3%. Evaluation of 47 configurations across 32 LLMs from 12 providers revealed significant variance in capability, with pass@1 rates ranging from 6.0% to 67.7%. Even with increased reasoning effort and 32 attempts per instance, pass@32 rates remained between 38.0% and 95.0%. The study identifies common failure modes in current models, including inability to match reference poses, follow precise motion trajectories, or coordinate multi-event sequences.
takeaways: **Benchmark Composition:** Contains 100 expert-curated instances based on real-world Lottie motion designs, available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench.
**Verification Methodology:** Uses deterministic, human-readable programs to verify animation requirements, achieving 93.3% agreement with human evaluators.
**Model Performance:** Across 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 rates vary widely from 6.0% to 67.7%, with pass@32 rates ranging from 38.0% to 95.0%.
**Baseline Comparison:** The programmatic verification method outperformed the GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline in both approval and rejection recall.

title: onóna: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings
author: Cheng Luo, Xinnan Dai, Zhongzhu Zhou, Zefan Cai
contentSnippet:
Authors: Cheng Luo , Xinnan Dai , Zhongzhu Zhou , Zefan Cai , Ruijie Zhu , Tianyu Zhang , Junjie Hu

Abstract: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

Notes: 18 pages

summary.tldr:
Researchers Cheng Luo et al. introduced 'onóna,' a parameterization technique designed to enhance language model output expressiveness while maintaining the parameter efficiency of weight tying. Unlike standard tied output heads that rely on a single softmax, onóna utilizes two embedding tables. The Transformer architecture processes the average of these two tables as input, while the output head computes a mixture of two softmax distributions derived from the same tables. A gate, conditioned exclusively on the current input token, determines the mixture weight, allowing for precomputation during inference without modifying the core Transformer body.

The team evaluated onóna across four distinct architectures—Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts (MoE), and Attention Residual—at 142M, 330M, and 1B parameter scales. Under matched token budgets, the method achieved lower validation loss and external perplexity in 11 out of 12 experimental comparisons. Furthermore, onóna improved average accuracy across eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12 cases. The only performance exception noted was in the 1B MoE model, where the method did not lower validation loss. The implementation cost is limited to one additional embedding table and one additional vocabulary projection.
takeaways: **Methodology:** Uses a two-table parameterization where the input is the average of two embedding tables and the output is a gated mixture of two softmax distributions.
**Performance:** Demonstrated lower validation loss and perplexity in 11 of 12 test cases across Dense, Gated DeltaNet, and Attention Residual architectures.
**Downstream Impact:** Achieved higher average accuracy on eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12 comparisons.
**Computational Overhead:** Requires one additional embedding table and one additional vocabulary projection, with no changes required to the Transformer body.

title: Energy-Tweedie: Score meets Score, Energy meets Energy
author: Andrej Leban
contentSnippet: Denoising and score estimation are classically linked through Tweedie's formula, which relates the posterior mean under Gaussian noise to the Stein score of the noisy marginal. In this work, we extend this perspective beyond Gaussian noise to a broad class of Gibbs (energy-based) noise distributions, with the generalized Gaussian family as an example. We derive the Energy-Tweedie identity: when the denoising posterior is viewed through the lens of scoring rules, the path derivative of a kernel scoring rule defined by the noise potential recovers the Stein score of the noisy marginal. Thus, the familiar correspondence between Gaussian noise, posterior means, squared loss, and Tweedie's formula is lifted to a distributional correspondence between Gibbs noise distributions, full posterior laws, kernel scoring rules, and the Energy-Tweedie identity, which gives a Tweedie-style relation for each noise potential. Among its consequences, this identity gives a posterior-samples-to-score route to score estimation, yields a principled criterion for estimating unknown noise parameters, and enables diffusion-style sampling along user-chosen paths through the noise-parameter space, supplying the score-based perspective on recent generative methods trained with scoring rules.

title: Longtail-SWE: High-Quality SWE Tasks for Underrepresented Languages
author: Vladimir Dobrovolskii, Ibragim Badertdinov, Alexander Golubev
contentSnippet: Challenging repository-level benchmarks remain limited for many programming language ecosystems, where filtering scarce candidates with ambiguous descriptions or defective tests can discard valuable engineering problems. We introduce Longtail-SWE, a benchmark of 202 issue-resolution tasks across 13 languages with limited coverage in existing repository-level benchmarks: Clojure, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Haskell, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, OCaml, R, Scala, and Swift. Its construction uses a solver--judge--repairer pipeline: a solver attempts each candidate task, and a judge reviews the task together with the solver's trajectory and test results to guide revisions to tests and task descriptions. These revisions aim to correct tests that reject valid alternative implementations or accept incorrect solutions while retaining challenging tasks and preserving their intended requirements. We evaluate nine model configurations, including frontier models, and analyze task-solving performance, consistency across repeated attempts, and resource usage. We release all benchmark instances, executable environments, complete construction and evaluation tooling, and agent trajectories, together with an additional set of easier tasks to support evaluation of smaller models.

title: Satellite Streaks in HETDEX: Spectra, Orbital Identification, and Survey Impact
author: Erin Mentuch Cooper
contentSnippet: We present a spectroscopic database and analysis of satellite streaks in Public Data Release 1 (PDR1) from the Hobby-Eberly Telescope Dark Energy Experiment (HETDEX), covering 6778 observations and $\sim$90 deg$^2$ of sky from January 2017 to July 2024. We detect 527 streaks across 492 observations, a contamination fraction of 7.3% that rises to monthly values above 20% by 2023--2024, although the streaks mask only 0.09% of the survey area. Of the 527 streaks, 475 (90.1%) are identified with a cataloged object using archival two-line elements: 258 (54%) lie in low or Earth orbit and 217 (46%) are geostationary or highly elliptical. Only 35% were launched since 2010; the rest are spent rocket bodies, debris, and older spacecraft. This reflects HETDEX's sensitivity to faint objects and its 2017--2024 observing baseline. The Hobby-Eberly Telescope's large 10\,m aperture and HETDEX's $\sim$6\,minute exposures result in similar observed magnitudes for low Earth orbit (LEO) and geostationary Earth orbit (GEO) objects (median $g_{\rm AB}=16.2\pm1.1$ for LEO, $16.7\pm1.1$ for GEO). However, once transit time is corrected for, instantaneous magnitudes differ widely: $g_{\rm inst}=7.4$ for LEO versus $g_{\rm inst}=13.0$ for GEO objects, a difference of 5.6\,mag, while the exposure-averaged magnitudes differ by only 0.5 mag. Normalized to 550 km, the 34 Starlink streaks give $g(550 {\rm km})=5.95$, consistent with the mean $V(550\,{\rm km})=5.92\pm0.04$ reported for VisorSat-design spacecraft. The spectra are consistent with reflected sunlight, with modest, signal-to-noise-driven differences in slope. The catalog, spectra, and code are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22962479.

title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet: Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security. The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It's unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats. We regret to inform you... Last Friday, Chainalysis said it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It's not clear why the company considered such information "non-sensitive." title: AVCORP: Identifying and Resisting Deception via Communication Theory and Theory of Mind
author: Fardin Saad
contentSnippet: Today's LLM-based agents are vulnerable to deception by users and other agents. Defending against deception requires Theory of Mind (ToM) reasoning to infer the beliefs and goals of others as well as modeling tactics based on communication theory. To enable training models to detect deception, we adopt the well-known deception game, Avalon. We present a corpus, AVCORP, of 5,000 annotated utterances from 250 games of Avalon. AVCORP includes (1) 37 tactics mapped to a 4x4 behavior matrix, and (2) reasoning traces capturing abductive hypotheses, suspicion levels, and nested ToM beliefs. We train Qwen3-8B on AVCORP and evaluate it on 25 held-out games and 20 games played by humans. On held-out games, our best trained detector outperforms its untrained baseline and frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro), matching Claude Opus 5.5. On human games, every trained detector exceeds the untrained model in F1 score across all rounds.

title: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints
author: Shantanu Tripathi
contentSnippet: When you deploy a model to a GPU endpoint, the smallest unit of GPU you can request is one whole accelerator. This constraint can cost you twice. First, you can’t host more models on an instance than it has accelerators. An ml.p4d.24xlarge has eight A100s, so it holds eight models, whether each one needs 40 GB or 14 GB. Second, and less obvious, it makes every deployment come down to a choice of which full GPU to deploy to. As your concurrency and prompt lengths grow, a full GPU on an older instance stops being enough, but a full GPU on a newer one is more than your model can use. You end up either under-served or paying for capability you never reach. Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation. This post covers both. The first part is the direct benefit: deploy more models than you have GPUs, with isolation between them. The second is the one customers ask about when the question turns to cost: how the granularity of partitioning helps you pick the right-sized unit, and what we measured when we did. One thing to know before you read further: GPU partitioning works on endpoints that use inference components , the construct you use to deploy several models to one endpoint and set the compute each model gets. Partitioning builds directly on it. A partition is a resource a component asks for, in the same place it already asks for CPU and memory. If you haven’t used inference components, this post introduces them. Single-model endpoints, serverless endpoints, and heterogeneous instance pools cannot be partitioned. What customers do today, and why each option falls short If you have more models than accelerators, you have had three choices. Run fewer, larger endpoints and batch harder – This raises utilization, but only when the models are interchangeable. A portfolio of fine-tuned variants or per-tenant models is not. Use multi-model endpoints –  These load and unload models from a shared GPU on demand, which fits sparse, bursty traffic.

title: Taxonomy of agentic primitives in AWS Quick
author: Thomas Delteil
contentSnippet: Over the past year, as we built AWS Quick, our agents went from answering questions to taking actions: scheduling meetings, running research, generating reports. As the system evolved, one problem kept resurfacing: there was no shared definition of the primitives that agentic work is built from. The same few ideas kept getting rebuilt under different names: an actor that does the work, a signal that starts it, a packaged procedure, and a memory that carries lessons forward. This repetition leaked into product design and onto the user. Take the user who says “ monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest ”. Is that a new agent, a scheduled instruction to an existing one, a workflow, or a skill? These are different questions, but without a shared vocabulary they collapse into one confusing choice. This post shares the taxonomy we converged on: one set of primitives found by decomposing agentic work into four plain questions: When? , What? , Who? , and How? Most of the framework stays invisible to end users by design, but a shared vocabulary makes the system easier to reason about for anyone building beneath it. This post describes these primitives and how they relate to one another. It’s the first post in a series, and upcoming posts cover our agentic operating system, background learning, proactive feeds, and much more. Triggers: What causes work to begin Triggers are the activation mechanism for getting work done, but they also carry instructions: a human message is both the moment of activation and the description of what to do. They are both the When? and the What? of a task. Human-initiated: A person opens a conversation and asks the agent to do something. Interactive, synchronous, conversational. Agent-delegated: One agent, mid-task, invokes another to handle a sub-problem. Programmatic, composable, potentially recursive. Scheduled: Time-based activation, like “run financial research every Monday at 9am.” Deterministic, with the same standing instructions applied across runs. title: Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate
author: Aishwarya Pawar
contentSnippet: Organizations building applications powered by artificial intelligence (AI) face a recurring challenge: giving large language model (LLM) agents access to enterprise data lakes without duplicating integration logic across every agent and application. Most teams begin by wiring agents directly to databases and APIs, with no shared gateway such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in between. Each new dataset demands custom code, and each agent reimplements its own access control. As the number of datasets or agents grows, permission enforcement drifts, and onboarding a new data source becomes a multi-day engineering effort. Our team supports Amazon’s North America Sort Center (NASC) network, where planning teams rely on operational data to manage capacity, labor, and package flow. To give those teams conversational access to that data, we built a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate to address this problem for planning teams in NASC. The server acts as a centralized, agent-agnostic gateway between AI agents and our enterprise data lake. Exposing a new dataset requires only a JSON metadata file that the server discovers automatically on the next pipeline sync. In this post, we describe the architecture, show how a metadata-driven approach removes the need for per-dataset integration code, and explain how the serverless infrastructure supports multiple agents and applications in a multi-tenant environment. Problem statement and design goals Two interrelated challenges shaped how we designed this system: fragmented data access patterns and an unsustainable onboarding model. Integration challenge at scale Our data lake contains thousands of datasets spanning operational metrics, business analytics, and domain-specific data. Multiple teams wanted AI assistants that could query this data conversationally, but each built its own integration from scratch. Each agent embedded its own SQL generation logic, schema knowledge, and connection handling, so a schema change meant patching every agent individually. Access control was fragmented, with no single audit point for data access decisions. Onboarding a new dataset required custom tool code, query validation, and redeployment, typically a multi-day effort per table. title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1
author: Hammad Ausaf
contentSnippet: An AI agent that updates a ticket or reads a customer record acts for a person, inside applications that person can reach. Your identity team then has to answer a question that per-app OAuth consent and shared service accounts leave open: which agent might act for which user in which application, and how you stop it. Okta Cross App Access (XAA) answers it in your identity provider (IdP). You register the agent in Okta, an administrator approves the applications it might reach, and Okta evaluates policy each time the agent asks to act for a user. In our tests, after an administrator removed a user’s assignment to the agent, Okta refused the agent’s new requests for that user within about 1 second, and tokens already issued expired within 5 minutes. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses two of its capabilities to carry out Okta’s decision on AWS. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates Okta’s grant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeems it for a short-lived access token with credentials your agent code doesn’t see, and keeps that token in its token vault. In our tests, AgentCore Identity added about 0.6 seconds to a request that took about 30 seconds end to end. In this post, the first of two, you build a task agent on AgentCore runtime that acts for signed-in users through XAA and AgentCore Identity. You configure the AgentCore Identity parts it needs, enforce each user’s authority in the tools, and see what we measured: what each check refuses, the practices we settled on, and how fast Okta’s controls take effect. Part 2 then puts the same governance behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Cedar policies, a second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and an audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch. Solution overview Okta is the governance plane: it decides which agent might act for which user, against which resource. AgentCore Identity is the execution plane: it holds the agent’s credentials, turns Okta’s decision into a token the resource accepts, and keeps both identities in that token. title: RidgeFill: Training-Free Late-Layer Cache Fill for Faster Prefill
author: Dylan Johnston
contentSnippet: RidgeFill shortens prefill by not computing most of a model's upper layers for the prompt. The lower layers run exactly up to a split; from the split layer's state a per-layer map predicts every later layer's input, and each late layer writes its cache from that prediction. The design follows YOCO and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, where the projection is trained into the model. RidgeFill retrofits it onto models that were never trained for it: the map is a ridge regression fitted once in closed form from one pass over calibration text, the layer's own projections run unchanged, and a chosen set of rows, the last few thousand tokens, and every decoding step run the full model. Nothing is trained and no token is dropped. Most of the work was in measurement, finding a repeatable methodology. Loss averaged over all tokens hides RidgeFill's error. Needle retrieval in the filled region, loss on tokens that depend on distant context, and splice tests that swap filled keys or values for exact ones show which component carries it: the keys on Llama-3.1-8B, half of it in their scale, and the values and the recurrent state on Qwen3.5-9B. On Qwen3.8-27B in a llama.cpp fork on an A100, time to first token is 1.25 to 1.31x faster at 16K to 120K tokens with the maps in VRAM; RULER changes by -1.2 and -1.4 points and LongBench v2 by -1.4; the 95 % intervals include zero but do not rule out losses of a few points. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in vLLM it is 1.50 to 1.60x faster than exact at 9K to 32K tokens, with RULER's needle tasks at 99.8 against 100.0 and perplexity on novel tokens 2.65 % higher [-0.02 %, +4.93 %]. On three 8 to 9B reference models, at the same split and tail as the identity fill, the fitted map retrieves 49.1 and 49.6 more filled-region RULER points on the two dense models (at that split Llama's loss is worse), and its long-document loss is +/-0.03 nats of the released SwiftKV checkpoint's.

title: Taxbit Assist: A grounded, role-aware AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Karan Nayak
contentSnippet: Taxbit is a digital-asset tax and accounting compliance platform. Founded in 2018, Taxbit helps enterprises such as exchanges, payment services, and brokers calculate gains and losses, collect tax documentation, and file information returns at scale. Now, a cited, permission-aware AI assistant helps compliance teams find answers right inside the product dashboard. But the knowledge needed to use that dashboard well was scattered across the public website, API documentation, and help-center articles, and a meaningful share was never written down at all. When a customer asked “what does this form status mean?”, they either went digging or filed a support ticket. Today more than 55 percent of users who ask Assist a question return to ask another within 24 hours, according to Taxbit’s internal production analytics. title: META-IR: Meta-Introspective Reasoning for Adaptive Safety Alignment in LLM
author: Mahabubur Rahman Miraj
contentSnippet: Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks and harmful-content prompts, particularly under adversarial distribution shifts where static alignment pipelines fail to generalize. Although introspective methods such as STAIR strengthen refusal consistency, they depend on fixed self-evaluation policies that cannot rapidly adapt to evolving manipulation strategies. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces META-IR, a meta-introspective reasoning framework that enhances safety alignment through meta-learning-driven adaptation. It employs a dual-loop architecture: an inner introspective loop that performs structured risk analysis, self-assessment, and reflective correction via SI-MCTS, and an outer meta-learning loop that optimizes the introspection policy across diverse jailbreak task families to enable rapid generalization to unseen attacks. A dynamic jailbreak simulation module further exposes the model to progressively harder adversarial prompts, enabling continual self-improvement without human supervision. Experiments across multiple models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2-7B-Instruct) and a broad suite of safety, helpfulness, generalization, and introspection metrics demonstrate that META-IR substantially improves adaptation speed, robustness, and reasoning stability compared with all baseline models. These results establish META-IR as an effective pathway toward building LLMs capable of sustained, adaptive safety alignment under dynamic and evolving threat environments.

title: How NVIDIA Open Source Tools Are Helping Researchers Build Next-Generation 6G Networks
author: Soma Velayutham
contentSnippet: A year ago, NVIDIA open sourced its Aerial wireless software , joining Sionna and a broader suite of open source tools for accelerating next-generation 6G network development. Together, they give researchers a foundation for testing ideas, comparing results and building on each other’s work — connecting simulation and AI training with experiments on real over-the-air wireless systems. Today, researchers and developers are using these tools to build 6G-ready networks that do more than just transmit data — receiving signals more effectively, keeping robots and autonomous systems connected when it matters most, and adapting in real time as devices move through the world. Over the past year, global developer adoption of NVIDIA AI Aerial and NVIDIA Sionna software has grown 10x, while NVIDIA’s open source 5G/6G tools have surpassed 1 million downloads. More than 8,000 research and academic institutions worldwide are using these platforms. The projects emerging today offer a view of how future networks could look. Each addresses a different challenge, but together point toward a broader ambition for building AI-native 6G networks that deliver connectivity, computing and sensing over a converged software-defined platform for billions of people, machines and agents. Networks That Help Robots React Faster A robot picking up an object needs to understand its surroundings and act before they change. When the AI powering that decision runs on a nearby server or in the cloud, the wireless connection becomes part of the response time. Researchers are exploring a more efficient approach called goal-oriented semantic communications. Instead of sending full images, robots transmit compact descriptions of objects, their positions and their relationships. Transmitting just as much information as needed allows robots to more quickly respond, especially in dynamic environments like workplaces and warehouses. At King’s College London , researchers connected a camera-equipped robot arm to an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin running NVIDIA Sionna, which supports both software-defined 5G network and edge AI processing. In fruit-packing and cube-stacking experiments with deliberately introduced faults, the approach reduced robot task completion time by up to 52.6% and improved task success compared with sending periodic images. title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
author: Grace Huckins
contentSnippet: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour. I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself. title: InstantHMR : Real-Time Human Mesh Recovery on Your Phone
author: Mohamed Adjel, Kahina Chalabi, Vincent Bonnet
contentSnippet: Real-time 3D human mesh recovery from a single image on mobile devices is a challenging problem with many applications, including robotics, biomechanics, AR/VR, and exergames. Current state-of-the-art models are either too slow to run efficiently on mobile devices or sacrifice accuracy for speed. We present InstantHMR, a family of open-source single-image regressors suited for mobile inference, based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) parametric model and trained exclusively on publicly available annotations from the SAM 3D Body dataset. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on a Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, recovering a 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.5 ms per person, and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. This speed surpasses all existing methods we evaluated. On mobile, it is 12x faster than the single mobile-compatible method that slightly outperforms ours in accuracy, while achieving competitive accuracy with 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB and 41.7 mm on RICH. To ensure fair comparisons, we re-evaluate 11 state-of-the-art methods under a unified protocol aligned with the closest MHR-based competitors, including Meta's official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, and report their reproduction results. Additionally, we measure latency across eight different targets, ranging from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR.

title: Analyzing Code Provenance in LLMs for Programming Education
author: Subhankar Maity
contentSnippet: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasing role in programming education, challenging traditional assessment methods as they can generate fully functional code instantly. This disrupts the reliability of student submissions as indicators of learning and effort. To address this issue, code provenance is essential for tracing the origins of code and distinguishing student-authored, AI-generated, and externally sourced components. We extend the Min-K% probability approach by incorporating synthetic non-member code generation and apply it to Python code for membership inference and provenance tracking. Evaluations cover free LLMs such as GPT-2, DistilGPT-2, and DialoGPT, as well as state-of-the-art commercial models including GPT-5, Gemini 2.5, Mistral, DeepSeek, and LLaMA 3.3. Before evaluating our approach on higher-education student assignments, we validate its feasibility using Stack Overflow data. The results show that free models enable more sensitive code memorization detection than commercial models. By systematically comparing these LLMs, we assess trade-offs between detection accuracy and privacy protection, taking an initial step toward effective assessment of AI-assisted programming education through combined provenance detection and process visibility.

title: Does Reasoning Improve Psychological Depth in Large Language Models?
author: Ruichen Zheng
contentSnippet: Benchmark gains from reasoning-enhanced large language models encourage the assumption that these models should broadly perform better on complex generative tasks, but this remains underexplored in open-ended, creative domains shaped by nuances of reader experience. We tested this assumption through the lens of psychological depth in short stories. We compared DeepSeek-R1 vs. DeepSeek-V3, our closest available contrast for reasoning-oriented post-training, and GPT-5 vs. GPT-4o, through 60 blinded pairwise evaluations in which seven human annotators and an ensemble LLM-as-a-Judge rated prompt-matched story outputs. Human evaluations showed no universal reasoning advantage: GPT-5 was slightly preferred over GPT-4o (60.0-62.9% across two reasoning-effort settings), whereas DeepSeek-R1 fell behind DeepSeek-V3 (42.9%). Although this pattern was marked by low inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's $α= 0.070$), our annotation-quality checks suggested genuine evaluative subjectivity, plausibly reflecting distinct annotator decision schemes rather than annotation failure. In contrast, the LLM-as-a-Judge showed a strong pro-reasoning bias (98.3% of pairs vs. 55.2% of human votes), consistent across its five configurations and partly tracking sentence length. These findings suggest that, at the frontier, reasoning-related quality differences are small enough to be dominated by reader subjectivity, and that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators can obscure this subjectivity in nuanced creative-generation tasks.

title: ISER-MoE: Dynamic In-Switch Replication of Hot Experts for Load Balancing in Expert-Parallel
author: Jintao Peng
contentSnippet: Expert-parallel mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers run at the pace of the most loaded GPU, and a few hot experts carry most of the excess load. Replicating them at every MoE layer balances the load only if their weights arrive within the layer, and broadcasting from the owner is the bottleneck: point-to-point copies overload it, and baseline broadcasts pay latency or bandwidth overheads. We present ISER-MoE (In-Switch Expert Replication for MoE), built in TensorRT-LLM, which multicasts hot experts through the NVLink switch to fixed GPU groups, so each byte leaves its owner once. A GPU scheduler assigns hot experts to groups per layer, and a multi-port broadcast spreads the injection over the group's ports, both overlapped with the shared expert. In trace replay, the scheduler removed 98-99% of the excess load; in prefill serving of DeepSeek-V4-Pro, throughput rose 17.4% on a math benchmark and 7.2% on agentic prompts.

title: e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)
author: Swann Bessa, Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré, Gergely Szilvasy, Hugo Touvron
contentSnippet:
Authors: Swann Bessa , Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré , Gergely Szilvasy , Hugo Touvron , David Picard , Matthijs Douze , Hervé Jégou

Abstract: Lloyd's k-means algorithm is a long-running standard for clustering, with applications in data analysis, retrieval, quantization and data curation. In this paper, we introduce an exponential moving average optimization procedure for k-means with mini-batch updates, powered by modern deep learning machinery and new insights. We also establish scaling laws on how decay rate and batch size impact final performance. This gives us a formulaic rule to fix them for multiple problem sizes and embedding datasets, without the need for any hyperparameter sweep. The resulting clustering algorithm, coined e-means, is much faster than Lloyd k-means and converges to lower losses, frequently even beating k-means++. On a wide array of embeddings datasets, it beats the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, which translates to 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedups compared to state-of-the-art k-means implementations. As an example, e-means partitions DINO10B, a dataset of 10 billion DINO embeddings, into 16 million clusters in only 2.5 epochs, reaching a loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs.

summary.tldr:
Researchers from Meta and associated institutions have introduced 'e-means,' an optimization procedure for k-means clustering that utilizes exponential moving average (EMA) updates within a mini-batch framework. By leveraging modern deep learning infrastructure, the authors established specific scaling laws governing the relationship between decay rates and batch sizes, effectively eliminating the requirement for hyperparameter tuning across various embedding datasets. The algorithm is designed to replace the traditional Lloyd's k-means approach, offering a more efficient path to convergence for large-scale data curation and quantization tasks.

Performance benchmarks demonstrate that e-means achieves lower loss values than standard Lloyd's k-means and frequently outperforms k-means++ initialization. In practical testing, the algorithm reaches the loss level of a 25-epoch Lloyd's run in just 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, resulting in GPU wall-clock speedups ranging from 10x to 45x. A notable demonstration involved partitioning the DINO10B dataset—comprising 10 billion DINO embeddings—into 16 million clusters in only 2.5 epochs, surpassing the loss metrics of traditional methods.
takeaways: **Algorithm Mechanism:** e-means replaces standard Lloyd's updates with an exponential moving average (EMA) optimization procedure optimized for mini-batch processing.
**Efficiency Gains:** The method delivers 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedups compared to state-of-the-art k-means implementations.
**Scaling Laws:** The authors derived a formulaic rule for setting decay rates and batch sizes, removing the need for manual hyperparameter sweeps.
**Large-Scale Benchmark:** The algorithm successfully clustered 10 billion DINO embeddings into 16 million clusters in 2.5 epochs.
**Performance Metric:** e-means consistently achieves lower loss values than Lloyd's k-means at 25 epochs within a fraction of the time.

title: RidgeFill: Training-Free Late-Layer Cache Fill for Faster Prefill
author: Dylan Johnston, Robert P. Smith
contentSnippet: RidgeFill shortens prefill by not computing most of a model's upper layers for the prompt. The lower layers run exactly up to a split; from the split layer's state a per-layer map predicts every later layer's input, and each late layer writes its cache from that prediction. The design follows YOCO and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, where the projection is trained into the model. RidgeFill retrofits it onto models that were never trained for it: the map is a ridge regression fitted once in closed form from one pass over calibration text, the layer's own projections run unchanged, and a chosen set of rows, the last few thousand tokens, and every decoding step run the full model. Nothing is trained and no token is dropped. Most of the work was in measurement, finding a repeatable methodology. Loss averaged over all tokens hides RidgeFill's error. Needle retrieval in the filled region, loss on tokens that depend on distant context, and splice tests that swap filled keys or values for exact ones show which component carries it: the keys on Llama-3.1-8B, half of it in their scale, and the values and the recurrent state on Qwen3.5-9B. On Qwen3.8-27B in a llama.cpp fork on an A100, time to first token is 1.25 to 1.31x faster at 16K to 120K tokens with the maps in VRAM; RULER changes by -1.2 and -1.4 points and LongBench v2 by -1.4; the 95 % intervals include zero but do not rule out losses of a few points. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in vLLM it is 1.50 to 1.60x faster than exact at 9K to 32K tokens, with RULER's needle tasks at 99.8 against 100.0 and perplexity on novel tokens 2.65 % higher [-0.02 %, +4.93 %]. On three 8 to 9B reference models, at the same split and tail as the identity fill, the fitted map retrieves 49.1 and 49.6 more filled-region RULER points on the two dense models (at that split Llama's loss is worse), and its long-document loss is +/-0.03 nats of the released SwiftKV checkpoint's.

title: Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching
author: Chuangtao Ma, Sriom Chakrabarti, Arijit Khan, Bálint Molnár
contentSnippet: Traditional similarity-based schema matching methods fail to resolve semantic ambiguities and conflicts in complex, domain-specific mappings due to a lack of commonsense and domain-specific knowledge. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) without sufficient background knowledge tend to hallucinate, further complicating schema matching. To overcome these limitations, we introduce KG-RAG4SM, a Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching. This method integrates novel retrieval mechanisms, including LLM-based, vector-based, graph traversal-based, and hybrid techniques with advanced reranking schemes to extract the most relevant subgraphs from large external KGs. Our approach achieves superior results without requiring re-training, as evidenced by improvements of 39.79% in precision and 30.56% in F1 score over LLM-based state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods (e.g., Jellyfish-8B) on the MIMIC dataset, and enhancements of 69.20% in precision and 21.99% in F1 score over pre-trained language model (PLM)-based SOTA methods (e.g., SMAT) on the Synthea dataset. Additionally, KG-RAG4SM scales effectively across KGs from commonsense KGs to domain-specific ones, while its instruction-tuning knowledge exclusion component ensures truthful performance in end-to-end schema matching tasks despite the suboptimal relevance of KG context. Our empirical analysis and case studies from real-world scenarios show that the hallucination problem in LLMs for schema matching is well mitigated by our solution.

Additionally, KG-RAG4SM scales effectively across KGs from commonsense KGs to domain-specific ones, while its instruction-tuning knowledge exclusion component ensures truthful performance in end-to-end schema matching tasks despite the suboptimal relevance of KG context.
