**Project Lightwell:** A $5 billion initiative unveiled by Red Hat and IBM in May 2026 aimed at securing open-source software within enterprise infrastructure.

title: Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics
author: Aditya Mehta
contentSnippet:
It feels like AI is cracking a new math problem every week. Last month, OpenAI alone released 719 manuscripts claiming solutions to some of the field’s hardest problems. Even the computer checks can slip . After years of AI slop, it’s fair to wonder whether math is next.

AxiomMath is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground. The $1.6B startup wants to build a verified foundation that AI agents can rely on to write software and, eventually, do science.

On Wednesday, the company announced it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans. Mathematicians often hold Stacks in rare regard—Columbia mathematician Peter Woit has claimed there’s “ nothing else really comparable ,” comparing the project to “ the famous Bourbaki books ,” a series that rebuilt math from its foundations in the 20th century.

Woit’s Columbia colleague Johan de Jong started the Stacks Project in 2005 as an open-source reference. Mathematicians have contributed to it ever since, building out results from college-level algebra all the way up to the field’s most advanced ideas across algebra, geometry, and number theory.

The company’s fleet of AI agents translates the library’s roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of computer-checked code.

Formalizing math is a way of making sure the structure underneath it is sound. Mathematicians rewrite the proof as code in a programming language called Lean, and a program called a proof assistant checks the code line by line. If the proof passes, mathematicians can trust that it’s logically sound.

Engineers use the same idea, called formal verification, to confirm their chip designs work , while researchers in France have used it to catch bugs in software that calculates family benefits.

For a library like the Stacks Project, checking each theorem is only part of the job. The theorems and definitions in Stacks are interconnected, and each one builds on the ones before it. Like a family tree, many results in Stacks trace back to the ones that came before it.

That interconnectedness made Axiom unsure the project would work at first. The team had to keep every connection intact across about 16 million lines of Lean code.

“Things that are big and things that are delicate in life just don’t go together,” Axiom CEO Carina Hong told TechCr

summary.tldr:
Axiom Math, a $1.6 billion startup founded in March 2025 by CEO Carina Hong, has announced the formal verification of the Stacks Project, a massive open-source repository of mathematical knowledge. By utilizing a fleet of autonomous AI agents, the company translated approximately 7,654 pages of human-written mathematics into 16 million lines of Lean code. This process ensures that the interconnected theorems and definitions within the Stacks Project are logically sound and free of paradoxes, providing a verified foundation for future AI-driven scientific and software development.

The technical methodology involved training proprietary models specifically for mathematical reasoning, moving beyond standard "vibe coding" to instill a sense of mathematical "taste" in the agents. These agents operated in parallel, identifying and executing tasks within a loose hierarchy to maintain the integrity of the project's complex, tree-like structure of dependencies. This formalization addresses a significant "black hole" in algebraic geometry, enabling researchers and AI agents to build new proofs and software infrastructure on a verified substrate rather than starting from scratch. Axiom Math, which raised a $200 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures, positions this work as a critical safeguard against the proliferation of "AI slop" in technical fields.
takeaways: **Project Scale:** The Stacks Project, originally started by Johan de Jong in 2005, was converted into 16 million lines of Lean-verified code.
**Company Valuation:** Axiom Math is currently valued at $1.6 billion following a $200 million Series A funding round led by Menlo Ventures.

**Technical Approach:** The company trained proprietary models to perform formal verification, allowing agents to self-organize and work in parallel to maintain logical consistency across interconnected mathematical results.

**Strategic Goal:** Axiom aims to provide a verified foundation for AI agents to write bug-free software and conduct scientific research, challenging other coding companies to adopt formalization at scale.

title: Detecting signs of hypertension using wearable sensors
author: Google AI Research Blog
contentSnippet:
November 5, 2026 Paolo Di Achille, Staff Research Scientist, and Ming-Zher Poh, Senior Staff Research Scientist, Google Research

We present a new AI system that leverages standard consumer smartwatch sensors to passively detect signs of high blood pressure.

Hypertension (i.e., high blood pressure), often called the "silent killer”, affects over one billion people globally, yet more than half of adults with the condition are unaware they have it . Because it rarely presents with obvious symptoms, high blood pressure (BP) is typically discovered only through incidental screening. This gap in awareness is particularly severe among younger adults aged 18 to 44 , where missing diagnoses can delay life-saving early interventions and significantly increase the long-term risk of adverse cardiovascular events like stroke or heart failure.

Office BP measurement serves as the primary initial screening gateway for detecting hypertension. In recent years, cuffless wearable devices have emerged as a potential tool to complement episodic office care. However, existing commercial solutions usually require regular calibration using a traditional arm cuff. This means they only track relative changes from a baseline cuff reading rather than identifying absolute hypertensive states, limiting their utility as independent screening tools.

In a new study published in Nature , we present a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of passively detecting signs of hypertension using a consumer smartwatch, without requiring any cuff calibration. Dubbed AI-PPG-ACC-HTN , we validated this system against the clinical gold standard of 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), and it achieves accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuff-based diagnostic workflows for both initial and confirmatory screening. These research findings helped inform the blood pressure trends Health Guardian feature in the Google Health app.

Instead of attempting to estimate exact, point-in-time systolic and diastolic blood pressure values, which are highly susceptible to transient environmental noise, our system reframes the problem. It focuses on identifying an individual’s underlying, persistent hypertensive state by aggregating passive physiological signatures over multiple days.

The system leverages data from two sensors already active on modern smartwatches:

Photoplethysmog

summary.tldr:
Google Research scientists Paolo Di Achille and Ming-Zher Poh have introduced AI-PPG-ACC-HTN, a multimodal AI system capable of detecting hypertension using standard consumer smartwatch sensors without requiring cuff-based calibration. Published in Nature, the system shifts the diagnostic paradigm from point-in-time measurements to the identification of persistent hypertensive states by aggregating physiological signatures over multiple days. The research, which informed the 'Health Guardian' feature in the Google Health app, was developed in collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School.

The system utilizes a two-stage machine learning architecture. Stage one employs a 1-D deep convolutional neural network trained via self-supervised contrastive learning on 492,347 hours of sensor data from 2,109 participants to create waveform embeddings from PPG (photoplethysmography) and ACC (accelerometry) signals. Stage two uses a regularized logistic regression classifier to process these embeddings alongside user height to output a hypertension probability score. By aggregating data over time, the model filters out transient noise, such as movement or temperature fluctuations, to isolate vascular and cardiac signatures like pulse wave reflections and ballistocardiogram (BCG) modulations.
takeaways: **Clinical Validation:** In a study of 196 participants, the system achieved 65.8% sensitivity and 90.0% specificity for initial screening, outperforming office-based screenings (55.3% sensitivity).
**Confirmatory Performance:** For confirmatory testing, the system reached 78.4% sensitivity and 96.7% positive predictive value (PPV), exceeding the performance of return office BP measurements.

**Sensor Fusion:** The model integrates PPG optical sensors for blood volume tracking and ACC motion sensors to capture the ballistocardiogram (BCG), specifically analyzing 'K waves' and 'IJK complexes' as indicators of cardiac mechanical function.
**Interpretability Findings:** High-risk hypertension scores correlated with reduced pulse width, slower systolic upstrokes, and lower d/a ratios, suggesting increased arterial stiffness.
**Training Scale:** The model's waveform encoder was pre-trained on a massive unlabeled dataset comprising 492,347 hours of sensor data from 2,109 consenting individuals.

title: The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models
author: Matthew Leib
contentSnippet: Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it. “We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers. Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is YouTube , where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents. “I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.” Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it. “Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.” That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents. “I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. title: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge
author: Amr Elmeleegy
contentSnippet: Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack. But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory. That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit. How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed. Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin platform, HBM capacity per GPU rose roughly 3%, while agentic throughput per dollar rose by up to 30x on SemiAnalysis AgentX. Agentic Inference Is Putting More Pressure on HBM Frontier models now have trillions of parameters — the values that hold what an AI model learned in training. KV cache, which holds the context the model needs to understand each active request without reprocessing the same information, is also expanding. Agentic trajectories carry prior context across repeated model and tool calls, in some cases processing up to 3 million tokens, so each request’s working memory grows over time. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) adds relevant enterprise information to prompts, creating even more context to process and retain. During inference, HBM primarily holds both model parameters and KV cache. The result: greater pressure on HBM. Why AI Factories Need a Memory Hierarchy Adding more HBM capacity per GPU is the obvious response to that pressure, but capacity delivers only what bandwidth can move. Think of HBM as a warehouse and memory bandwidth as its loading docks. A lar

summary.tldr:
NVIDIA is addressing GPU memory constraints through a full-stack codesign strategy that integrates hardware (GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage) and software to optimize the memory hierarchy. Rather than relying solely on increasing High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) capacity, the company focuses on maximizing the utility of every byte across the hierarchy, which includes HBM, CPU memory, local SSDs, and shared storage. This approach aims to mitigate the bottleneck created by the competing demands of model weights and KV cache within the limited HBM tier.

Technical benchmarks provided by NVIDIA indicate that while HBM capacity per GPU increased by approximately 3% between the Blackwell Ultra and the upcoming Vera Rubin platform, agentic throughput per dollar improved by up to 30x, as measured by the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark. This efficiency is critical as agentic applications and RAG workflows drive context windows up to 3 million tokens, significantly increasing the working memory required for KV cache and model parameters during inference.
takeaways: **Memory Hierarchy Strategy:** NVIDIA optimizes data movement across HBM, CPU memory, local SSDs, and shared storage to balance speed and cost-per-bit.
**Throughput Gains:** Agentic throughput per dollar increased by up to 30x on the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark between the Blackwell Ultra and Vera Rubin generations.
**HBM Scaling:** HBM capacity per GPU saw a modest 3% increase during the transition from Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin platform.
**Inference Pressure:** Growing KV cache requirements for agentic trajectories and RAG workflows are creating significant contention for HBM capacity alongside model weights.

title: Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M to bolster its AI infrastructure
author: Lauren Forristal
contentSnippet:
Dropbox is making a big push into AI infrastructure with a $350 million acquisition of cloud technology company Tigris Data, marking what appears to be its largest acquisition to date.

Announced Thursday, the deal is expected to strengthen Dropbox’s AI infrastructure capabilities and support the development of DBX Agent Cloud, a new storage platform aimed at businesses and developers building AI models and agents.

Dropbox told TechCrunch via email that the transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. The company also said it currently has no plans to reduce headcount as part of the acquisition. The company already cut 9% of its global workforce last month, WSJ reported.

DBX Agent Cloud will initially offer object storage as a stand-alone product, allowing businesses to purchase storage independently and use it with existing tools and applications built for Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service), which is a cloud storage service that enables businesses to store and retrieve large volumes of data.

Beyond its infrastructure ambitions, Dropbox is also bringing more AI capabilities to its core product. Users will be able to ask AI to perform supported tasks using their files, choose between different AI models, and connect their Dropbox content to third-party tools, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Muse.

The company also plans to expand DBX Agent Cloud with additional capabilities designed to help AI systems work with different types of content, including documents, images, audio, and video. Other planned additions include filesystem features that will allow AI agents to manage files and maintain continuity across tasks and sessions.

Dropbox says the updated experience has already reached more than 70,000 teams. The initial rollout is available to eligible Standard and Advanced customers in the U.S., U.K., and Australia, with broader availability planned for 2027.

Tigris Data was founded by former Uber engineers who helped develop the ride-hailing company’s storage infrastructure. The company provides cloud storage technology that helps businesses store and access data across different regions. Its platform automatically positions data closer to the users and computing resources that need it, helping reduce access times and improve performance.

Tigris Data raised $25 million in a Series A funding round last year.

title: AI Text Watermarking May Not Be Able to Meet the E.U.’s New Rules
author: Anna Desmarais
contentSnippet: The European Union now requires AI-generated text to be watermarked so that it can be identified as such. But tests on OpenAI’s new textGrain watermark, released in October and developed to comply with the new E.U. law , show that these watermarks often do not survive additional editing of the text or when it’s under 150 words. With no clear legal benchmark for how well watermarks should work, it’s uncertain whether textGrain will meet Europe’s transparency rules, which could cost the company significantly and make it difficult to detect AI-generated text as models grow more sophisticated. AI models calculate the probabilities of different possible next “tokens” (the next word or word fragment it generates) based on the text already written, then select one and repeat that process until the response is complete. After the prompt “today the weather is…,” for example, says Xiang Li , coauthor of the textGrain technical report and a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Pennsylvania, the model might weigh “warm” or “cool” as possible next words. A watermark uses a secret key to generate pseudorandom values—numbers produced by a mathematical process that influence which token the model suggests. This creates a statistical pattern in the text that a detector with the same secret key can look for, Li says. What makes textGrain different from other watermarks is that it uses entropy, a measure of how unpredictable a model’s word choices are, as a resource that can be budgeted when embedding a watermark. Developers specify how much entropy or unpredictability they want to allow, and textGrain adjusts to that target. This gives developers more control over the balance between embedding a detectable signal and preserving variation in the model’s output, Li says. “We can think of entropy as a resource, a kind of money.… In our approach, we can accurately determine how much of that resource we want to consume.” Limits of AI Watermark Detection The watermark is invisible to readers. But a positive result does not show how much a person contributed to a passage, and a negative result does not prove that a text was human-written. OpenAI’s false-positive rate is 1 percent, meaning the detector is designed to wrongly flag about one in 100 unwatermarked passages. title: The hidden supply chain costs of the AI boom
author: Nilay Patel
contentSnippet: Today, I’m talking with Willy Shih, an economist, a professor of management practice at Harvard Business School, and the author of the upcoming book, Where Does My Stuff Come From? The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains . Willy is one of my all-time favorite Decoder guests — his way of looking at the world through our supply chains is just a fascinating way of making sense of the global economy. I first met Willy in 2019, while The Verge was covering Foxconn’s promise to build an LCD fab in Wisconsin. That obviously never happened, but Willy called it right away because he could see the supply chain to support a fab simply wasn’t in place. We also had Willy on the show in 2021 to talk about what was then the pandemic-era chip shortage. Now, five years later, we’re in another manufacturing mess, as we stand in the middle of a political fight over whether globalization is coming to an end. Trumps’ tariffs keep changing, the factories that were supposed to reshore in America mostly haven’t materialized, and AI is devouring the planet’s computing resources during an unprecedented infrastructure buildout. Willy’s new book is all about the economics underlying these complex systems, which our politicians and regulators seem to insistently ignore. You’ll hear us talk about why the markets have reacted to all these disruptions the way they have, and why China remains a global manufacturing powerhouse even though every other country thinks that’s so risky. I loved this conversation — it’s in the weeds, and Willy really knows his stuff. Okay: economist Will Shih on his new book Where Does My Stuff Come From? Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Willy Shih, you’re an economist and professor of management practice at Harvard. You’re also the author of the new book, Where Does My Stuff Come From: The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains . Welcome back to Decoder . Well, thanks for having me back. I am very excited to talk to you. You and I first started talking ages ago when The Verge was covering Foxconn in Wisconsin. You are a reliable source of information on what it takes to actually build an LCD plant anywhere, not just in Wisconsin. The Foxconn in Wisconsin thing was funny because I tend to go on first principles on these things. Once I knew they weren’t going to build a glass plant across the street, it’s

summary.tldr:
Harvard Business School professor and economist Willy Shih discusses the structural realities of global supply chains in the context of his new book, 'Where Does My Stuff Come From? The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains.' The conversation highlights the persistent gap between political rhetoric regarding domestic manufacturing reshoring and the actual economic and logistical requirements necessary to sustain large-scale industrial projects, such as semiconductor fabrication facilities.

Shih critiques the current AI infrastructure boom, noting that the massive surge in computing resource demand is occurring within a volatile global manufacturing environment. He emphasizes that despite political shifts, tariff changes, and widespread concerns over supply chain risk, China remains a dominant manufacturing powerhouse due to the deep-rooted, complex ecosystems that are not easily replicated elsewhere. The discussion serves as a case study on why high-profile industrial projects, such as the previously proposed Foxconn LCD plant in Wisconsin, often fail when they lack the foundational supply chain support required for viability.
takeaways: **Expertise:** Willy Shih is a professor of management practice at Harvard Business School and author of 'Where Does My Stuff Come From? The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains.'
**Industrial Reality:** The failure of the Foxconn Wisconsin LCD project was attributed to the absence of a local glass manufacturing plant and the necessary supporting supply chain infrastructure.
**Manufacturing Context:** Despite geopolitical tensions and tariff fluctuations, China maintains its status as a global manufacturing powerhouse due to established, complex industrial ecosystems.
**AI Infrastructure:** The current AI boom is characterized by an unprecedented demand for computing resources that is straining existing global supply chain systems.

title: Automated Video-to-QA Pipeline: End-to-End Question Generation and Verification Using Large Language Models
author: Jaival Chauhan
contentSnippet: The exponential growth of educational and informational video content on platforms like YouTube presents a challenge for efficient knowledge retrieval and assessment. This paper proposes an end-to-end automated pipeline for extracting structured summaries and generating high-fidelity Question-Answer (QA) pairs from video streams. The framework integrates a cascade of state-of-the-art models: audio extraction is handled via FFmpeg, followed by automatic speech recognition (ASR) using Whisper (A library in Python) to generate accurate transcripts. Due to the token constraints of Large Language Models (LLMs), transcripts are segmented and summarized using Facebook's BART. A key innovation of this work is a Self-Verification and Fine-Tuning Loop. We utilize meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8BInstruct to generate candidate QA pairs from transcript chunks, which are then fed back into the model to rigorously assess their relevance and importance. Only verified, high-quality pairs are retained to construct a synthetic dataset. This dataset is subsequently used to fine-tune the Llama model using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), resulting in a specialized model capable of generating domain-aligned assessment questions. This approach demonstrates a scalable method for creating self-improving educational tools without the need for manual data annotation. The proposed model can be downloaded from Kaggle with all the codes from GitHub.

title: Together AI Releases Together Compiler: Agents Make Inference Up to 2.6x Faster
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Together AI has introduced Together Compiler (TKCC), an agent-driven system that keeps re-optimizing inference as production traffic changes. Together Compiler already runs on several of Together’s serverless endpoints. The core claim for developers: an engine tuned once goes stale, so tuning should never stop. TL;DR System: It is an optimization system, tested on Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash and Llama 1B. Runs on: NVIDIA B200, B300, GB300, H100, AMD MI355X and AWS Trainium2. Each run used at most 2 nodes per model. Performance: Up to 2.6x higher TPS than the best published InferenceX configurations, in under 24 hours per setting. Best: 1,111 P90 TPS per user on MiniMax M3.1 Flash (B200, batch size 1), 1.8x over the 633 TPS baseline. Worst: GLM 5.3 on MI355X moved only from 463 to 480 TPS (about 4%). What is Together Compiler? Together Compiler is a continual compilation loop from Together AI that uses coding agents to rewrite a model’s forward pass. It takes a server launch command, a traffic profile and a hardware configuration. Agents propose faster forward passes, and a persistent engine measures each one. The winning code ships into the serving engine. When traffic drifts, the loop runs again. Why does inference need continual compilation? Together AI team reports that its traffic shape never sits still. Prompt lengths in one country ran about 97K tokens versus 70K elsewhere. One customer’s P90 input length grew from 18K to 33K tokens in 3 days. Kernels tuned on random data can also mislead. Random inputs activated 13 to 38% more MoE experts than real traffic. One agent-written top-k kernel took 20 µs on random data. On real data at 70K context, it took up to 62 ms. How does the persistent engine work? Most agent loops restart vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM for every experiment. The research team measures 761 seconds of cold startup for MiniMax M3.1 Flash on TensorRT-LLM. Together Compiler starts the engine once. Agents submit a candidate forward pass over RPC. The server swaps the forward function pointer and re-captures CUDA graphs. Two measurement tiers balance speed and fidelity. A fast tier serves 12 layers for quick screening. A slow tier serves 60 layers to confirm gains on real distributions. Two tiers tested 8.1x more candidates than one slow tier (1,354 vs 168). They also found a solution 7.2% faster. Together AI tea

summary.tldr:
Together AI has launched Together Compiler (TKCC), an agent-driven optimization system designed to perform continual inference re-optimization based on real-time production traffic patterns. Unlike static compilation methods that rely on random data, TKCC utilizes coding agents to rewrite a model’s forward pass, which is then validated by a persistent engine. The system is currently operational on Together’s serverless endpoints and supports a wide range of hardware, including NVIDIA B200, B300, GB300, H100, AMD MI355X, and AWS Trainium2, with tests limited to a maximum of two nodes per model.

The system addresses the issue of "traffic drift," where prompt lengths and expert activation patterns fluctuate significantly, rendering static kernels inefficient. By avoiding the cold-start overhead of frameworks like vLLM or TensorRT-LLM—which can take up to 761 seconds for models like MiniMax M3.1 Flash—TKCC swaps forward function pointers and re-captures CUDA graphs in real-time. It employs a two-tier measurement strategy: a fast tier for screening 12 layers and a slow tier for validating 60 layers against real traffic distributions. This approach allowed the team to test 1,354 candidates compared to 168 in a single-tier setup, resulting in a 7.2% performance gain.

Performance benchmarks demonstrate significant throughput improvements, with the system achieving up to 2.6x higher tokens-per-second (TPS) than existing InferenceX configurations. Notable results include MiniMax M3.1 Flash on NVIDIA B200 reaching 1,111 P90 TPS, a 1.8x increase over the 633 TPS baseline. While gains vary by model and hardware—such as the GLM 5.3 on AMD MI355X showing a more modest 4% improvement—the system effectively mitigates the performance degradation observed when using random data for kernel tuning, where expert activation can be miscalculated by 13% to 38%.
takeaways: **Performance Gains:** Achieved up to 2.6x higher TPS compared to InferenceX configurations, with a peak of 1,111 P90 TPS on MiniMax M3.1 Flash.
**Hardware Support:** Compatible with NVIDIA B200, B300, GB300, H100, AMD MI355X, and AWS Trainium2.
**Optimization Methodology:** Uses a two-tier measurement system (12-layer screening vs. 60-layer validation) to test 8.1x more candidates than traditional single-tier approaches.
**Traffic Sensitivity:** Addresses real-world performance gaps where random data tuning led to kernel execution times jumping from 20 µs to 62 ms under 70K context loads.
**Operational Efficiency:** Eliminates cold-start overhead by maintaining a persistent engine and swapping forward function pointers via RPC rather than restarting the serving stack.

title: Google AI Research Releases Agile Deliberation Framework for Gray-Area Image Classifiers
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Google Research has released Agile Deliberation , a human-in-the-loop framework for building image classifiers around subjective concepts. Think ‘healthy food’, ‘inspiring artwork’ or clickbait in content moderation. Most tooling assumes users already know the concept boundary. Agile Deliberation assumes they do not, and helps them find it. TL;DR Framework : It prompts Gemini 2.5 Pro and Gemini 2.5 Flash through the API, without fine-tuning. Runs on: A Jupyter or Colab notebook. Retrieval uses CLIP embeddings and a FAISS index on CPU or GPU. The demo index starts at about 260 MB. Performance: 10.5 F1 points above zero-shot Gemini 2.5 Flash on average, across 2 concepts and 18 live sessions. Best: Paid to play F1 of 0.59 vs 0.48 zero-shot, with precision up 22 points (0.35 to 0.57). Worst: Recall drops 17 points on paid to play (0.80 to 0.63) and 15 points on healthy food. What is Agile Deliberation? Agile Deliberation is a Google Research’s framework that turns a vague concept into a structured written definition. That definition does two jobs. It is a human-readable policy, and it is the text prompt for a VLM classifier. Each round keeps the candidate definition with the best F1 on the user’s labels. The design came from interviews with a group of content moderation experts . Experts scoped a concept first, then refined it on borderline images. Finding those images was the slow part. How does concept scoping work? Stage 1 breaks the concept into at most 3 unit concepts, using prompt chaining with Gemini 2.5 Pro. Each unit gets candidate positive and negative subconcepts, shown with retrieved images. For healthy food, positives might be salads or grain bowls. Negatives might be processed food or raw, unprepared ingredients. The user keeps, flips or drops each one. How does concept iteration find borderline images? Stage 2 skips classic uncertainty sampling. The classifier is a prompted generative VLM, so its confidence scores are often uncalibrated. Instead, the system hunts for images that are borderline in meaning. The pipeline runs 4 steps: Gemini 2.5 Flash writes borderline queries, such as ‘salads with heavy mayo dressings’. Each query retrieves 50 to 100 images. Images are de-duplicated, encoded, and grouped into clusters with dictionary learning. A UCB multi-armed bandit picks the next cluster. It favors clusters where users corrected the model or lef

summary.tldr:
Google Research has introduced Agile Deliberation, a human-in-the-loop framework designed to refine image classifiers for subjective, ambiguous concepts such as 'healthy food' or 'clickbait.' Unlike traditional approaches that assume fixed concept boundaries, this framework utilizes Gemini 2.5 Pro and Gemini 2.5 Flash via API to iteratively build structured, human-readable definitions that serve as both policy documents and VLM prompts. The system operates within Jupyter or Colab environments, leveraging CLIP embeddings and FAISS indexing (with a base index size of approximately 260 MB) to manage image retrieval and classification without requiring model fine-tuning.

The framework functions in two primary stages: concept scoping and iterative refinement. In the scoping phase, Gemini 2.5 Pro uses prompt chaining to decompose a target concept into up to three unit concepts, which users then validate. The refinement phase replaces standard uncertainty sampling—which is often uncalibrated in generative VLMs—with a semantic-focused search. Gemini 2.5 Flash generates queries for borderline cases, which are then retrieved, de-duplicated, and clustered using dictionary learning. A UCB (Upper Confidence Bound) multi-armed bandit algorithm selects clusters for user review, prioritizing areas where the model previously required corrections.

Performance benchmarks across 18 live sessions and two concepts show an average F1 score improvement of 10.5 points over zero-shot Gemini 2.5 Flash. In the 'paid to play' category, the framework achieved an F1 of 0.59 compared to 0.48 zero-shot, with precision increasing by 22 points. However, the framework exhibits trade-offs in recall, which dropped by 17 points in 'paid to play' and 15 points in 'healthy food' scenarios.
takeaways: **Performance Metrics:** Agile Deliberation improved average F1 scores by 10.5 points over zero-shot Gemini 2.5 Flash, with a 22-point precision gain in 'paid to play' classification.
**Technical Stack:** The framework runs in Jupyter/Colab, utilizing Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash APIs, CLIP embeddings, and a FAISS index (starting at ~260 MB) for retrieval.
**Refinement Methodology:** The system replaces uncalibrated uncertainty sampling with a UCB multi-armed bandit that targets semantically borderline image clusters.
**Recall Trade-offs:** The framework experienced recall declines of 17 points for 'paid to play' and 15 points for 'healthy food' compared to zero-shot baselines.
**Concept Scoping:** The process uses prompt chaining to break complex concepts into a maximum of three unit concepts, each with user-validated positive and negative sub-labels.

title: Who May Overrule the Agent? Evidence-Gated Authority in LLM Review Institutions
author: Fuad Ali
contentSnippet:
Authors: Fuad Ali

Abstract: Multi-agent language-model systems often add a reviewer to improve an upstream agent's decision. Yet a reviewer can both repair errors and replace decisions that were already correct. We study this as a problem of institutional jurisdiction: conditional on the same proposal, task information, model, and review output, when is the reviewer authorized to make its recommendation binding? We compare broad override authority with an evidence gate that permits replacement only after the reviewer produces a mechanically valid record of a binding-constraint violation and a compliant repair. Across two locally run open-weight models, 96 spatial-policy tasks, and a 96-task portfolio-transfer benchmark, the gate sharply reduces corruption of correct proposals while retaining most repairs of violations. The directions of this tradeoff are partly implied by the rule; its magnitude depends on reviewer transitions and upstream proposal states. A prospective validation then gives the reviewer an explicit choice to retain, replace, or escalate. This eliminates correct-proposal corruption for Qwen, but Mistral still replaces all 48 correct proposals; Qwen also declines every welfare-only repair that Mistral frequently attempts. Thus interface design changes reviewer behavior but is not a model-independent safeguard. The result is not that restricted review is universally better. It is that reviewer competence, action interface, and binding jurisdiction jointly determine both the correction domain and the corruption surface.

Notes: 11 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code, frozen outputs, and reproduction instructions: this https URL

summary.tldr:
In 'Who May Overrule the Agent? Evidence-Gated Authority in LLM Review Institutions,' author Fuad Ali investigates the institutional jurisdiction of multi-agent systems, specifically focusing on when a reviewer agent should be permitted to override an upstream agent's decision. The study evaluates a mechanism called an 'evidence gate,' which restricts the reviewer from replacing an upstream proposal unless it generates a mechanically valid record of a binding-constraint violation alongside a compliant repair. This approach is contrasted against broad override authority, where reviewers frequently replace correct decisions with inferior ones.

Testing across 96 spatial-policy tasks and a 96-task portfolio-transfer benchmark using open-weight models Qwen and Mistral, the research demonstrates that the evidence gate significantly reduces the corruption of correct proposals while maintaining the ability to repair actual violations. However, the efficacy of these interface constraints is model-dependent. When provided with a prospective validation interface—allowing the reviewer to explicitly choose to retain, replace, or escalate—Qwen successfully eliminated the corruption of correct proposals and declined welfare-only repairs, whereas Mistral continued to replace all 48 correct proposals. The findings conclude that reviewer competence, the action interface, and binding jurisdiction are interdependent factors that determine the balance between correction and corruption.
takeaways: **Methodology:** Evaluated multi-agent review systems across 96 spatial-policy tasks and a 96-task portfolio-transfer benchmark.
**Evidence Gate Mechanism:** Restricts reviewer overrides to instances where the reviewer provides a mechanically valid record of a binding-constraint violation and a compliant repair.
**Model Performance Variance:** Qwen eliminated correct-proposal corruption under prospective validation, while Mistral continued to replace all 48 correct proposals.
**Core Finding:** Interface design and binding jurisdiction are not model-independent safeguards, as reviewer behavior varies significantly based on the underlying model architecture.

title: Agent Harness Awareness: Turning Verified Telemetry into Operational Control for Tool-Using Agents
author: Manu Agrawal, Shrey Nagpal
contentSnippet:
Authors: Manu Agrawal , Shrey Nagpal

Abstract: Tool descriptions tell an agent what an action can do, but they do not necessarily reveal whether that action is healthy or suitable at the moment of use. Execution harnesses often possess this information through monitors, traces, and recent failures while the model choosing the next action does not. We call this gap operational blindness. We introduce Agent Harness Awareness, a trust-separated design in which the host supplies a small, fresh, verified state snapshot before a consequential action while retaining measurement, enforcement, evaluation, and final dispatch authority. We test its tools-and-network instance with ToolRoute, a controlled isolation benchmark that holds the task and candidate semantics constant and varies the operational information available to the model. In a 216-decision ablation across GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.7 Flash, verified tool-health state reduced mean observable policy regret by 96.9% against a same-shape neutral control (4,252 ms to 131 ms) and raised single-dispatch completion from 69.4% to 95.8%. In a separate 27-decision end-to-end replication with live local TCP/HTTP execution, OpenTelemetry client spans, and Toxiproxy-injected faults, verified state reduced mean regret from 8,956 ms to 0 ms (zero excess observable operational cost) and completed the live action in 9/9 model-by-fault cases versus 5/9 for the neutral control. These studies establish the tools-and-network instance of Agent Harness Awareness: selected host telemetry materially improves pre-dispatch operational choice. Runtime state, hardware pressure, economics, retry-aware recovery, and heterogeneous selection remain open empirical extensions of the same architecture.

Notes: 9 pages, 3 figures

summary.tldr:
Researchers Manu Agrawal and Shrey Nagpal have introduced 'Agent Harness Awareness,' a design pattern addressing 'operational blindness' in tool-using AI agents. The framework bridges the gap between static tool descriptions and real-time execution health by having the host system provide a verified, fresh state snapshot to the model immediately before a consequential action. This trust-separated architecture keeps measurement, enforcement, and final dispatch authority with the host, while the model uses the telemetry to inform its decision-making process.

In a 216-decision ablation study using GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.7 Flash, the inclusion of verified tool-health state reduced mean observable policy regret by 96.9%, dropping from 4,252 ms to 131 ms, and improved single-dispatch completion rates from 69.4% to 95.8%. A secondary end-to-end replication involving live TCP/HTTP execution, OpenTelemetry spans, and Toxiproxy-injected faults demonstrated even more significant gains, reducing mean regret from 8,956 ms to 0 ms and achieving a 100% completion rate (9/9) compared to 55.5% (5/9) for the neutral control group.
takeaways: **Performance Impact:** Verified tool-health state reduced mean observable policy regret by 96.9% across three major LLM architectures.
**Completion Metrics:** Single-dispatch completion rates increased from 69.4% to 95.8% when agents were provided with real-time host telemetry.

**Live Fault Testing:** In a 27-decision replication using Toxiproxy-injected faults, the framework achieved zero excess observable operational cost (0 ms regret) compared to 8,956 ms in the control group.
**Architectural Design:** The system utilizes a trust-separated model where the host retains final dispatch authority while supplying fresh state snapshots to the agent.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Resource Orchestration for Agentic AI Systems
author: Masoud Shokrnezhad, Tarik Taleb
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.05392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems powered by large language models (LLMs) execute as autonomous multi-step pipelines that dynamically invoke tools, integrate observations into memory, and iterate until a task is resolved or a resource budget is exhausted. Unlike classical workflows with fixed graphs, the aggregate compute, bandwidth, and end-to-end latency demands of such pipelines are unknown at dispatch time: they emerge at runtime from intermediate observations and stochastic token sampling, yielding heavy-tailed, multi-modal random variables. This unpredictability forces infrastructure orchestrators into a dilemma: under-provisioning risks mid-execution throttling and deadline violations, while over-provisioning wastes scarce edge or cloud capacity. Existing schedulers require a fully known pipeline graph, while edge resource-management methods rely on parametric or stationary demand models, and neither fits the unknown, non-stationary profiles of agentic pipelines. We formalize this setting as the uncertainty-aware agentic orchestration problem, where the goal is to reserve, at dispatch time, compute and bandwidth allocations that cover actual pipeline demands, and to verify that the pipeline can meet its deadline, each with a prescribed probability. We then propose Conformal Reservation for Orchestration (CRO), an online algorithm that translates a sliding window of past execution traces into dispatch-time resource allocations with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees via conformal prediction. Simulations over heterogeneous task mixes with multi-modal and heavy-tailed profiles show that CRO is the only evaluated method that simultaneously satisfies target probabilistic coverage across all risk levels while, among coverage-feasible methods, attaining the lowest over-reservation, roughly halving the resource waste of the Chebyshev-bound baseline.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced Conformal Reservation for Orchestration (CRO), an online algorithm designed to manage compute and bandwidth resources for agentic AI pipelines. Unlike traditional static workflows, agentic systems exhibit non-stationary, heavy-tailed, and multi-modal resource demands that emerge dynamically at runtime. CRO addresses the orchestration dilemma—balancing the risk of mid-execution throttling against the inefficiency of over-provisioning—by utilizing conformal prediction to provide finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees for resource reservations at dispatch time.

The algorithm operates by analyzing a sliding window of historical execution traces to calculate resource allocations that satisfy specific probabilistic deadlines. In simulations involving heterogeneous task mixes, CRO outperformed existing baselines, including those relying on Chebyshev bounds. It is the only tested method capable of maintaining target probabilistic coverage across all risk levels while simultaneously minimizing resource waste, effectively halving the over-reservation overhead compared to traditional statistical approaches.
takeaways: **Problem Definition:** Agentic AI pipelines create unpredictable, multi-modal, and heavy-tailed resource demands that render classical fixed-graph scheduling and stationary demand models ineffective.
**Core Methodology:** CRO uses conformal prediction to translate past execution traces into dispatch-time resource allocations with formal, distribution-free coverage guarantees.

**Performance Benchmark:** CRO achieved the lowest over-reservation rates among all coverage-feasible methods in simulation, reducing resource waste by approximately 50% compared to Chebyshev-bound baselines.
**Research Identifier:** The methodology is detailed in arXiv:2611.05392v1, focusing on the uncertainty-aware agentic orchestration problem.

title: Challenge-Aware Knowledge Recruitment with Meta-Agent Supervision for Medical Multi-Agent Reasoning
author: Riccardo Riccio, Haitz S\'aez de Oc\'ariz Borde, Pietro Li\`o
contentSnippet:
Authors: Riccardo Riccio , Haitz Sáez de Ocáriz Borde , Pietro Liò

Abstract: Large language models perform strongly on standard medical QA but degrade on harder reasoning tasks, where multi-agent debate often fails to beat strong single-model prompting. We argue that a key limitation is that existing systems select experts and retrieve knowledge from the question alone, rather than from gaps that emerge during reasoning. We propose challenge-aware adaptive recruitment: an external CHALLENGER inspects the evolving reasoning trace and identifies specific factual or expertise gaps. These signals trigger targeted knowledge retrieval or mid-discussion specialist recruitment. On the MEDAGENTSBENCH hard subset (862 questions across nine biomedical datasets), upfront retrieval provides little benefit, while challenge-aware in-between retrieval performs better; on a multi-specialist backbone it improves accuracy on 8 of 9 datasets and adds 6 percentage points over Challenger Only. Ablations indicate benefits from both retrieval timing and gap-specific query signals, and a live web-search experiment shows that the timing advantage persists across retrieval backends. For specialist recruitment, self-triggered adaptation is unreliable, whereas Challenger-triggered recruitment raises GPT-4.1-mini MedQA accuracy from 46% to 54%, with positive direction on all tested generalization datasets. Naively combining retrieval and specialist recruitment degrades performance, highlighting the need to coordinate adaptive intervention channels. These results show that when and why external resources are recruited is a key design choice in multi-agent medical reasoning.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Riccardo Riccio, Haitz Sáez de Ocáriz Borde, and Pietro Liò have introduced 'Challenge-Aware Knowledge Recruitment,' a framework designed to improve medical multi-agent reasoning by shifting from upfront knowledge retrieval to dynamic, gap-based intervention. The system utilizes an external 'CHALLENGER' agent that monitors the evolving reasoning trace of a multi-agent system, identifying specific factual or expertise deficits in real-time. This mechanism triggers targeted knowledge retrieval or the recruitment of specialized agents only when necessary, addressing the performance degradation often seen in standard multi-agent debate models when faced with complex medical reasoning tasks.

Testing on the MEDAGENTSBENCH hard subset—comprising 862 questions across nine biomedical datasets—demonstrated that challenge-aware in-between retrieval consistently outperforms upfront retrieval. The approach improved accuracy on 8 of 9 datasets, providing a 6 percentage point gain over a 'Challenger Only' baseline. Furthermore, the study found that while self-triggered specialist recruitment is unreliable, Challenger-triggered recruitment increased GPT-4.1-mini MedQA accuracy from 46% to 54%. The authors note that naively combining retrieval and specialist recruitment can degrade performance, underscoring the necessity of precise coordination between intervention channels.
takeaways: **Benchmark Performance:** The framework improved accuracy on 8 out of 9 biomedical datasets within the MEDAGENTSBENCH hard subset.
**GPT-4.1-mini Gains:** Challenger-triggered specialist recruitment boosted MedQA accuracy for the GPT-4.1-mini model from 46% to 54%.
**Methodological Shift:** The research identifies that 'when' and 'why' external resources are recruited is more critical than static, upfront retrieval strategies.
**Intervention Coordination:** Naive integration of retrieval and specialist recruitment leads to performance degradation, necessitating structured coordination of intervention channels.

title: A Feasibility Condition for Confidence-Gated Tiered LLM Inference
author: Sumit P. Ahuja
contentSnippet:
Authors: Sumit P. Ahuja

Abstract: Tiered inference distributes large language model computation across a hierarchy of devices, from on-device and edge hardware to the datacenter, and is increasingly offered as the route to cheaper, lower-latency, and more private serving. Most such systems orchestrate frozen model checkpoints, and most decide what to resolve locally and what to escalate using a confidence signal produced by a forward-deployed model. We give a closed-form condition for when no threshold on that signal makes a tiered cascade worthwhile relative to sending every query to the backstop. Modeling the routing decision as a binary test and separating local from escalation cost through an architecture cost ratio $\kappa$, we derive a feasibility condition bracketed by a signal-free floor, below which a cascade is feasible at any signal quality, and a perfect-signal ceiling, above which none is. Read along the $\kappa$ axis the condition inverts: where local compute is billed, cost binds, matching a recent empirical finding; where it is sunk, on decentralized hardware, feasibility becomes unconditional and signal quality instead sets what the cascade achieves. We turn the condition into three design requirements that existing trained-in primitives satisfy only in isolation, and we propose, as future work, a co-designed architecture and a protocol to test it. The condition and the inversion hold independently of that architecture; they are the paper's contribution.

Notes: 21 pages, 2 figures

summary.tldr:
In the paper 'A Feasibility Condition for Confidence-Gated Tiered LLM Inference,' author Sumit P. Ahuja provides a mathematical framework for evaluating the viability of tiered LLM inference systems, which distribute computation between edge devices and datacenters. The study models the routing decision as a binary test, utilizing an architecture cost ratio (κ) to distinguish between local and escalation costs. The research establishes a closed-form condition that defines the boundaries of when a tiered cascade is economically or operationally superior to routing all queries directly to a backstop model.

The paper identifies two critical thresholds: a 'signal-free floor,' where cascades are feasible regardless of signal quality, and a 'perfect-signal ceiling,' beyond which tiered systems fail to provide value. A key finding is the inversion of this condition along the κ axis: when local compute costs are billed, cost constraints dominate, aligning with recent empirical observations; conversely, when local compute is treated as a sunk cost—common in decentralized hardware—the feasibility of a cascade becomes unconditional, with signal quality determining the system's performance ceiling. The author concludes that existing tiered inference primitives fail to satisfy the derived design requirements simultaneously, proposing that future systems require co-designed architectures and standardized testing protocols.
takeaways: **Mathematical Framework:** The paper derives a closed-form feasibility condition for confidence-gated tiered inference, independent of specific model architecture.
**Cost Ratio (κ):** The model uses an architecture cost ratio to differentiate between local compute costs and datacenter escalation costs.
**Threshold Dynamics:** Feasibility is defined by a signal-free floor and a perfect-signal ceiling, with the condition inverting based on whether local compute is billed or treated as a sunk cost.
**Design Gap:** The author identifies that current tiered inference systems satisfy necessary design requirements only in isolation, necessitating a shift toward co-designed architectures.

title: Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments
author: Shijue Huang, Hangyu Guo, Hengheng Zhang, Guo An, Zhitao He, Qi Tian, Yiren Feng
contentSnippet:
Authors: Shijue Huang , Hangyu Guo , Hengheng Zhang , Guo An , Zhitao He , Qi Tian , Yiren Feng

Abstract: As agents become more capable, they are moving beyond one-off tasks toward sustained assistance across successive user goals. Such assistance requires agents to discover how unfamiliar environments work, reuse what they learn across tasks, and keep that experience current as environments evolve. Existing benchmarks increasingly study experience reuse and adaptation, but provide limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain, or lose. To address this gap, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark for the experience lifecycle across 18 interactive environments. It distinguishes structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. To study how experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. It builds task streams around shared experience and introduces silent environmental changes. We evaluate task performance and track changes in saved experience throughout each stream. Across 20 models, we find that retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always complete tasks successfully. These findings identify selective maintenance and effective use as complementary challenges for long-lived agents.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Shijue Huang, Hangyu Guo, et al. have introduced ReScopeBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate the experience lifecycle of long-lived AI agents across 18 interactive environments. The framework specifically categorizes agent knowledge into 'structural experience'—pertaining to environment organization and access—and 'rule experience,' which covers reusable principles and constraints. By utilizing an 'experience-first construction' approach, the benchmark generates task streams that incorporate silent environmental changes, allowing researchers to track how agents acquire, reuse, and revise their internal knowledge bases over time.

Evaluation of 20 distinct models reveals a significant gap in agent performance: while retained experience generally correlates with improved task success, agents frequently fail to update their knowledge when environments evolve. The study highlights that even when agents correctly record necessary information, they often struggle to apply it effectively to complete tasks. These results suggest that the primary bottlenecks for long-lived agents are not just the acquisition of data, but the selective maintenance of experience and the ability to translate that experience into successful task execution.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** ReScopeBench evaluates agent performance across 18 distinct interactive environments.
**Experience Taxonomy:** The framework distinguishes between structural experience (environment organization) and rule experience (reusable principles).
**Methodology:** The benchmark utilizes an experience-first construction approach that introduces silent environmental changes to test agent adaptability.
**Performance Findings:** Testing across 20 models shows that agents often fail to keep experience current, even when the information is correctly stored.

title: Can Large Language Models Review the Scientific Literature? A Test Against a 102-Article Benchmark
author: Abdullah Al Kalbani, David M. Schultz, Alexandra K. Anderson-Frey, Zhonghua Zheng, Catherine McGuire
contentSnippet:
Authors: Abdullah Al Kalbani , David M. Schultz , Alexandra K. Anderson-Frey , Zhonghua Zheng , Catherine McGuire

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support scientific literature reviews, yet evaluations often examine individual tasks rather than the review process as a whole. We assess six AI tools across four stages: finding relevant articles, interpreting them, synthesizing across them, and proposing future research. The benchmark is a published review of the Spanish plume weather pattern and its 102-article corpus. In the initial searches, five tools collectively identified 57 articles, with the best individual tool finding 42. Institutional library access increased discovery from 42 to 82 articles for Codex and from 15 to 79 for Claude Code. Given the complete corpus of 102 PDFs, three tools correctly identified all 18 articles discussing the Spanish plume substantially, but incorrectly classified 40% to 79% of the 84 passing mentions as substantial. The same three tools produced syntheses evaluated blindly by two domain experts. Although largely accurate, the syntheses provided limited insight and sometimes contained unsupported claims, quotation errors, and exaggerated statements of consensus. Finally, all three tools proposed research directions broader than the Spanish plume literature, although two approached questions identified in the benchmark review. No single tool performed best across all tasks. We provide eight recommendations for researchers using AI tools in literature reviews. Our findings suggest that LLMs can assist with discovering and interpreting scientific literature, particularly when institutional access is available, but cannot replace expert judgment in evaluating evidence or synthesizing research.

Notes: 34 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Data, prompts, analysis scripts and results: this https URL (GitHub: this https URL )

summary.tldr:
Researchers Abdullah Al Kalbani, David M. Schultz, Alexandra K. Anderson-Frey, Zhonghua Zheng, and Catherine McGuire evaluated six LLM-based tools across four stages of scientific literature review: discovery, interpretation, synthesis, and research proposal generation. Using a benchmark corpus of 102 articles related to the 'Spanish plume' weather pattern, the study assessed the tools' ability to replicate a published review. The findings indicate that while LLMs can assist in discovery—especially when integrated with institutional library access—they struggle with the nuanced classification of evidence and the synthesis of complex scientific consensus.

In the discovery phase, the top-performing tool identified 42 of 102 articles, a figure that rose to 82 when provided with institutional library access. When tasked with classifying the relevance of articles, three tested tools correctly identified all 18 articles containing substantial discussions of the Spanish plume but misclassified 40% to 79% of the 84 articles that only contained passing mentions. Blind evaluations by domain experts revealed that while the generated syntheses were largely accurate, they frequently suffered from unsupported claims, quotation errors, and exaggerated consensus. Furthermore, the tools struggled to propose research directions specific to the provided corpus, often defaulting to overly broad topics.

**Classification Accuracy:** While tools achieved 100% recall for substantial articles, they exhibited high false-positive rates, misclassifying 40% to 79% of passing mentions as substantial.
**Synthesis Quality:** Expert blind reviews identified recurring issues in AI-generated syntheses, including unsupported claims, citation errors, and artificial consensus inflation.
**Research Proposal Limitations:** AI tools failed to generate highly specific research directions, instead producing broad queries that often drifted outside the scope of the provided literature.
**Tool Consistency:** No single model outperformed others across all four stages of the literature review process, necessitating a multi-tool approach for researchers.

title: SlackBench: Benchmarking Agents on Collaborative Projects Grounded in Real Code Repositories
author: Mingxuan Li, Huanzhi Mao, Ruitao Zheng, Jarod Stanbury James, Yunze Li, Natanya Anderson, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Alex Dimakis
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.05512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI Agents are becoming digital coworkers that can browse the web, write code, run experiments, and assist humans over extended horizons. Yet existing benchmarks fall short of real knowledge work: many rely on synthetic data or isolated tasks, missing the complex, multi-party dynamics of collaborative projects, where critical information is scattered across conversations, code, and evolving decisions. Even simple workplace questions may require locating relevant channels and direct messages, recovering context from long discussions, inspecting repository state, reconciling stale or conflicting evidence, and synthesizing across sources. We introduce SlackBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on realistic research and engineering workflows that require joint reasoning over workplace communication and evolving repository state. Grounded in privacy-preserving reenactments of real academic research projects, SlackBench provides reproducible environments with realistic multi-party dialogue, evolving decisions, and corresponding code changes grounded in GitHub repositories and Google Docs. It contains 140 queries spanning heterogeneous-source agentic search, abstention on unanswerable or false-premise questions, goal-directed summarization, and circumstance inference over long conversations. These tasks are not reducible to static corpus question answering: agents must determine which conversations matter, traverse threads, inspect repository state, and synthesize evidence across communication and code artifacts. Across 33 frontier models and agent harnesses, the best system scores around 80% and most agents score below 66%, highlighting substantial headroom for improvement. SlackBench thus provides an extensible framework for evaluating agents in collaborative work environments. The SlackBench dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuanzhiMao/SlackBench .

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced SlackBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on complex, collaborative engineering and research workflows that require reasoning across multi-party communications and evolving code repositories. Unlike existing benchmarks that rely on synthetic or isolated tasks, SlackBench utilizes privacy-preserving reenactments of real-world projects, integrating data from GitHub repositories, Google Docs, and multi-party dialogue. The dataset comprises 140 queries that test an agent's ability to perform heterogeneous-source search, goal-directed summarization, circumstance inference, and abstention from answering false-premise or unanswerable questions.

Technically, SlackBench forces agents to move beyond static corpus question answering by requiring them to traverse communication threads, reconcile conflicting evidence, and inspect the state of code repositories over time. The benchmark evaluates performance across 33 frontier models and agent harnesses. Current results indicate significant room for improvement, with the top-performing system achieving approximately 80% accuracy, while the majority of evaluated agents score below 66%. The dataset is currently available on Hugging Face for further research and development.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** Contains 140 queries focused on collaborative research and engineering workflows involving multi-party dialogue and repository state.
**Data Sources:** Integrates real-world artifacts including GitHub repositories, Google Docs, and long-form workplace communication threads.
**Performance Metrics:** Evaluates 33 frontier models and agent harnesses, with a top score of 80% and a median performance below 66%.
**Core Capabilities:** Tests agentic search, context recovery, evidence synthesis, and the ability to abstain from answering false-premise questions.
**Availability:** The dataset is hosted on Hugging Face under the repository HuanzhiMao/SlackBench.

title: MA-SafeDiffuser: Safe Multi-Agent Planning with Diffusion Probabilistic Models
author: Kiran Ravish, Ankita Kushwaha,  Preeti, Pawan Kumar
contentSnippet:
Authors: Kiran Ravish , Ankita Kushwaha , Preeti , Pawan Kumar

Abstract: We propose MA-SafeDiffuser, a multi-agent extension of SafeDiffuser that equips diffusion-based trajectory planners with finite-time diffusion invariance guarantees for joint-agent safety specifications. Building on the single-agent construction that embeds control barrier function (CBF) constraints into reverse-diffusion updates, we: (i) formalize joint safe sets as intersections of per-agent and pairwise barrier sets; (ii) derive centralized and decentralized (communication-aware) constrained denoising procedures with provable invariance under mild assumptions; (iii) address local-trap and deadlock phenomena via time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs; and (iv) develop a lightweight benchmarking suite including a multi-agent Maze2D domain. Empirically, MA-SafeDiffuser reduces violation counts relative to unconstrained diffusion baselines, while retaining planning quality. We provide algorithms, proofs, and reference implementations.

Notes: Accepted at AAMAS 2026. 14 pages, including supplementary material

summary.tldr:
MA-SafeDiffuser, presented by Kiran Ravish, Ankita Kushwaha, Preeti, and Pawan Kumar, is a multi-agent trajectory planning framework that extends the single-agent SafeDiffuser architecture. Accepted at AAMAS 2026, the model integrates Control Barrier Function (CBF) constraints directly into the reverse-diffusion denoising process to ensure finite-time diffusion invariance for joint-agent safety specifications. The framework is designed to handle complex multi-agent environments by formalizing joint safe sets as the intersection of individual agent constraints and pairwise safety requirements.

The methodology introduces both centralized and decentralized denoising procedures, the latter of which is communication-aware, to maintain safety guarantees under varying connectivity conditions. To mitigate common multi-agent planning failures such as local traps and deadlocks, the authors incorporate time-varying specifications and liveness-focused CBFs. The researchers validated the approach using a custom benchmarking suite, including a multi-agent Maze2D domain, demonstrating that the model significantly reduces safety violation counts compared to unconstrained diffusion baselines while maintaining trajectory planning performance.
takeaways: **Core Methodology:** Integrates Control Barrier Function (CBF) constraints into reverse-diffusion updates to enforce joint-agent safety.
**Architectural Variants:** Supports both centralized and decentralized (communication-aware) constrained denoising procedures.
**Failure Mitigation:** Addresses local-trap and deadlock scenarios through the use of time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs.
**Validation:** Benchmarked against unconstrained diffusion baselines using a multi-agent Maze2D domain, showing improved safety violation metrics.
**Publication Status:** Accepted at AAMAS 2026, with a total length of 14 pages including supplementary materials.

title: Towards Efficient Whole Page Ranking with One-Pass Inference
author: Qi Xu, Zhigang Hua, Zijie Lei, Yan Xie, Jizhe Zhang, Lynn Lu, Delun Du, Sha Hua, Ren Mao, Ke Pan, Haomin Yu, Sandeep Pandey, Luke Simon
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.05542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whole-page ranking jointly optimizes advertisements and organic content to balance business outcomes and user engagement under complex layout and business constraints. Existing non-autoregressive (NAR) approaches enable efficient page generation but typically score candidate items independently of previously selected items, limiting their ability to capture order-dependent interactions. Autoregressive (AR) methods address this limitation through sequential conditioning, but incur substantial inference overhead that challenges large-scale deployment. Bridging this quality-efficiency gap remains a challenge in industrial whole-page ranking. We propose Multi-Item Scoring (MIS), a prefix-aware NAR-style framework that incorporates sequential context into efficient multi-item scoring. MIS integrates global candidate interactions, localized prefix conditioning, and position-aware scoring within a shared representation architecture. By computing reusable representations once per request and performing lightweight prefix-conditioned scoring during constrained beam search, MIS captures important sequential dependencies without repeated full-model inference. Experiments on KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS demonstrate that MIS approaches the generation quality of an autoregressive CGA baseline while achieving 4.07x and 3.54x faster CPU decoding, respectively. In a randomized evaluation on a large-scale social-video platform, MIS improves the realization metric by 0.104% and watch time by 0.058%, while reducing ranking-service CPU consumption by 9.73%. These results demonstrate that prefix-aware multi-item scoring can narrow the quality gap between NAR and AR generation while retaining the efficiency required for industrial scalability.

title: Iterated creation, grading, and revision of data science projects by language models
author: Rohan Alexander
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.05548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We evaluate the extent to which agentic AI models can complete an end-to-end data science project, and how this improves with feedback. A 'writer' model with specific tools creates a complete data science project including downloading, cleaning, and analyzing a dataset, and writing a short paper about it. The project is executed and a 'grader' model evaluates it. The writer can then revise its submission, and this repeats for a total of three rounds. We consider seven models from five developers: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, and Z.AI. Each model is both a writer and a grader, so there are 49 writer-grader pairs and we run each pair three times. Of the 147 initial submissions, 107 run and render, and the average score increases from 59 per cent to 76 per cent after the final round of feedback. By writer the extent of the increase ranges from 3 percentage points for Anthropic's Opus 5.5 to 46 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5, and by grader it ranges from 13 percentage points for Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash to 32 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5. When a model grades its own writing the score tends to be about 9 percentage points higher than the average of what the other models give it. About half of the difference that we see from round to round is within the grader's own noise. Feedback generally results in the highest marks, but even just having the chance to revise, or having the additional budget, in terms of time or tool calls, without any feedback, results in considerable increases for some of the models but not for others. We find that how much such a loop helps depends on which model plays which role, but weaker models generally do not improve stronger models.

title: Whose Transparency is it Anyway? Understanding Generative AI Transparency Needs and Gaps Across Stakeholders
author: Genevieve Smith, Sahiba Chopra, Natalia Luka, Min Kyung Lee
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.05549v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transparency has become a central principle in AI governance, yet there is little agreement about what transparency means, for whom, and in what contexts. Drawing on interpretive flexibility within the Social Construction of Technology, this paper examines how different stakeholders understand and experience transparency in generative AI. This study draws from a global survey of 400 end-users, AI builders, and policymakers, complemented by a structured focus group with end-users, grounding the quantitative findings in qualitative insights from the group most underserved by current transparency practice. We present three key findings. First, all three groups share similar understandings of what transparency means and what it should afford, centered on ensuring accuracy and privacy. Second, gaps between the importance of transparency features and their perceived availability are substantially larger for end-users than builders, revealing how power shapes what gets built and who it serves. Only 28% of end-users report that current transparency practices reflect their needs very well, compared to 53% of builders and 49% of policymakers. Third, transparency is situationally constructed, priorities shift with context and task structure, with role-specific frames activating when context demands them and receding when it does not. We argue that meaningful AI transparency requires moving beyond a one-size-fits-all solution, including current emphases on AI disclosure and static documentation, toward pluralistic transparency infrastructures that reflect the needs of diverse users and stakeholders.

title: VirtualTrialHarness: Coordinating Agentic Operationalization of Virtual Trial Protocols Across Complex Clinical Schemas
author: Pengze Li, Jingna Feng, Yue Yu, Yining Wu, Xinyue Hu, Jie Lin, Avanti Bhandarkar, Cui Tao
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.05551v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Virtual trials use routinely collected clinical data to evaluate treatment strategies, but translating a study protocol into an executable analysis requires determining how clinical concepts and study requirements should be represented in the available data and applied consistently across the workflow. These decisions depend on local data representations and operational conventions and can involve source selection, patient and encounter identity, linkage, and temporal interpretation. Here we introduce VirtualTrialHarness (VTHarness), an agent framework that coordinates virtual-trial operationalization by selecting reusable procedural skills for each workflow stage and uses explicit contracts to maintain consistent study decisions across stages. We also introduce VTBenchmark for evaluating source selection and cohort construction. Across three complex synthetic environments, VTHarness successfully produced all required cohort outputs matching the references in 95.1% of workflows after requirement clarification, compared with 60.4% using retrieval from the same procedural corpus. Procedural skills improved source recovery across three language models and increased source overlap with analyst code in 13 Mayo Clinic cases. Site-specific adaptation enabled reference-matched cohort execution across eight MIMIC-IV tasks. Within the Mayo Clinic Virtual Trials Program, the framework supported investigator review of cohort construction and endpoint analysis. These findings support coordinating procedural guidance with workflow decisions to improve virtual-trial implementation across complex clinical schemas.
