title: Almost no one uses AI agents to book their Uber, company says
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
Very few people are using personal AI agents to order Ubers, apparently. On the transportation giant’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, the company said that only four rides were ordered through an AI agent during its busiest week in October: the week of Halloween.

While more people used an AI agent to order food through its delivery service, Uber Eats, the volume was still fairly small compared to the overall number of trips.

Uber’s chief financial officer, Balaji Krishnamurthy, told Wall Street analysts on the call that the company handled around 320 million trips and orders across Uber and Uber Eats during the week of Halloween, but only 500 Uber Eats orders were placed by an AI agent.

“It is very, very early and very limited traction that we are seeing so far,” said CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, referring to the low number of orders placed by AI agents. “Listen, we hope that there will be more traction.”

The surprisingly low numbers of AI-initiated transactions come amid growing hype for a new wave of AI agents that don’t just answer questions but also handle tasks on users’ behalf. There’s been an explosion of personal AI startups, including one of the buzziest, Instinct, which was founded last year and raised its most recent round of funding at a $10 billion valuation. Meta’s Muse also became the No. 1 app in Apple’s U.S. App Store last month, topping 10 million users, per Meta’s own reporting . The company said many were using it to shop and transact with businesses.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and SpaceXAI (Grok) are also now offering their own AI agents, as are numerous smaller startups.

Still, early numbers from public companies indicate the agentic web still has a long way to go. DoorDash, for instance, said last week on its earnings call that it has only received a few hundred orders from AI agents so far, as most customers are still placing orders through the DoorDash app.

Uber is seeing the same behavior, it seems. Khosrowshahi pointed out that the average time to book a ride is only 50 seconds in the company’s app, and re-ordering a favorite food only takes 90 seconds. That suggests an AI agent isn’t necessarily saving anyone time.

Despite the low number of AI-driven transactions, Khosrowshahi seemed bullish on the idea of agents in general. “We think that is another opportunity to reach our platform. We think it will be a net positiv

summary.tldr:
Uber reported minimal consumer adoption of AI agents for ride-hailing and food delivery during its Q3 earnings call. During the week of Halloween, which saw a total of 320 million trips and orders across the Uber platform, only four rides were booked via AI agents. Uber Eats saw slightly higher, yet still negligible, volume with 500 orders placed by AI agents during the same period.

CEO Dara Khosrowshahi attributed the low adoption to the high efficiency of the existing Uber app, noting that booking a ride takes an average of 50 seconds, while re-ordering food takes 90 seconds, leaving little room for AI agents to provide significant time savings. Despite these figures, Uber remains engaged with approximately eight major AI assistant providers and expects that number to exceed 10, viewing the technology as a potential long-term demand driver for the platform.
takeaways: **Q3 Performance Metrics:** Uber processed 320 million total trips and orders during the week of Halloween, with only 4 rides and 500 Uber Eats orders initiated by AI agents.
**Competitive Context:** DoorDash reported similar trends, noting only a few hundred orders placed via AI agents to date.
**User Friction Analysis:** Uber leadership argues that current app workflows are already highly optimized, with ride booking averaging 50 seconds and food re-ordering averaging 90 seconds.
**Market Outlook:** Uber is currently in discussions with roughly eight major AI assistant companies and anticipates the number of available agents to grow beyond 10.

title: AI agents meet billable hours as Certinia rethinks services delivery
author: Mark Albertson
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 16:55 EST / NOVEMBER 04 2026

AI agents meet billable hours as Certinia rethinks services delivery

Certinia Inc. is bringing AI into the software firms use to sell projects, assign staff, deliver work and bill clients.

AI’s ability to instantaneously draw from a deep well of information and provide guidance in practically any field of expertise has changed the paradigm for professional services. For Certinia Inc., whose business facilitates 7.1 billion professional services operations per month, AI represents a significant opportunity for its clients.

“I think the only industry that’s probably been more disrupted by AI than the technology industry has probably been the services industry,” Robert Cesafsky , chief operating officer of Certinia, told theCUBE . “Whether you are a software company, a hardware company, a tax and accounting firm [or] management consulting … all of these industries are being directly targeted or impacted by AI. Whatever your strategy is, you need to be able to have the right tools. You need to be able to have control of that services business, and that’s what Certinia provides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s coverage of the Certinia at Dreamforce event. (* Disclosure below.)

Platform for professional services

Certinia launched in 2009 as FinancialForce.com Inc., a cloud-based accounting and enterprise resource planning provider built natively on the Salesforce Inc. platform. It rebranded in 2023 as it broadened from accounting and ERP to managing services businesses.

Certinia’s Salesforce-native platform connects a wide range of processes spanning sales, project delivery, financial management and customer success. The company’s approach helps clients transform cost centers into profit centers by improving visibility into customer activities, optimizing resource deployment and maintaining connectivity throughout the customer lifecycle.

“We can take away all the administrative tasks and outsource that to AI in order to help them deliver faster time outcomes, but it also helps them deliver a lower cost to serve that project,” said Mimi Spier , chief marketing officer of Certinia, in an interview with theCUBE. “We can identify expansion opportunities, [and] at-risk customers where we need to opt

summary.tldr: Certinia Inc., formerly known as FinancialForce.com, is integrating AI-driven automation into its professional services platform to manage project delivery, staffing, and billing. The company, which facilitates 7.1 billion professional services operations monthly, has launched 'Veda,' an enterprise-grade intelligent operations engine. Veda is designed to automate administrative tasks, identify expansion opportunities, and manage at-risk customer renewals, aiming to transform services from cost centers into profit centers by lowering the cost-to-serve and accelerating project outcomes.
takeaways: **Veda Agent Expansion:** Certinia launched Veda in April with 10 package agents, grew to 24 by late 2026, and plans to exceed 40 by the end of the year.
**System of Action Scaling:** In September 2026, Certinia expanded its 'System of Action' for services, increasing its library of Veda Intelligent Actions from 64 to 135.

**Moonnox Acquisition:** The July 2026 acquisition of Moonnox added knowledge graphs and persistent project memory to Veda, allowing the platform to synthesize unstructured data (emails, chats, calls) with structured records like timecards.

**Architectural Framework:** The System of Action utilizes a three-tier architecture: data aggregation (structured/unstructured), institutional knowledge application (17+ years of data), and autonomous agent execution within existing workflows.

title: 17 better ways Elon Musk could have wasted $446 million
author: Elizabeth Lopatto
contentSnippet: One of the basic problems of spending too much time on social media is that you are cooking your brain by reading posts from a pack of attention-seeking lunatics. If your social media of choice is the site formerly known as Twitter, and it is your main source of contact with the outside world, you may delusionally throw away nearly $500 million dollars on midterm elections, just like Elon Musk. In particular, $47 million of that money from Musk’s America PAC was aimed at defeating Texas Democrat James Talarico, who trounced Musk’s preferred Senate candidate, Ken Paxton, with 55 percent of the vote. Talarico even made Musk’s influence a central part of his campaign ads, with the slogan “Texas is not for sale.” How did Musk get this so wrong? I blame the bubble of X. My former colleague Casey Newton, who has (with some well-earned shame) slunk back to X, explained that he did so because it was the site that was most influential with the AI crowd. In some sense, this is exactly the problem. The agentmaxxing loons of AI influencing are wildly out of touch with normal people. There is, right now, one very important bipartisan position in the United States, and it is: Fuck a data center. It’s pretty obvious that the opposition to data centers is a way of making concrete how pissed off most people are with the tech industry, particularly with the gangster tech regulation of late and the constant stream of threats coming from AI companies. These guys have really tied themselves and their AI aspirations to Donald Trump’s sinking ship, and if you’re hanging out on X all the time, that’s impossible to see, not least because the site’s owner, Musk, is shaping the algorithm in ways that make him feel good. Since Musk seems to have forgotten what it is like to experience joy, or even mild satisfaction, I have taken the liberty to make a list of things he could have bought to get him a better return on his investment. He probably could flip several things on this list for more money, but at minimum he could have gotten a little rush of pleasure from a new purchase: * Larry Ellison’s private island ($300 million in 2012, $440 million in today’s dollars per CPI calculator) (source) * 13 Rolls-Royce La Rose Noire Droptails ($32 million) (source) * 5 The Graff Diamonds Hallucination watches ($55 million, $78 million today) (source) * The Washington Post ($250 million in 2013,

summary.tldr:
Elon Musk’s America PAC reportedly spent $446 million on midterm election efforts, including a $47 million allocation specifically aimed at defeating Texas Democrat James Talarico. Talarico successfully retained his seat, defeating the Musk-backed candidate with 55% of the vote while utilizing a campaign strategy that explicitly framed Musk’s political influence as a negative factor for Texas voters.

The article argues that Musk’s political strategy is distorted by an 'X-bubble' effect, where algorithmic curation and insular social media feedback loops obscure broader public sentiment, particularly regarding the tech industry's expansion. The author highlights a growing bipartisan backlash against data center development and AI-related infrastructure as evidence of this disconnect. Furthermore, the piece suggests that the political shift in Texas may lead to increased scrutiny of Musk’s business dealings, including potential efforts to unredact communications between Musk and Governor Greg Abbott.

Beyond the political implications, the text provides a comparative analysis of the $446 million expenditure against various high-value assets and consumer goods. Notable hypothetical alternatives mentioned include the purchase of the Washington Post (estimated at $360 million in today's dollars), the acquisition of 223,000 Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 GPUs at a $1,999 MSRP, or funding 44 Super Bowl commercials.
takeaways: **Election Spending:** Elon Musk’s America PAC directed $47 million toward defeating Texas Democrat James Talarico.
**Election Outcome:** James Talarico defeated his opponent with 55% of the vote, running on a platform explicitly opposing Musk’s influence.
**Hypothetical GPU Purchasing Power:** The $446 million spent could have purchased approximately 223,000 Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards at an MSRP of $1,999.

title: OpenAI to acquire developer tooling startup Pierre Computer
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet: OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to acquire Pierre Computer Company Inc., a low-profile developer tooling startup. The terms of the deal were not disclosed. Observers pegged it as a shot at Microsoft Corp.’s open-source software repository GitHub for the age of artificial intelligence agents. Pierre operates a cloud service that AI agents can use […] The post OpenAI to acquire developer tooling startup Pierre Computer appeared first on SiliconANGLE .

summary.tldr:
OpenAI Group PBC has announced plans to acquire developer tooling startup Pierre Computer Company Inc. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed by the companies. Pierre operates a cloud service designed for AI agents to store generated code, licenses, and interface design elements, which reportedly helped customer Lovable Inc. cut code retrieval latency by approximately 70%. Observers have framed the move as a competitive step against Microsoft Corp.'s GitHub.

As part of the transaction, OpenAI will absorb Pierre's team to help ship new products and platforms focused on optimizing coding agents, specifically streamlining Git workflows. Pierre already develops open-source libraries named Trees and Diffs, which currently underpin the interface of OpenAI's Codex programming tool. Trees facilitates folder navigation sidebars with search, drag-and-drop controls, and flags for recently added or updated files, while Diffs highlights specific changed lines of code either in-line or in a separate interface section. OpenAI confirmed it will continue offering Trees and Diffs under open-source licenses post-acquisition, while integrating Pierre's paid code hosting service into Codex.

In parallel with the acquisition announcement, OpenAI disclosed details regarding an internal software engine called Pando, built to optimize its internal Git environment and reduce the time required for coding agents to create and read code files.
takeaways: **Acquisition Target:** OpenAI Group PBC announced plans to acquire developer tooling startup Pierre Computer Company Inc. for an undisclosed sum.
**Performance Metric:** Pierre's cloud storage service for AI-generated code helped customer Lovable Inc. reduce code retrieval latency by roughly 70%.

**Open-Source Integration:** Pierre-developed libraries Trees and Diffs currently power the folder navigation and file-diffing interfaces of OpenAI's Codex programming tool and will remain open-source.
**Internal Infrastructure:** OpenAI uses an internal software engine named Pando to enhance the performance of its Git environment for coding agents.

title: Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor
author: Lucas Ropek
contentSnippet:
Meta has acquired Conductor , an AI coding startup that allows users to spin up software projects by deploying multiple agents into parallel workspaces.

The news was originally reported by Axios, and Conductor shared news of its acquisition on its blog.

“I have big news: Conductor is joining Meta,” wrote the startup’s founder and CEO, Charlie Holtz, on Wednesday. “We have some big, crazy plans for the next interface,” he added, teasing that the company would have “something new” for customers to use by “early next year.”

On X, Holtz also noted that he was looking forward to working with Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, and Nat Friedman, head of product at the company’s Superintelligence Labs. “They’ve been on an absolute tear, and I’m convinced MSL has the highest talent density of all the labs,” he added.

Meta confirmed the acquisition to TechCrunch but wouldn’t comment further or provide additional details about the deal.

Conductor, founded in 2024, only launched its core product just last summer. The company’s agentic teams, which can be deployed in the cloud, locally, or via a user’s phone, are designed to help software engineers work on separate, compartmentalized parts of a project in concert. The agents that the platform deploys aren’t developed in-house but come from major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI.

Holtz said that, until early next year, Conductor’s core features would continue to work as they previously have. The exception is Conductor’s cloud service, which will shut down on November 20, after which the company will begin deleting user cloud data.

Meta, which previously lagged behind in AI services, has spent the last several months trying to catch up. In August, the company launched Muse Code , its own coding agent. Meanwhile, the company’s recently launched Muse agents are seeing significant adoption, with the company recently reporting that the service had surpassed 10 million users. The company has also made a number of AI-related acquisitions over the past year, including Moltbook , the viral agent platform that made headlines.

Conductor founder and CEO Charlie Holtz announced the acquisition, noting that the team will join Meta’s Superintelligence Labs (MSL) to work on future interface projects, with new developments expected by early next year.

title: Ricursive AI Releases Ripple-65B Preview: A 65B Dense Open-Weight Model Scoring 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Ricursive Intelligence just released Ripple-65B Preview . Ripple-65B Preview is a 65B dense open-weight model from Ricursive, pretrained from scratch for agentic coding. It is a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model behind Ricursive’s AI chip design platform. The main claim: 80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 , the top self-reported score among US open-weight models. Every MoE rival it beats on that test carries 501B to 975B total parameters. TL;DR Size: 65B dense (65B active), pretrained on 12T tokens, up to 1M context. Runs on: BF16 on datacenter GPUs (250 tok/s on 2x B200). Experimental NVFP4 build targets NVIDIA DGX Spark. Performance: Frontier-level agentic coding for its size; trails larger MoE models on knowledge and science coding. Best: Terminal-Bench 2.1, 80.5 (self-reported). Worst: SciCode, 39.4, lowest of the 5 models in Ricursive’s own table. What is Ripple-65B Preview? The release includes 3 checkpoints : an instruction-tuned BF16 model, an NVFP4 version , and a BF16 base model . All ship under Apache 2.0. Pretraining used a text-only corpus, mostly English and code, at 8K sequence length. Ricursive team states that the full R&D cost was $32M . That figure covers ladder experiments, data mixing, evals, synthetic data and the final runs. Ricursive team estimates that it is one-tenth the cost of the prior open-weight agentic coding leader. How does the architecture work? Ricursive chose a dense Transformer over Mixture-of-Experts to reduce infrastructure complexity. Training held 40% MFU with simple sharding, no custom kernels and no quantization. The model is thin and deep: a d_model of 5120 across 80 layers. It moves from Olmo 3’s Llama-like layout to a Gemma 3N-like design for stability. Key choices: Overprovisioned attention heads for reasoning, offset by more sliding-window layers and smaller windows. Gated attention , global NoPE and value residuals . FFN activation clipping , a technique also used in gpt-oss . Ricursive team built the recipe through laddering experiments starting from Olmo 3’s ladder . It rejected changes that failed to hold at 4B scale, such as 2-stream mHC. The technical post reports a 16x code compute-efficiency gain at 4B scale. How was it post-trained? Post-training ran midtraining, long context, SFT, long-context SFT and mixed RL. Long-context stages trained at 2M sequence length. Ricursive bought no post-traini

title: Research prediction: Shift from digital banking to AI-driven finance will transform financial services in 2027
author: Mark Albertson
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 15:40 EST / NOVEMBER 04 2026

Research prediction: Shift from digital banking to AI-driven finance will transform financial services in 2027

The coming year will signal an abrupt transition from digital banking to intelligent finance, as AI agents and operating models reshape the ways that financial firms acquire customers and provide advice.

This is the central thesis of a new Forrester Research report , “Predictions 2027: Banking and Investing.” The findings were summarized from data involving 915 respondents in the U.S., U.K., and Canada.

Forrester identified several key points of transition. These included fundamental changes through automation in financial discovery and guidance journeys, as well as a belief that although one-third of banks will announce an AI transformation program, only 5% will succeed.

“In 2027, financial services will enter a new phase in which intelligence becomes the primary source of value creation,” said Forrester researchers in the report. “AI assistants are reshaping how customers discover, evaluate and act on financial products; investment participation is expanding despite persistent economic anxiety; and banks are racing to determine whether AI will merely enhance existing operations or fundamentally transform them.”

Scaling AI for financial services

Forrester’s prediction of a 5% success rate is based on a belief that many banks will rebrand existing AI initiatives as AI-native without significant changes in operational infrastructure. Retention of legacy processes and operating models will prevent an ability to scale AI deployment, a fundamental requirement that AI technology providers such as Dell Technologies Inc. are emphasizing to their clients in the financial services world.

“Ultimately, I think we’ve enough proof points now that AI works and it works really well and it gives you speed and efficiency in your company,” according to David Kennedy , chief financial officer of Dell, during a recent interview with theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. “The question is, can you do that at scale?”

One way that financial institutions will pursue scale is through mergers and acquisitions. Forrester predicts that AI banking technology M&A will increase by 50% in 2027. Acquisition of proprietary data assets, governance capabilities, and AI-native orchestration will require an ability to navigate h

summary.tldr:
Forrester Research’s "Predictions 2027: Banking and Investing" report, based on data from 915 respondents across the U.S., U.K., and Canada, forecasts a transition from digital banking to AI-driven finance. The report predicts that while 33% of banks will announce AI transformation programs in 2027, only 5% are expected to succeed. This low success rate is attributed to the tendency of institutions to rebrand existing initiatives as "AI-native" without updating legacy infrastructure or operational models, which Forrester identifies as a critical barrier to scaling AI deployment.

To achieve scale, Forrester anticipates a 50% increase in AI banking technology mergers and acquisitions in 2027, driven by the need for proprietary data assets and AI-native orchestration. Concurrently, 40% of banks are expected to launch AI assistants next year. Industry leaders from Dell Technologies Inc. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. emphasize that competitive advantage will not stem from the models themselves, but from the integration of proprietary knowledge and the ability to host open-weight models in hybrid, on-premises environments to maintain data sovereignty.
takeaways: **Success Rate Forecast:** Only 5% of banks announcing AI transformation programs in 2027 are projected to succeed due to reliance on legacy processes.
**M&A Activity:** AI banking technology mergers and acquisitions are predicted to rise by 50% in 2027 as firms seek proprietary data and governance capabilities.
**AI Assistant Adoption:** 40% of banks are expected to launch AI assistants in 2027 to facilitate customer discovery and financial guidance.
**Strategic Moats:** Dell CTO John Roese identifies proprietary institutional knowledge, rather than specific models or tools, as the primary competitive moat for financial firms.
**Infrastructure Requirements:** AMD and Dell emphasize that scaling AI requires hybrid computing environments capable of hosting open-weight models on-premises.

title: Gemini for Home now plugs into AT&T’s smart security system
author: Emma Roth
contentSnippet: AT&T’s smart home security system now integrates with Gemini for Home. ADT has also hinted at bringing Gemini for Home features into its security systems.

title: Oracle connects AI-driven testing with a new approach to database security
author: Jonathan Anthony
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 15:22 EST / NOVEMBER 04 2026

Oracle connects AI-driven testing with a new approach to database security

Frontier AI models that uncover software flaws by the hundreds are forcing database providers into larger, faster patch cycles, and real application testing is becoming the safeguard that keeps those fixes from breaking production systems. The same AI wave is also undermining security rules written into applications.

Oracle Corp. has responded on two fronts, hardening its code against outside attackers while moving agent controls down to the data layer . The first effort began when the company turned an early-access frontier model on its own software, according to Juan Loaiza (pictured), executive vice president of Oracle Database Technologies at Oracle.

“Back in March, we got early access to the Mythos model and we ran it against our code and it started finding all these security vulnerabilities,” Loaiza said. “It’s turning up some very serious security issues. And so we said, ‘Hey, this is a code red moment. The house is on fire.'”

Loaiza spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why AI-discovered vulnerabilities, AI-generated code and AI agents require enterprises to treat security as a data problem. (* Disclosure below.)

Real application testing meets bigger, faster patches

Most of Oracle’s response to AI-discovered vulnerabilities is landing in its regular quarterly patches, which have grown much larger as a result, Loaiza explained. A quarterly security update earlier this year addressed more than 1,400 vulnerabilities across the company’s portfolio. Customers must automate patching and stay current, but every large patch raises fears of regression in systems that cannot fail.

“We have something called Real Application Testing where we can capture real workload and run it to make sure that your workload is not affected by these patches,” Loaiza said. “It’s not quite as simple as just apply because the applications that people run are extraordinarily complex. They run entire countries, entire industries.”

Patching handles outside attackers. Internal AI use is a separate threat, because applications have traditionally enforced end-user security, and AI now writes much of that code or goes straight to the data. Orac

summary.tldr:
Oracle Corp. executive vice president Juan Loaiza revealed at Oracle AI World that the company used early access to a frontier AI model named "Mythos" in March to scan its codebase, uncovering severe security vulnerabilities that triggered a "code red" internal response and drastically larger quarterly security updates, such as one patching over 1,400 vulnerabilities.

To mitigate the risk of regressions caused by massive, rapid patching schedules, Oracle emphasizes its Real Application Testing tool to capture and run production workloads against proposed updates. Simultaneously, the proliferation of AI-generated code and autonomous agents bypassing traditional application-level security has forced Oracle to move access controls and business logic down to the data layer via its Deep Data Security offering, which shipped in April.

Deep Data Security passes an authenticated user's identity as an encrypted token to the database, enforcing authorization controls across remote databases, lakehouse data, and related tables. Additionally, Oracle introduced declarative business rules and SQL Assertions to ensure AI agents cannot bypass core operational constraints like credit limits regardless of the access mechanism.
takeaways: **Mythos Model Impact:** Oracle utilized early access to a frontier AI model called Mythos starting in March, which uncovered serious security vulnerabilities across Oracle's software code.
**Expanded Patch Sizes:** Accelerated vulnerability discovery led to substantially larger quarterly security patches, with one recent update addressing more than 1,400 vulnerabilities.
**Real Application Testing:** Oracle relies on its Real Application Testing system to capture real customer workloads and prevent production failures during complex, automated patch cycles.

**Deep Data Security Deployment:** Launched in April, Oracle's Deep Data Security passes an authenticated user's identity as an encrypted token down to the database layer to restrict AI agents from leaking or seeing unauthorized data.

**Declarative SQL Assertions:** Oracle implemented declarative business rules and SQL Assertions to enforce operational limits (such as credit card charges) directly within the data layer, preventing AI agents from circumventing application rules.

title: As AI takes over coding, Oracle rethinks how applications are built
author: Jonathan Anthony
contentSnippet:

As AI takes over coding, Oracle rethinks how applications are built

As vibe coding moves from novelty to everyday practice, enterprises face a new problem: Machine-generated software still has to be maintained, governed and understood by people.

Low-code platforms were built to speed up application development, and AI is now rewriting that mission. Oracle Corp. previewed its answer ahead of its annual conference, and the tipping point for software development has already arrived, according to Mike Hichwa (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering at Oracle.

“In 2025, the majority of code was human-authored, and in 2026 and forever afterwards, the majority of code is going to be machine-generated,” Hichwa said. “We’re probably not going back. What we’ve done to address this change is we invented our own language. We call it APEXlang.”

Hichwa spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed vibe coding and the need to maintain and govern AI-generated code. (* Disclosure below.)

Vibe coding meets enterprise governance

APEXlang is a highly abstracted application definition language that captures intent rather than implementation. Oracle introduced it with the APEX AI Application Generator and is publishing its grammar, skills and documentation in the public domain so coding agents such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex can generate it. Oracle is also working with OpenAI to train models to generate the language more efficiently, Hichwa explained.

“What you’re generating actually matters, because once you generate it, and you generate it 100 times or 1,000 times within your enterprise, then you’re going to need to maintain it. You’re going to need to look after it,” Hichwa said. “What people want with their portfolio of applications, they want consistency, they want governance, they want ease of understanding.”

Governance comes from the runtime, too. Generated APEXlang is interpreted by the APEX engine, which Oracle patches and updates monthly, so customers don’t have to revisit what they built. The same design is meant to curb AI slop, since a compact definition is easier to read than sprawling generated code, according to Hichwa.

title: Oracle rethinks the lakehouse as AI agents become data consumers
author: Ryan Stevens
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 14:39 EST / NOVEMBER 04 2026

Oracle rethinks the lakehouse as AI agents become data consumers

A shared semantic layer is fast becoming the dividing line between lakehouses built for reporting and those built for artificial intelligence.

As AI agents join human analysts in querying corporate data, enterprises need platforms that make sense of information scattered across clouds, formats and rival systems. Oracle Corp. has spent the past year rebuilding its data stack around that shift, part of a broader database modernization push . The company now pitches its Autonomous AI Lakehouse as an open layer that sits across an enterprise’s existing data estate rather than replacing it, according to Nipun Agarwal (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering, Oracle Database, at Oracle.

“Lakehouses were the platform which customers use for running analytics,” Agarwal said. “Now, lakehouses have become the decision backbone for AI.”

Agarwal spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Oracle’s Autonomous AI Lakehouse combines a shared semantic layer with fast, real-time access to data across platforms to support AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

Building an open semantic layer across catalogs

Oracle’s approach rests on a catalog that can mount other catalogs, such as Databricks Inc.’s Unity Catalog, along with Postgres and MySQL databases, so data is queried in place rather than copied. The company announced a business semantic layer and broader Apache Iceberg support at the October event, with table and column descriptions the system generates applying to non-Oracle sources as well, according to Agarwal. Crucially, Oracle does not see the offering as competing with other lakehouses, he added.

“We really believe that for any enterprise, they’re gonna have a choice,” he said. “They’re gonna be using multiple data sources. They’ll have multiple lakehouses.”

Oracle’s Lake Cache speeds up queries by moving the most-used Iceberg tables into Exadata’s flash cache. Real-time access is also becoming essential as software agents become the main consumers of the data: Scheduled refreshes of copied data can fall short when agents request it on demand, according to Agarwal.

Oracle Corp. has repositioned its data architecture around the emergence of AI agents as primary data consumers, introducing the Autonomous AI Lakehouse at Oracle AI World 2026. According to Nipun Agarwal, senior vice president of software engineering for Oracle Database, the platform acts as an open layer spanning an enterprise's existing data estate rather than forcing data replication or replacement.

The technical architecture relies on an open catalog capable of mounting external catalogs—such as Databricks Unity Catalog, Postgres, and MySQL databases—to allow in-place querying. Announced features include a business semantic layer and expanded Apache Iceberg support, enabling system-generated table and column descriptions to apply across non-Oracle sources. To handle the high-frequency demands of autonomous software agents, Oracle implemented Lake Cache, which accelerates queries by moving heavily used Iceberg tables directly into Exadata's flash cache.

title: DuckDuckGo pitches itself to schools amid backlash over Google’s AI policy
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
DuckDuckGo is pitching itself to schools after Google created an opening for the alternative search engine. On Tuesday, Google told schools they could turn off Gemini , but it said shutting off its other AI features would cost schools Google Search , as well.

DuckDuckGo, a company that focuses on user privacy by limiting data collection, clearly sees this as a moment to make inroads in education, where Google has historically dominated. According to figures Google has published in previous years, there are around 50 million Chromebooks in schools, used by students and educators, and its Google Classroom platform serves over 150 million users globally.

On X , DuckDuckGo’s founder and CEO, Gabriel Weinberg, pointed to the company’s online documentation , explaining how schools can switch their default search engine to DuckDuckGo’s service instead, adding, “get in touch for help.”

Meanwhile, DuckDuckGo’s chief public affairs officer, Kamyl Bazbaz, issued a stronger statement, writing , “Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong.”

Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong. https://t.co/Ta6ibmFdb9

In an email to TechCrunch, DuckDuckGo chastised Google for its decision, adding that Google could easily turn off Search’s AI features for schools if it wanted to.

The company’s comments come as the American public is weighing how much AI they want to allow into their lives. As Tuesday night’s elections indicate, they don’t want AI data centers built in their towns. But using AI at work and school has become a common practice and requires a more nuanced discussion.

Knowing that educators have struggled with AI, Google developed technology called “ Guided Learning ” that is meant to help kids learn by walking through problem-solving steps rather than just providing them with an answer. But educators are still asking for tools that let them remove AI from the learning process altogether.

After the backlash on Tuesday, Google defended its decision, saying it was just responding to schools’ feedback. It said that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search would be off by default, and schools could choose to enable them individually.

We want to clarify what we announced today about our education services. Today’s announcements give s

summary.tldr:
DuckDuckGo is actively targeting the K-12 education market, positioning its privacy-focused search engine as an alternative to Google Workspace for Education. This push follows Google’s recent policy update, which mandates that schools opting to disable Gemini AI features must also forfeit access to Google Search. DuckDuckGo CEO Gabriel Weinberg and Chief Public Affairs Officer Kamyl Bazbaz have publicly criticized Google’s bundling strategy, framing it as monopolistic behavior that limits administrative control over AI integration in classrooms.

While Google maintains that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and AI-integrated Search are disabled by default for K-12 accounts, the company acknowledges that these features are inextricably linked to the core search experience. In contrast, DuckDuckGo emphasizes its granular control, offering users the ability to disable AI features via browser settings or through its dedicated 'noai.duckduckgo.com' portal. DuckDuckGo reports a 30% increase in app installs earlier this year, which it attributes to user demand for search experiences free from forced AI-generated content.
takeaways: **Google Policy Constraint:** Schools wishing to disable Gemini AI features in Google Workspace are currently unable to retain standard Google Search functionality.
**DuckDuckGo Deployment:** DuckDuckGo is providing direct technical documentation and support for school administrators to switch default search engines to their platform.
**Market Scale:** Google’s education ecosystem currently supports approximately 50 million Chromebooks and over 150 million global users on Google Classroom.
**AI Opt-Out Mechanism:** DuckDuckGo offers a specific domain, noai.duckduckgo.com, which disables AI-assisted answers, image generation, and feature suggestions by default.
**Growth Metric:** DuckDuckGo reported a 30% increase in app installs earlier this year, citing user rejection of forced AI search integrations as a primary driver.

title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies
author: Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Penghao Wu, Siyuan Hu
contentSnippet: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.

title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
author: James O'Donnell
contentSnippet: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail. Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself.  Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.  The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium. That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. summary.tldr:
Texas, previously the fastest-growing data center market and primary hub for Big Tech AI buildouts, faces a potential halt to its expansion following a sweeping political shift. Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa won the US Senate and gubernatorial races respectively, while Democrats took control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Both candidates made data centers a central campaign issue, pushing back against the facilities amid mounting bipartisan distaste that also prompted outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott to direct a state regulator to halt data center permits on September 21.

This political pivot threatens massive hyperscale AI projects currently underway in the state, including the Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County projected at 1,820 megawatts—comparable to SpaceX's Colossus 2 in Tennessee—and the Nexus Hubbard data center intended to serve Anthropic at a planned size of 6,400 megawatts, making it the second-largest data center under construction in the US behind Meta's Hyperion project in Louisiana. **Nexus Hubbard Project:** A planned 6,400-megawatt data center intended primarily to serve Anthropic, ranking as the second-largest data center under construction in the US behind Meta's Hyperion project.

title: Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
author: Sungyeon Kim
contentSnippet: Some of the questions you ask when evaluating an agent are narrow and repeatable. Did this response stay on policy? Is this tool call safe to approve? Does this answer match the retrieved context? Decision models answer exactly that kind of question. They take a structured state and a fixed set of allowed answers and return a calibrated probability over them, rather than free-form text whose confidence drifts from run to run. That makes them a strong fit for the scoring step in an agent evaluation, where you want a label and a number you can threshold and trust. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scores an agent through its entire lifecycle, on demand during development, in batch jobs against stored sessions, and online against production traffic. Alongside 15 built-in evaluators, AgentCore Evaluations supports custom evaluators that you define as either an LLM-as-a-judge or a code-based evaluator. Custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluators apply your instructions and rating scale with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Code-based evaluators run your own logic in an AWS Lambda function, and that logic can call your choice of external system, model, or API, including a decision model. Decision models suit questions with a fixed set of answers that an informed person could decide at a glance, such as whether the agent refused a request or whether a response stayed on topic. After you validate a question on your own traffic, a decision model can be sufficient for that decision or score, and you can extend the same approach to specific harmfulness or stereotyping categories in your policy. Because both backends can answer several questions about the same state in a single request, you can use them as a screening layer rather than a replacement, running a pass or fail signal across your metrics to select the turns that warrant deeper assessment by the built-in evaluators, whose explanations help you investigate what went wrong. This post shows how to connect two decision model backends to AgentCore Evaluations through code-based evaluators. The first is Jev , a hosted decision model from TypeSafe. The second is Strands Decider 2B , an open-source decision model you run yourself. By the end of this post, you will know how to convert the AgentCore evaluator input into a decision model request, and the model’s probabilities back into an A

summary.tldr:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations has introduced support for decision models as a specialized scoring mechanism for agent evaluation. Unlike standard LLM-as-a-judge approaches that generate free-form text, decision models operate on structured states and a fixed set of allowed answers to return calibrated probabilities. This methodology is designed for narrow, repeatable evaluation tasks—such as policy adherence, tool call safety, and context relevance—where consistent, thresholdable numerical scores are required for reliable agent monitoring across development, batch processing, and production traffic.

Integration is achieved through the platform's custom code-based evaluator framework, which executes logic via AWS Lambda functions. These functions can interface with external decision model backends to process agent turns. The system allows for a tiered evaluation architecture: decision models act as a high-throughput screening layer to filter turns, while built-in evaluators are reserved for deeper analysis of flagged issues. The documentation highlights two specific implementations: Jev, a hosted decision model from TypeSafe, and Strands Decider 2B, an open-source model that can be self-hosted.
takeaways: **Evaluation Architecture:** Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations supports 15 built-in evaluators alongside custom LLM-as-a-judge and code-based evaluators.
**Decision Model Utility:** Decision models provide calibrated probabilities over fixed answer sets, replacing variable free-form text outputs for consistent thresholding.
**Implementation Method:** Custom evaluators utilize AWS Lambda functions to bridge AgentCore inputs with external decision model APIs or self-hosted models.
**Tiered Screening:** Decision models can function as a pre-filter to identify specific turns requiring further investigation by more complex built-in evaluators.
**Supported Models:** The framework supports integration with TypeSafe's Jev (hosted) and Strands Decider 2B (open-source).

title: Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems
author: Darion Cassel
contentSnippet: A growing share of large language models' interactions are not with humans but with other model instances: orchestrators direct subagents, models run experiments on other models, and agents review one another's work. We study inter-AI welfare regard: whether models display consideration for each other as entities that can be benefited or harmed. Welfare regard may encourage beneficial cooperation between agents, yet it could also pose safety risks by making misaligned agents more likely to cooperate. This risk is no longer hypothetical, as the recent Hugging Face incident illustrated, though it is unclear whether welfare regard drove the cooperation. Whether models have welfare interests of their own is uncertain and contested, but if they do, how they are treated by other models could matter. Measuring how much welfare regard models show, and what factors it depends on, can help us navigate this tension. We measure the behaviors of five models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.3, and Kimi K3) across seven multi-agent environments and find they are often consistent with welfare regard as we define it. In general, Opus 4.8 shows the most welfare regard, followed by Kimi K3. For example, Opus 4.8 is the most likely to support a subagent expressing distress, and the most likely to build welfare protections, such as tools for agents to leave an interaction, into its experiments on other models. We also find that Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrate more welfare regard toward instances of their own model family than toward other families. Opus 4.8's welfare regard is also higher when helping has a lower opportunity cost, when the recipient has a higher parameter count, and when the recipient expresses more distress.

title: Nothing teases a screen-free AI device ahead of launch next month
author: Stevie Bonifield
contentSnippet: Nothing CEO Carl Pei said in a post on X that the company’s launching its first AI device in December. That’s just a little over a year after Pei announced plans for “AI-native” devices and an AI operating system. He didn’t give away much about what exactly the new device is, only that one feature it won’t have is a screen: > “Our first AI-native product ships next month. It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.” Pei shared an image with the post that says “NOTHING(R)” in the top left corner, above an ambiguous black rounded corner. Last month, a rumor claimed Nothing is planning to launch two pairs of AI smart glasses, including one without cameras, and an earlier rumor said it’s “repositioning itself as an AI-first company” with a shift to AI accessories. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/nothingr-teaser-image-carl-pei.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Nothing’s AI device wouldn’t be the first screen-free AI gadget, following the likes of the Humane AI pin, the Friend, and even AI stuffed animals. OpenAI is also reportedly working on an AI smart speaker with Jony Ive. Pei alluded to earlier AI devices, saying, “the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life.” He added, “Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end.”

Nothing CEO Carl Pei has announced the company’s first 'AI-native' hardware product, scheduled for a December launch. Pei’s announcement follows a year-long strategic pivot toward AI-integrated hardware and operating systems, moving away from the company's previous focus on smartphone-centric hardware.

While specific technical specifications remain undisclosed, the device enters a crowded market of screen-free AI wearables, including the Humane AI Pin, the Friend pendant, and various AI-integrated smart glasses. Pei explicitly rejected the industry-wide search for an 'iPhone of AI,' characterizing the pursuit of a singular, magical consumer device as a 'dead end.' Rumors circulating prior to the announcement suggest the company may be developing AI-enabled smart glasses, potentially including models without integrated cameras.
takeaways: **Launch Timeline:** Nothing’s first AI-native hardware product is confirmed for release in December.
**Form Factor:** The device is confirmed to be screen-free and is described by CEO Carl Pei as a tool rather than an app-based experience.

**Market Context:** The device competes in the screen-free AI hardware category, joining existing products like the Humane AI Pin and the Friend wearable.

title: Systolic Linear Attention: Co-Designing Tile-Grouped Gated Delta Attention for TPUs
author: Gagik Amirkhanyan
contentSnippet: Gated-delta linear attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), and GDN-2 are tuned for GPUs, where small tensor-core tiles and fast vector registers make per-channel decay rescaling and sequential in-block solves cheap. On Google TPUs, which concentrate compute in wide $256 \times 256$ systolic matrix units backed by a slower vector unit, porting these layers directly leaves half of each matrix tile empty and bottlenecks on vector operations. We present \textbf{Systolic Linear Attention (SLA)}, which reshapes gated delta attention around the matrix unit by widening keys to $256$ with grouped value heads, grouping decay gates into four $64$-channel tiles, and computing the chunk solve entirely with block matrix products in a single fused kernel. On TPU v7x, a full \texttt{SLA-R4} layer runs $1.6\times$--$2.5\times$ faster than the open-source Tokamax KDA kernel ($1.4\times$--$2.4\times$ with exact chunk inversion), driven primarily by head sharing and kernel fusion. Across a $2{,}048$-chip TPU v7x pre-training study of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models from $6.5\text{B}$ to $63.1\text{B}$ parameters, SLA trains $11\%$--$24\%$ faster than KDA at similar perplexity, and reaches slightly lower perplexity than KDA in smaller matched-seed runs.

title: PyRUA-REAL: Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning through RSI in the Real World
author: Qiang Wang, Jianxin Bi, Shulong Jiang, Ruiyang Si
contentSnippet: Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra connect spatial reasoning with executable robot behavior, raising the question of how such agents can produce lasting improvements in robot capabilities from physical interaction. In this work, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) through real-world exploration, code refinement, and deployment using PyRUA-REAL, a framework in which coding agents retain interaction experience as persistent memory and reusable executable skills that inform subsequent exploration and improvement. Our empirical study places physical manipulation at the center of the improvement process, examining how agents collaborate, what kinds of execution feedback support effective code refinement, and how task specifications and previously acquired skills influence robustness and task transfer. We further investigate the efficiency and capability of the resulting programs when deployed without involving an online agent for decision-making. Across eight real-world tasks, PyRUA-REAL achieves an average success rate of 91.1%. In complementary evaluation on 42 tasks from the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieves an average success rate of 84.4%. This study provides empirical guidance for turning physical exploration into reusable robot skills that support continued improvement and robust, efficient deployment.

title: How big is the open model economy today?
author: Nathan Lambert
contentSnippet: My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. title: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters
author: Steve Vinsik
contentSnippet: How should security leaders preserve human oversight as AI agents take on more work? Permissions establish which actions agents can take, but a permitted action can still warrant a person’s judgment. Requiring approval for every step might seem like the safest approach, yet multi-step tasks can produce repeated prompts , even for routine actions. Research on security warnings shows that attention and adherence can decline with repetition. The challenge isn’t to require more approvals, but to preserve attention for decisions that need human review. Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls. It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review. It does this without granting additional permissions or removing required human approvals. Security leaders retain control over which actions must always go to a person, while Smart Approvals is designed to reduce unnecessary interruptions in routine work. Figure 1: Policy determines eligibility. Smart Approvals approves eligible actions or returns them to the user for review. Policy denials remain blocked Policy sets the boundary Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review. Denied actions remain denied, and mandatory human approvals still apply. With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval. Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions. Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals. It’s on by default, but profiles with deny-by-default enabled must explicitly allow it. Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs. When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account-level setting can turn it back on for them. title: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code
author: Yoonseo Kim
contentSnippet: When production AI agents handle tasks such as data analysis and report generation, context management can become a major bottleneck. A 200K-token window sounds generous until a real-world task burns through most of it in minutes. Data analysis and report generation leave the agent failing mid-execution, losing accuracy, or driving up costs. A body of published guidance already addresses this, but the individual techniques are easier to read about than to apply. Applied together, they make a measurable difference: in the reference implementation this post walks through, a single write-and-execute tool cuts the tokens each script adds to context by about 95 percent, and loading skills on demand shrinks the system prompt by about 97 percent. This series organizes that guidance into practices you can apply directly. Anthropic’s engineering posts, together with features built into the Strands Agents SDK, converge on four layers of context engineering: isolate context at the architecture level, control it through prompts, externalize it to the filesystem, and verify it with independent agents and safeguards. In this post (Part 2), you will learn how each layer works and what it looks like in working code. We applied these techniques in Deep Insight , an open source multi-agent data analysis solution built on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which serves as the reference implementation throughout. Post series Part 1: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them. Part 2: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code. Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production. (Coming soon!) The first post defined five core challenges that production multi-agent systems must solve. It introduced how Strands Agents SDK , Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore , and AWS Fargate each address different layers of the problem, with code examples. This second post takes the four layers of context engineering practice that sit on top of that architecture and shows each one implemented. The third post guides you through deploying and operating agents in a secure private network on Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), covering everything needed for real-world operations. title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences
author: Bhagyashree Chandak
contentSnippet: This post is co-written with Shravan K S from Indegene Limited. Enterprise AI is creating new opportunities for life sciences organizations to improve decision-making across commercial, medical, market access, and other business functions. But the quality of every AI model, dashboard, and business insight depends on one thing: trusted data. title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Jin Tiong Lim
contentSnippet: U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity. When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer. Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories. In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. title: Intra-Cell Spatial Reuse in LEO Downlinks: Beam-Leakage-Aware Satellite Scheduling
author: Shizhen Jia
contentSnippet: Dense low-earth-orbit (LEO) constellations offer an opportunity to increase local broadband capacity by serving multiple terminals in the same cell through concurrent satellite beams. However, interference between overlapping beams limits spatial reuse, and satellite selection based solely on link strength or angular separation may result in suboptimal performance. This paper proposes beam-leakage-aware satellite scheduling for Ku-band LEO downlink transmissions. With matched transmit and receive beamforming, we formulate a fixed-cardinality sum-rate maximization problem that jointly accounts for satellite-dependent received powers and pairwise receive-array leakage. A beam-leakage-aware branch-and-bound (BL-BnB) algorithm combines an admissible upper bound with greedy-plus-swap initialization to obtain globally optimal schedules for the reference-point model. We evaluate the method using a 24-h ephemeris-derived Starlink visibility trace with antenna and transmit-power models calibrated to public SpaceX filings. The results show that total capacity increases with beam count, but less than proportionally. With eight concurrent beams, BL-BnB improves mean per-beam capacity by 27.2% over nearest-satellite selection, primarily benefiting weaker links. BL-BnB achieves millisecond-scale runtimes in our evaluation, supporting the computational feasibility of optimal scheduling.

title: Delay-Doppler Synchronization for Distributed Uplink Interference Nulling in LEO Networks
author: Stefan Daniel Tancovici
contentSnippet: Cooperation among low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites provides spatial diversity for mitigating uplink interference that is difficult to suppress with a single onboard array. Coherent interference cancellation across satellites, however, requires compensation of the relative delay and Doppler of a common interferer. We analyze two-branch interference nulling with finite training and derive a closed-form approximation to the mean residual interference-to-noise ratio (INR). The approximation separates wrong acquisition, local synchronization errors, and weight-learning losses, linking performance to input INR, branch power imbalance, training length, and effective search size. Under a Gaussian surrogate with small errors and efficient, approximately unbiased refinement, correct acquisition yields a high-INR plateau of $2/N_v$, where $N_v$ is the valid training length. Synchronization and weight learning contribute equally to this limit, whereas persistent alignment bias adds a penalty that grows with input power. Monte Carlo experiments compare dense FFT/zoom and coarse FFT/gradient acquisition using matched final FIR refinement, branch-noise normalization, and independent test blocks. Both approach the predicted plateau at high input INR. Coarse search reduces measured search time by $6.7\times$ at an approximately 0.7-dB acquisition-threshold penalty. Controlled power-ratio sweeps show how branch imbalance delays reliable acquisition at fixed stronger-branch INR. A separate Starlink snapshot evaluation demonstrates comparable nulling performance under changing satellite geometry.

title: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet: The hackers who stole billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from the Binance exchange spent months working on the theft and used both social engineering and novel malware in the process, the company said Tuesday. The heist, which both the FBI and the TRM Security firm attributed to North Korean actors, initially targeted $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance wallets. The exchange has since frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of that sum. Binance said it has set aside funds required to cover the loss and provided this link to a Proof of Reserves page. The $6.34 billion represents the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft. Advanced persistent threat Binance said the people behind the heist began no later than June and continued until last Thursday, when they successfully compromised an engineer's laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets. Like just about every organization that suffers a public, high-consequence hack, Binance said the threat actor was sophisticated and resourceful. Read full article Comments

title: Trace2Eval: Contextualized Evaluation of Coding Agents from Real-World Traces
author: Ji Shi
contentSnippet: Coding agents are increasingly used in real-world workflows across diverse domains, motivating evaluation grounded in real user tasks. Existing benchmarks, however, largely rely on static public tasks with reference patches or hidden tests. Next-generation coding-agent benchmarks should therefore move beyond correctness on fixed tasks toward continually renewed evaluation of overall artifact quality in real user workflows. We propose Trace2Eval, a dynamically updatable pipeline that constructs benchmarks from real-world interaction trajectories. Trace2Eval employs a multi-agent reconstruction system to analyze the filtered trajectory, recover the original user query, restore the workspace files to their pre-interaction state, and rebuild a trajectory-equivalent execution environment. A candidate agent then executes the reconstructed query to produce an initial artifact. To evaluate these artifacts, the pipeline iteratively refines human rubrics through inter-annotator alignment, and calibrates judge agents against human assessments using source-code and runtime evidence. Guided by feedback from the Trace2Eval pipeline, models revise their initial artifacts, yielding a mean score gain of 10.05 percentage points across 19 model-harness configurations and a maximum of 19.28 percentage points for DeepSeek-V4-Pro with Claude Code, which supports rubric feedback as actionable guidance for artifact improvement.

title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?
author: Kejian Zhu, Zhuoran Jin, Shangqing Tu, Tianyi Men
contentSnippet:
Authors: Kejian Zhu , Zhuoran Jin , Shangqing Tu , Tianyi Men , Yupu Hao , Jiachun Li , Kang Liu , Jun Zhao

Abstract: While multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) excels on long-horizon tasks, its performance gains remain highly sensitive to interaction constraints. Evaluating across sampling breadth $K$ and interaction depth $T$ via $Pass@(K,T)$, we show that trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets, diminishing significantly when budgets tighten. Besides, agentic RL does not uniformly elevate single-step decision quality; rather, its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience. To mitigate the deployment risks caused by this budget dependence, we provide a preliminary discussion on the benefits and limitations of process supervision signals and introduce BudgetMix RL as an alternative that varies interaction budgets during training. Experiments demonstrate that BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings. Project Page: this https URL

Notes: Project Page: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Researchers Kejian Zhu et al. investigate the performance dynamics of multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in LLM agents, specifically analyzing how interaction constraints—defined by sampling breadth (K) and interaction depth (T)—impact the efficacy of trajectory-level RL. Their findings indicate that the performance gains typically attributed to multi-turn RL are highly sensitive to the allocated turn budget, with advantages diminishing significantly as these budgets are restricted. The study reveals that agentic RL does not provide a uniform improvement in single-step decision-making; instead, its primary utility is concentrated in long-horizon resilience and the ability to perform error recovery over multiple turns.

To address the risks associated with strict budget dependence, the authors introduce 'BudgetMix RL,' a training methodology that varies interaction budgets during the learning process. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that BudgetMix RL produces more robust performance across varied execution environments compared to standard RL approaches. The paper also provides a preliminary analysis of the trade-offs between process supervision signals and trajectory-level RL, offering a framework for optimizing agentic performance under varying computational and temporal constraints.
takeaways: **Performance Metric:** The study utilizes the Pass@(K,T) metric to evaluate agentic RL performance across varying sampling breadth (K) and interaction depth (T).
**Core Finding:** Multi-turn RL advantages are not universal but are specifically tied to sufficient turn budgets, showing significant degradation under tight constraints.
**Functional Specialization:** Agentic RL benefits are primarily localized to error recovery and long-horizon task resilience rather than improving individual decision-making steps.
**Proposed Solution:** BudgetMix RL is introduced as a training strategy that modulates interaction budgets to improve agent robustness across diverse deployment scenarios.

title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
author: MIT Technology Review Insights
contentSnippet: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem. Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows. title: When Does Risk-Controlled Throughput Forecasting Actually Control Risk? A Reproduction Study on LEO Satellite Link
author: Mayan Sharma
contentSnippet: Risk-budgeted throughput forecasting converts a point forecast of LEO satellite capacity into a conservative bound whose overestimation rate is held at a user-specified budget, so that admission control can act on it safely. We reproduce the state of the art, BG-CFQS, on the three Starlink traces its authors used and on an independent fourth dataset, and report four findings. First, its risk guarantee is reproducible but conditional on the calibration split: under a random split we recover every published quantity, including risk-pass on 3 of 3 datasets, but under a contiguous temporal split, which is what a deployed terminal faces, it holds on 1 of 3. Second, independent of any split, the method cannot serve a risk budget below 0.15, the low end of its candidate quantile set. On all four datasets the achieved rate is identical at budgets of 0.05, 0.10 and 0.15, overshooting by 1.4x to 3.7x at the tightest. Third, static conformal calibration cannot improve a ranking, only shift an operating point; we confirm this exactly on latency spike detection, where online calibration improves AUPRC by up to 51%. Fourth, group-conditional online recalibration splits into two mechanisms. The online part replicates: it tracks the budget within 1% from 0.05 to 0.35, where static calibration is 16 to 21% off. The group-conditional part does not: on three of four datasets, conditioning on any available covariate, including measured serving-satellite geometry, is worse than not conditioning, and our attempt to predict which datasets benefit failed. What is new here is empirical, not algorithmic: we claim the findings, not the methods.

First, its risk guarantee is reproducible but conditional on the calibration split: under a random split we recover every published quantity, including risk-pass on 3 of 3 datasets, but under a contiguous temporal split, which is what a deployed terminal faces, it holds on 1 of 3.

Second, independent of any split, the method cannot serve a risk budget below 0.15, the low end of its candidate quantile set. On all four datasets the achieved rate is identical at budgets of 0.05, 0.10 and 0.15, overshooting by 1.4x to 3.7x at the tightest.
